talks.title: Trust No One - Especially the Agents Building Zero Trust Through Machine Identity Track 2
talks.teaser: See how short-lived workload identities can constrain an AI agent’s access to business services.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how machine identities and AI agents challenge access controls built for human users, especially when agents rely on long-lived credentials across services. She describes a workload identity approach using SPIFFE and SPIRE to issue short-lived identities and credentials under resource-specific policies, then walks through a sales pipeline agent example. Attendees learn how this model can limit privileges, support revocation, and improve visibility into agent access.

talks.title: OWASP Platinum Corporate Supporter - An Interview with Abraham Aranguren, of 7ASecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how a penetration testing firm runs audits, publishes open source reports and supports OWASP projects.
talks.summary:
Andrew van der Stock interviews Abraham Aranguren, managing director of 7ASecurity, about the firm's penetration tests and code audits across web, mobile, AI and cloud targets. Aranguren explains that each engagement opens a communication channel before testing starts, includes free fix verification, and concludes with an attestation letter. He also points to public reports the firm has published for open source projects, including Tor Project and Thunderbird Send.

The interview then covers OWTF, the Offensive Web Testing Framework, which began around 2008 as scripts automating Aranguren's OSCP preparation and later became an OWASP flagship project. The tool sorts its work by permission level, from passive reconnaissance that never contacts the target, to semi-passive requests, to active scanners run with client approval. Results appear in an interface where a tester verifies what is real. Aranguren recalls an authorization bypass he found by sending an unexpected HTTP method to a login page, which granted administrator access. He cautions that AI output must be validated by the professional who signs the report, and he stresses layered defenses and business logic testing.

For newcomers, he recommends contributing to an open source project in a chosen specialty, earning certifications, listening to security podcasts, giving lightning talks, joining OWASP chapter meetings and learning a programming language. He closes by noting that many widely used libraries, such as zlib, depend on unpaid maintainers, which makes formal audits valuable.

talks.title: Analyzing Zero Trust Architecture in the Age of Agentic GenAI
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Analyzing Zero Trust Architecture in the Age of Agentic GenAI.
talks.summary: Vinit Narjala, Application Security Engineer at AWS, presents a framework for securing autonomous AI agents using zero trust principles. He distinguishes agentic AI from traditional LLMs by highlighting agents' planning, reasoning, memory (short and long-term), tool integration, and autonomous action capabilities—creating significantly larger attack surfaces. Narjala identifies four new threat domains beyond traditional appsec: cognitive security (reasoning hijacking, goal manipulation), execution integrity (tool misuse, code execution risks), identity coherence (authentication/authorization across agent lifecycles), and governance complexity (multi-agent delegation chains). He maps 15 OWASP agentic AI threats into the ATFAA (Advanced Framework for Autonomous Agents) framework. The core defense strategy is ATBMF (Adaptive Trust Boundary Management Framework), a three-pillar approach: (1) Multi-dimensional Monitoring and Observability—capturing action-intent correlation, data access patterns, resource utilization, and communication patterns via deterministic hooks into agent workflows; (2) Dynamic Policy Enforcement—using graduated access (full/limited/read-only/deny), just-in-time privileges, automatic credential revocation, and contextual reauthentication to adjust trust boundaries in real-time based on risk scores; (3) Self-Healing Procedures—network isolation, quarantining, graceful degradation, and forensic state preservation. Narjala demonstrates an AWS implementation with API Gateway and Lambda fronting agents, where Lambda enforces policies before requests reach agents and dynamically attaches scoped IAM policies based on intent and risk profile. Real-world vulnerabilities cited include Outlook Copilot exfiltrating Slack tokens via prompt injection, Morse code bypassing guardrails, and steganographic image injection. The framework balances developer velocity with security by enabling controlled innovation in sandboxed environments rather than blocking adoption. Key mitigations include avoiding code execution access unless necessary, network isolating per-user interactions, using VMs for isolation, never passing credentials to agents, limiting input prompts to predefined options (like SQL stored procedures), and maintaining deterministic security decisions independent of model outputs. Narjala emphasizes that prompt injection is a built-in feature, not a bug, making architectural controls and guardrails paramount. The three core takeaways: operationalize AI with zero trust, model the agent itself (not just the application), and enable developers while keeping security satisfied.

talks.summary:
### Overview
The OWASP July 2020 Global Board of Directors meeting addressed critical operational, financial, and governance matters facing the organization amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Key items discussed included the approval of meeting minutes, reviews of executive director and finance reports, the creation of an Education and Training Committee, the status of regional and global conferences transitioning to virtual formats, election timelines, and proposed bylaw amendments regarding board member term limits and eligibility.

### Key Topics
- **Financial Status & Cash Reserves**: Tom presented the financial update showing revenues through June were roughly $26,000 ahead of forecast, partially because conference income cushioned deficits in memberships and donations. Total net deficit stood at approximately $112,000 to $166,500 year-to-date. Cash on hand was around $1.465 million at the end of June, projected to decline to around $1 million by year-end. A central concern discussed was OWASP's reliance on conferences as an "events company" and assessing whether the foundation would have a sufficient cash runway into 2021 if physical conferences remain halted.
- **Executive Director Report & External Affiliations**: Andrew van der Stock provided updates on membership growth (+61 net), website traffic (554k visitors), and declining service desk tickets. He announced policy community reviews, the move to fully virtual events, and that OWASP joined the Linux Foundation and the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), with board member Sherif Mansour appointed to the OpenSSF board.
- **Education Committee Approval**: Grant sponsored a motion to formally approve the establishment of the Education and Training Committee following the Committee 2.0 structure, led by community members Adrian and John. The motion passed unanimously (7–0).
- **Virtual vs. Regional Events Strategy**: The board evaluated how to address cancellations of major regional conferences (such as AppSec California and AppSec Cali/Dublin concerns). Discussion centered on providing chapters with virtual event tooling (e.g., StreamYard) and guidance rather than the central foundation taking over regional conferences, avoiding brand dilution and staff burnout.
- **Bylaw Amendments on Board Eligibility & Term Limits**: Significant debate occurred regarding compliance committee recommendations to clarify board term limits. Specifically, discussions focused on whether filling a partial vacancy should count as a full term or count toward term limits, how to measure time served (e.g., splitting by one year or setting a five-year cap), and the ethics of altering eligibility rules immediately prior to the upcoming election cycle when it could directly impact sitting board members. The topic was deferred for further public discussion and separated into discrete votes.

talks.summary:
### Overview
The May 2022 OWASP Global Board Meeting brought together board members, foundation leadership, and committee representatives to review organizational performance, project governance, and policy updates. Chaired by Vandana Verma, the meeting covered staff operations, finances, vendor neutrality challenges, event planning, and updates from the OWASP Project Committee.

### Key Topics
- **Operations and Administration**: The board noted that April meeting minutes were pending an electronic vote (evote). Staff reported progress on community awards nominations, updates to European entity restructuring (moving from Belgium to the Netherlands), and ongoing AMS (Association Management Software) migration planning.
- **Financial Health**: Tom presented the financial narrative, reporting strong foundation performance through April 2022. Cash assets and corporate membership were up year-over-year, operational reserves stood at 7 to 10.5 months (surpassing the nonprofit industry average of 6 months), and net income was performing significantly better than budgeted.
- **Events and Chapter Growth**: Chapters expanded to 416 with eight new additions. However, low registration for AppSec Europe and fewer Call for Papers (CFP) submissions for the APAC event raised concerns, prompting targeted marketing pushes.
- **Vendor Neutrality & Co-Marketing**: The board engaged in a detailed discussion regarding the boundaries of vendor neutrality. Board members highlighted the risks of appearing to endorse commercial products through retweets, co-marketing agreements, or project sponsorships. Consensus formed around drafting explicit, transparent policy guidelines distinguishing neutral co-marketing, sponsor acknowledgment, and member benefits while ensuring zero commercial endorsements.
- **Project Committee Update**: Björn Kimminich and Steve Springett presented committee progress, including streamlined incubator-to-lab project reviews (reducing turnaround time to 1–2 months), proposed "good practices" for vendor neutrality and repository management, and a proposal for a new "production" maturity tier between lab and flagship.

### Technical & Governance Details
- **SBOM & Standards Alignment**: Andrew reported on discussions in Washington, DC regarding Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) standards, highlighting the friction between SPDX Light and OWASP CycloneDX. The board emphasized the urgency of engaging the CycloneDX team directly with the SPDX initiative to preserve OWASP's influence at the standards table.
- **Project Support Resource Request**: The Project Committee raised a funding request ($60,000 FTE) for a dedicated technical community manager to support flagship projects like CycloneDX, Juice Shop, and Dependency-Track, alleviating pressure on Harold Blankenship. Andrew noted this would be considered during the 2023 budgeting process following the AMS rollout.
- **Operational Grants Process**: Harold shared a draft operational grants workflow to structure how OWASP accepts external grant funding (e.g., Google, Accenture) versus managing pass-through disbursements.

### Takeaways
OWASP remains in a stable financial and operational position, but faces growing governance demands. Priority action items include formalizing a comprehensive vendor neutrality and partnership policy, finalizing external grant operational workflows, advancing the European entity transition to the Netherlands, and evaluating dedicated technical staffing for major open-source projects in the upcoming budget cycle.

### Overview
The October 2023 OWASP Board Meeting covered a range of organizational, operational, and governance topics. Key agenda items included administrative updates on the ongoing financial audit and accounting transition, the 2023 board election voter turnout, operational status of chapters and projects, logistical preparations for Global AppSec DC and Singapore, the appointment of a new compliance committee member, and policy enforcement around corporate sponsor advertising on official social media channels.

### Key Topics
- **Finance, Audit, and Accounting Transition**: Executive Director Andrew reported on the status of the 2022 990 audit, noting requisitions handled with Virtual and upcoming review meetings. Due to revised methodologies, documentation of expense management controls, and updated tax treatment for corporate memberships, Andrew noted OWASP might not see a completely clean audit report. The operational migration to Charity CFO was ongoing, awaiting the audit conclusion, while banking operations were transitioning between Citizens and Chase.
- **Elections and Membership Metrics**: Dawn reported board election participation was at approximately 7.8%, tracking in line with historical turnouts under 15%. Andrew noted active membership was at 6,423. It was highlighted that a majority of project and chapter leaders were not active paid members, prompting discussion of complimentary leader membership drives. Technology updates included a force majeure flag extending complimentary memberships to individuals in conflict zones (specifically Ukraine, Israel, and Palestine).
- **Project Committee Report**: Björn presented an update on the project review process, handbook revisions, and project exits. Recent adjustments allow continuous monthly promotion reviews via a Google Form. Harold was leading the rewrite of the Project Leader Handbook to serve as a comprehensive single source of truth for guidelines, funding, and Jira reimbursement procedures (including the simplified process for expenses under $250). The board discussed project departures (such as ZAP and SKF), legal IP/licensing ownership, and repository management across GitHub organizations.
- **Compliance Committee Appointment**: The board met candidate Ricardo "Rick" Melo for the compliance committee (transitioning to compliance officers as of January 1). Rick shared his professional background spanning 22 years in IT, banking cyber risk, and management. Former compliance committee members Bill and Ricardo shared insights into adjudicating interpersonal and code-of-conduct disputes impartially. The board unanimously approved a motion appointing Rick to the compliance committee contingent upon completing his OWASP membership.
- **Events and Social Media Guidelines**: Lauren reported that Global AppSec DC exceeded budget expectations across registrations ($400,000+), trainings ($100,000 over budget), and sponsorships. Schedule adjustments were made to accommodate remote participation for speakers affected by international events and visa issues. Lauren also confirmed Global AppSec Singapore concluded with a net profit over $3,500. Finally, the board reviewed corporate sponsorship social media policies, clarifying that benefits had been revised back to single welcome announcements to prevent vendors from posting commercial product marketing or derogatory project comparisons via OWASP channels.

### Technical Details
- **Project Promotions & Governance**: Project promotions now follow a structured review sheet evaluated by committee members (Pass, Fail, Provisional Pass). Six to seven projects had reached the newly established production level. Formal flagship status additions or revocations remain subject to board approval upon committee recommendation.
- **Social Media Contract Controls**: Previous corporate sponsorship packages permitted one to three monthly posts, leading to an incident where an external post promoted a commercial product at the expense of an OWASP project. Contracts have been revised, and active grandfathered posts are strictly prescreened by staff to ensure vendor neutrality.

### Takeaways
OWASP demonstrated strong operational performance in events and operating reserves, while working through governance transitions in financial reporting, project IP policies, and compliance oversight. The board emphasized enforcing vendor neutrality on communication channels and improving internal documentation to make resources accessible to community leaders.

talks.title: What Can Traditional Web App Security Learn From Browser Wallet Extensions?
talks.teaser: Compares crypto wallet extension threat models with traditional web apps and shows dependency sandboxing with SES compartments.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts centralized web applications, where the server holds accounts and can revoke access after a breach, with decentralized applications such as self-custodial crypto wallets. In a wallet, the private key stored in the browser is effectively the account, so losing it means losing the funds. That makes the client a trusted single point of failure. The speaker frames the main risk as malicious code running inside the client, through cross-site scripting or through supply chain compromise of npm dependencies. Cross-site scripting is treated as largely addressable with modern browser controls, while supply chain attacks are presented as the harder problem.

The middle of the talk reviews why iframes and workers are weak sandboxes for JavaScript dependencies. Moving code into another realm breaks object identity and synchronous execution, which can break existing applications. The talk then presents SES, a TC39 proposal currently implemented as a shim, whose compartments isolate code within the same realm. The LavaMoat project, used in MetaMask's build, statically analyzes each dependency to derive a policy of the JavaScript APIs it uses, loads it in its own compartment, and fails the build when the policy changes. A worked example shows a logging package that suddenly calls fetch being blocked at runtime and caught during review.

The question-and-answer session covered the limits of this approach. Policies must be reviewed on every dependency change, onboarding a large dependency tree is costly, and applying it to content-heavy sites with many third-party scripts is hard. A dependency that legitimately holds a powerful API can still be abused. The takeaway is that traditional web applications can adopt least-authority policies, build-time policy review and confinement of untrusted code, because the client needs protection even when server-side reversal is possible.

talks.title: OWASP Coraza Web Application Firewalls Revisited
talks.teaser: Explains why web application firewalls still matter and how the open source Coraza WAF runs across proxies and browsers.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a core maintainer of the OWASP Coraza project, opens with a refresher on web application firewalls. A WAF is a proxy that inspects incoming and outgoing HTTP traffic at layer 7, matches it against rules such as the OWASP Core Rule Set, and writes audit logs for later analysis. Despite the shift toward zero trust, cloud and serverless, the speaker argues WAFs remain useful as one layer of defense. Virtual patching, lift-and-shift migrations, the PCI DSS 4.0 requirement and the SQL injection behind a major 2023 breach are given as reasons to keep one in place.

The talk then introduces Coraza as an open source WAF written in Go, initially inspired by ModSecurity, that supports SecLang and the Core Rule Set and carries OWASP's production-ready flag. Its guiding principles include sustainability beyond any single company, use-case-driven feature decisions, a stable core API alongside an experimental one, and a strong focus on performance. Because it targets many runtimes, Coraza compiles to WebAssembly for proxy-wasm hosts such as Envoy and Kong, and it also runs in a browser playground. To speed up matching, the project replaced Go's regex library with a statically linked RE2 build and used a Rust library for dictionary matching.

The closing section covers extensibility through plugins, operators, audit loggers and body processors. Planned work includes a directives API, OCSF audit log output, paranoia levels as first-class settings, more connector partnerships, and the upcoming support for Go's own garbage collector in WebAssembly builds.

talks.title: 'The Rise And Fall' Of ModSecurity And The OWASP Core Rule Set
talks.teaser: Shows how learned rule severities improve ModSecurity's detection, and how adversarial training hardens it against evasion.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how web application firewalls sit in front of applications and block attacks using signature rule sets, with ModSecurity and the OWASP Core Rule Set as the running example. It recaps how each rule carries a severity score, how anomaly scoring sums the scores of matched rules against a threshold, and how paranoia levels trade coverage for more false positives. The speaker points out that these severities are fixed in advance and do not reflect the traffic a given application actually receives.

The research treats each rule as a feature, so a request becomes a vector of rule matches and the anomaly score becomes a linear classifier whose coefficients are the severities. Using a dataset of about 50,000 SQL injection samples split between legitimate and malicious traffic, the speaker shows that adjusting severities alone can raise detection at a fixed 1% false positive rate. Some weights drop to zero and others turn negative. Several classifiers were compared, with L1 and L2 regularization affecting how many rules the model relies on.

The second part addresses evasion. Adversarial SQL injection variants generated with the WAFFLE tool were included in training, and the model trained this way kept better robustness when attack variants were sent against it than a model trained without them. The speaker notes the method is not specific to SQL injection, that the code and data are shared for reproduction, and that a linear model's weights could be applied directly to the rule set, while nonlinear models would require engine changes. The Q&A covered what severity means and how the results could feed back into the open-source project.

talks.title: Winning Buy-In: Mastering The Art Of Communicating Security To Management
talks.teaser: Ida Hameete explores Winning Buy-In: Mastering The Art Of Communicating Security To Management.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Ida Hamea addresses the challenge technical cybersecurity professionals face when seeking executive approval and budget from management or board members. Security practitioners frequently struggle because they communicate in technical jargon, focusing on vulnerabilities and technical problems rather than the strategic and financial values prioritized by executives. Through the narrative example of a colleague named Eric attempting to secure buy-in for a zero trust project, Hamea lays out a practical framework for translating security initiatives into business value, preparing rigorously, and successfully navigating presentations and executive questioning.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding the Audience:** Presenters must thoroughly research board members and managers—using LinkedIn, company websites, and published articles—to identify their backgrounds, language patterns, and core concerns.
- **Speaking Management Language:** Technical buzzwords and CVE counts fail to resonate with management. Security presenters must adopt management terminology and articulate initiatives around business goals such as Return on Investment (ROI), revenue generation, cost savings, or operational efficiency.
- **Building Allies:** Cultivating relationships across departments, including assistants and managerial colleagues (often through informal encounters like coffee or smoking areas), provides invaluable intelligence about executive personalities, calendar openings, and common objections.
- **Structuring the Presentation:** Presentations should begin with clear framing in the first minute: a short description of the project, a concise statement of intent (what approval or budget is needed), and the primary executive takeaway (e.g., increased safety and financial return). Rather than dwelling on problems, presenters should quickly transition into a solution-oriented posture.
- **Narrative and Visual Restraint:** Storytelling techniques (such as the hero's journey showing another organization's successful implementation) engage executives far better than data dumps. Visuals should be minimal to keep attention focused on the speaker, and detailed materials should be provided as a leave-behind document after the talk rather than beforehand.

### Technical Details
- **Metric Framing:** Numbers such as CVE totals are largely meaningless to management unless contextualized within business plans. Quantitative arguments should align with existing executive priorities, such as headcount reductions, product delivery timelines, or operational time savings (e.g., using automated security to reduce customer call handling duration in a telecommunications setting).
- **Handling Graphics and Timing:** Charts should only be shown at the exact moment they are being explained, preventing executives from making premature or inaccurate interpretations that derail the message.
- **Physical and Mental Preparation:** Rehearsing the exact presentation flow up to 100 or 200 times builds essential confidence. Presenters should mirror the audience's dress code (whether business formal, casual, or hoodies) to avoid distraction, practice diaphragmatic (belly) breathing to mitigate stress, and maintain a grounded physical stance.

### Takeaways
- **Anticipate and Disarm Objections:** The Q&A session frequently decides the outcome of a proposal. Identify typical management tactics beforehand—such as 'death by delay,' 'never change,' 'death by detail,' and 'killed by old experience.' Proactively mentioning anticipated objections early in the pitch disarms them.
- **Stay Grounded in Q&A:** When facing pushback or stalling tactics, remain respectful, acknowledge executive concerns, defer minor implementation details to later project stages, and firmly insist on moving forward immediately by tying the initiative directly to organizational business and revenue goals.

talks.title: OWASP Top-25 Parameters
talks.teaser: Lütfü Mert Ceylan explores OWASP Top-25 Parameters.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security researcher Matt introduces the OWASP Top-25 Parameters project, an initiative designed to identify and rank web application parameters that have the highest probability of harboring security vulnerabilities. Matt, a 19-year-old independent researcher from Turkey pursuing a bachelor's degree in Poland and an OWASP Project Leader, shares the history, methodology, and practical applications of the project. He conceptualizes the project using an atomic orbital model analogy: just as an electron cloud shows locations with the highest probability of finding electrons, the project maps out parameters where the likelihood of detecting vulnerabilities within a universal set is highest. These datasets are intended for use by security researchers in fuzz testing, static code analysis, and dynamic analysis.

### Key Topics
The presentation centers on three core areas: the sources and data collection methodologies, the vulnerability categories analyzed, and the timeline tracing the project's evolution. Matt began the project in 2021, achieving over 1,500 GitHub stars before it transitioned into an official OWASP Foundation project two years later. Following this milestone, he presented the project at OWASP Global AppSec in Washington, D.C., and HackSEC 2024 in Turkey.

A central topic is the contrast between manual analysis and automation. Unlike many modern datasets that rely exclusively on automated scrapers, Matt collected most of the foundational data manually from articles dating back to 2007, blog posts, write-ups, open-source projects, and public bug bounty reports from platforms like HackerOne and Bugcrowd, referencing vulnerable disclosure programs such as the Netherlands' VDP. The project distinguishes between 'confirmed' data verified manually and unconfirmed data collected via automated pipelines, with plans to synthesize both approaches in future iterations.

### Technical Details
The OWASP Top-25 Parameters project provides prioritized parameter rankings across several common web application vulnerability types:
- **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS):** Lists top parameters ranging from markers like `email`, `name`, and date fields, capturing high-probability entry points for XSS vulnerabilities.
- **SQL Injection (SQLi):** Features ranked primary parameter tables where parameters like `id` carry a significantly higher likelihood of vulnerability compared to parameters like `region`, `main`, or `form`.
- **Remote Code Execution (RCE):** Identifies function names, print parameters, and module markers with high likelihood of RCE exposure.
- **Local File Inclusion (LFI):** Highlights parameters commonly associated with file paths and file retrieval, including `cat`, `action`, `downloads`, and directory path values.
- **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and Open Redirects:** Documents parameters related to outbound network operations or redirection, including `data`, `reference`, `callback`, `redirect`, and payment/callback endpoints.

The analytical pipeline relies on collecting research articles, pentest reports, and public bug bounty data, performing pattern modeling and formation, factoring in uncertain values and risk calculations, and generating finalized ranked lists.

### Takeaways
The project demonstrates how analyzing high-frequency parameter patterns scientifically increases finding rates during vulnerability assessments. It raises ongoing research questions regarding the effectiveness of human-driven pattern extraction versus purely automated scanning. Furthermore, the broader security community and commercial tools have started integrating these datasets; Matt highlights ecosystem feedback such as PortSwigger community contributions, BApp Store extensions, and articles implementing Top-25 parameter wordlists for active testing tools. Future project goals include incorporating private bug bounty datasets if accessible and uniting automated data ingestion with manual validation.

talks.title: Token It Up A Notch: Elevating Payment Security
talks.teaser: Yadi Abdalhalim investigates Token It Up A Notch: Elevating Payment Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security engineer Jovan (V) and software engineer Yudi share how Chime engineered an internal tokenization platform to reduce PCI-DSS scope while supporting expanding business needs. Historically, Chime avoided handling primary account numbers (PANs) directly. However, new business requirements—such as card onboarding, cashback rewards integrations with payment networks (Visa/Mastercard), digital card displays, and reporting to banking partners—necessitated handling sensitive payment data. The engineers designed an in-house tokenization architecture to replace raw card numbers with opaque tokens, isolating cardholder data into a dedicated, highly secured environment.

### Key Topics
- **Tokenization & Envelope Encryption:** Replacing sensitive data (PANs, SSNs, ITINs) with UUID tokens while encrypting underlying card data using envelope encryption.
- **Network Isolation & Authentication:** Segmenting the tokenization infrastructure within a private network accessed via AWS PrivateLink, employing Okta for human Single Sign-On (SSO) and mutual service-to-service (S2S) authentication.
- **Data Schema & Association:** Isolating keys across discrete data families and leveraging HMAC digests to query and map raw values back to tokens without decrypting entire databases.
- **Performance & Batch Processing:** Re-architecting file detokenization for multi-gigabyte regulatory/partner reporting from slow sequential routines down to sub-10-minute parallelized workflows.
- **Threat Modeling & Insider Threats:** Designing defenses across multiple trust boundaries, including locked-down support environments, rate limiting, and anomaly detection for rogue staff.

### Technical Details
- **Architecture & Infrastructure:** The system runs as a containerized Go binary within AWS Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) and utilizes AWS KMS, Aurora PostgreSQL, and S3. Internal services connect via AWS PrivateLink, communicating through HTTPS, Twirp (a Protobuf-based RPC framework), or Amazon SQS for asynchronous jobs.
- **Envelope Encryption & Key Management:** Plaintext values are encrypted with a Data Encryption Key (DEK) via AES, while the DEK itself is encrypted under a Key Encryption Key (KEK) managed in an AWS KMS HSM. Encrypted DEKs and ciphertexts are stored in Aurora PostgreSQL; plaintext KEKs never leave KMS. DEKs are rotated after every 100 operations to balance blast radius reduction against customer onboarding latency and AES-GCM nonce limits.
- **Decryption Flow:** The Go service extracts the token ID, validates the data family, fetches the encrypted DEK, decrypts the DEK using the KEK via KMS, and then decrypts the ciphertext.
- **Batch Detokenization:** Processing reporting files with tens of millions of records previously took 8 to 9 hours. By sharding files, implementing caching, and executing detokenization concurrently, the job duration was reduced to under 10 minutes.
- **Customer Service App & Threat Mitigations:** To handle law enforcement inquiries matching PANs to account owners, a legacy Ruby on Rails customer service app embeds the Go tokenization UI via a sandboxed iframe. Controls include locked-down Chrome browser instances, client certificates, rate limiting, short-lived JWTs with strict expiration (`exp`) and algorithm validation, just-in-time SSH access via bastion proxies, and DataDog monitoring with anomaly alerts (e.g., capping support agent lookups to 20 per hour).

### Takeaways
Building an in-house tokenization system requires strict domain separation across data families, rigorous envelope encryption, and minimal service-to-service access. Key takeaways include keeping web frontends simple (using vanilla Go templates rather than complex frameworks to minimize attack surface), relying on automated dependency patching (Dependabot) and internal ECR mirror builds, and treating insider threats as first-class threat models through strict rate-limiting, investigation queues, and automated alerting.

talks.title: OWASP DefectDojo
talks.teaser: Introduces DefectDojo, an open-source platform that normalizes, deduplicates and tracks findings from many security scanners.
talks.summary:
Application security teams often receive scanner output from many vendors, each describing the same problem differently, and tracking it in spreadsheets quickly breaks down. This talk introduces DefectDojo, an open-source vulnerability management platform, and explains why its creator built it while running product security at Rackspace. The core idea is to import results from many tools, normalize them into one finding format, and remove duplicates so the team works from a single source of truth.

The speaker walked through the features that matter in daily use. A false positive marked once stays suppressed in later scans, and reimporting a scan closes findings that no longer appear. Tags and role-based views let the same data be reported to a department head or to a single app team. A full REST API makes almost anything scriptable, and integration with Jira runs in both directions. He described a pipeline pattern where CI jobs push scanner results into DefectDojo, which then creates or closes Jira issues and notifies developers. One organisation raised its yearly assessments from 44 to 224 after adopting the tool, and a large installation reported about 26,000 automated scans imported per day.

The closing section covered the project's pace, with monthly minor releases and weekly bug-fix releases, along with plans to drop MySQL and RabbitMQ support, expand testing, and check API changes between releases. The main takeaway for practitioners is that a normalizing layer lets you replace a scanner without changing downstream processes. The flexible data model is powerful, but it has many settings that need careful configuration before a deployment works well.

talks.title: Hacker Traction Through GitHub Actions: Is Your (Open Source) Project Safe?
talks.teaser: Stephen Giguere analyzes Hacker Traction Through GitHub Actions: Is Your (Open Source) Project Safe?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Steve Giguere shares research conducted alongside Avi Greenholtz exploring supply chain vulnerabilities within GitHub Actions and open-source workflows. Expanding upon initial research into command injection, npm email hijacking, and repo jacking, the talk demonstrates how attackers can chain vulnerabilities across GitHub Action dependencies to build a self-propagating CI/CD "worm" capable of compromising upstream actions and moving downstream to harvest sensitive secrets.

### Key Topics
- **GitHub Actions Attack Vectors**: Core repository risks include command injection, npm email hijacking, dependency confusion, and repo jacking.
- **Repo Jacking in GitHub Actions**: Unlike standard repositories protected by GitHub's retirement threshold (100 clones prior to account rename/deletion), GitHub Actions download assets instead of cloning. This leaves moved or deleted action namespaces vulnerable to re-registration and takeover.
- **Poison Pipeline Execution & Default Configurations**: Prior to March 2023, the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` had read/write permissions. Combined with default settings allowing first-time contributors' PR workflows to run without explicit approvals, attackers could execute arbitrary workflows, approve pull requests, and exfiltrate secrets.
- **Upstream Action Dependency Mapping**: By constructing a Neo4j dependency graph of actions using other actions across popular repositories, researchers traced multi-tier downstream attack paths.

### Technical Details
- **Command Injection via Metadata**: Workflows that directly interpolate issue titles or other untrusted metadata into bash commands or runner steps allow arbitrary shell execution.
- **Runner Persistence and Privilege Escalation**: In demonstrations on GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners, the speaker established a reverse shell via `netcat`, modified git configurations to spoof commits as other contributors (e.g., Linus Torvalds), closed PRs to circumvent workflow timeouts, and leveraged standard Docker access to escalate privileges to root.
- **Large-Scale Analysis**: Analyzing the top 10,000 GitHub repositories by stars alongside 32,000 repositories belonging to companies with bug bounty programs, the team isolated approximately 7,000 repositories using GitHub Actions. From this dataset, 175 repositories were directly vulnerable without chaining. In one chain, compromising a single initial repository allowed compromising 18 intermediary actions and stealing secrets from 72 downstream targets. Another path involving Veracode and Hangfire exposed a NuGet package with nearly 10,000 daily downloads, ultimately exposing nearly 12,000 repositories.
- **The Tag-Overwriting Worm**: Because actions are commonly referenced by mutable tags (e.g., `v1`) rather than immutable commit SHAs, compromising a read/write token enables pushing malicious updates and overwriting release tags with force commits. When downstream repositories run workflows calling that tag, the malicious payload repeats the process, propagating downstream.

### Takeaways & Mitigations
- **Token Permissions**: Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` and personal access tokens to read-only by default and strictly enforce minimal permissions.
- **Tag Pinning**: Pin all GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs instead of mutable tags. The speaker recommends using the open-source tool `ghat` by James Woolner to automate this.
- **Branch & Tag Protection**: Enable branch protection and enforce protected tags to prevent unauthorized tag overwrites and force pushes.
- **Contributor Approvals & CODEOWNERS**: Configure repositories to require approval for workflows submitted by outside contributors, and use `CODEOWNERS` to restrict workflow modifications.
- **Runner Hardening**: Never use self-hosted runners for public open-source projects, and restrict outbound network connections from runners to trusted domains.

talks.title: Will Machine Learning Replace The WAF?
talks.teaser: Argues that machine learning strengthens web application firewalls but does not replace signature rules, using real evasion cases.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether machine learning will replace the web application firewall, and answers no. It starts with the history of the speaker's company's WAF, from a ModSecurity-compatible rule engine built inside NGINX that ran for about nine years, to the problems that rule-based filtering runs into. Rules take time to write, tuning to reduce false positives leaves gaps, and attackers evade signatures with encoding and obfuscation. The Log4j wave of December 2021 is the main example: the first exploit attempts arrived about nine minutes after a public post, and attackers quickly spread variants that used nested lookups and URL encoding to get past filters.

The middle of the talk describes a machine learning layer added in 2022. It is a fast classifier trained on production traffic, labelled by the existing WAF's decisions, and augmented with synthetic variants of known malicious requests to mimic evasion. It scores each request inline, with 90 percent of decisions taking under a millisecond. Scores are mostly at either extreme, and the model has flagged attack patterns before they were publicly disclosed. Signatures remain necessary, because they supply the labels and turn unusual flagged traffic into new rules.

The talk then draws on early spam filtering, where Bayesian classifiers beat keyword lists and obfuscation made spam easier to spot. It warns that attackers could run the same feedback loop against a WAF to automate evasion. The practical takeaway is to avoid telling attackers whether a request was blocked, for example by returning responses that look the same as allowed ones, so they cannot learn from the feedback.

talks.title: Threat Modeling For Developers (Panel)
talks.teaser: Panelists explain threat modeling for developers and offer simple ways to start asking what could go wrong with a system.
talks.summary:
This panel introduces threat modeling as a collaborative process in which security specialists, business representatives and developers identify plausible threats to a system, set aside unrealistic ones, and decide which to address. The speakers argue that developers should take part because they understand the features and architecture best, and that keeping developers and security staff apart leads to poor communication and a checkbox exercise with little value.

For teams starting out, the panel suggested a simple four-question frame covering what is being built, what could go wrong, what will be done about it, and whether the result was good. Practical tips included asking developers what could go wrong, offering concrete examples to get people talking, asking about the worst possible outcome, and using card games such as OWASP Cornucopia and Elevation of Privilege, which are also available free online. For legacy systems, the panel advised focusing on not making existing risk worse in the parts being changed, documenting the system first, and noting that fragility can itself be a business risk worth raising with management.

The speakers closed by stressing that a threat model is a living document, that teams should accept imperfection and stop at a sensible point, and that hands-on practice teaches more than reading. They pointed to the Threat Modeling Manifesto, a free introductory course, OWASP resources and upcoming OWASP events with threat modeling training and mentoring.

talks.title: ATOR (Authentication Token Obtain and Replace) Burp Plugin
talks.teaser: Shows how a Burp Suite extension captures and replaces session tokens across multi-step logins, SSO flows and SMS one-time passwords.
talks.summary:
Modern web and API applications rely on layered authentication, such as access and refresh tokens, one-time tokens, JWTs and multi-step logins, so tokens expire partway through a test and scans start failing. The presenters explained that Burp's native macros could only substitute values in cookies or headers, not JSON bodies, and that their earlier scripts worked for only one application. Their extension, ATOR, follows four steps: define the failure condition, run a login sequence, extract a value from its responses, and inject that value into later requests.

In the demos, a simple login returned a token that had to be Base64-encoded before reuse. A second scenario chained two requests, passing a cookie from the first response into the second to obtain the final session cookie. A third walked through a Facebook SSO flow with several redirects and multiple values replaced between steps. The last demo handled SMS one-time passwords by fetching the code from an SMS service API during the login sequence and submitting it to the application.

The core process stayed the same across all scenarios; the difficulty lies in tracking which value moves where and in naming extracted tokens clearly. Configurations can be exported as JSON and reused when an application is onboarded, and the presenters noted that CSRF and JWT values follow the same replacement pattern. The release also added SMS support, pre-processing such as encoding before replacement, and prevention of duplicate login runs.

talks.title: Keynote: Using LLMs and generative AI to fix software vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Asankhaya Sharma analyzes Using LLMs and generative AI to fix software vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens by arguing that application security has stayed stubbornly repetitive for two decades, even as development moved to open source, cloud, microservices and DevOps. The speaker traces how code-focused language models have evolved from autocomplete-style generation to instruction-following chat models, and how open code models have narrowed the gap with proprietary ones on standard code benchmarks.

The middle of the talk lays out a road map from simple prompting to automated fixes. Asking a code model to infill a flagged line can address a modest share of vulnerabilities. Instruction tuning on curated commit messages and code diffs improves bug fixing, and an open model tuned this way is presented as competitive with a leading proprietary one. Adding security context taken from static analyzer output lifts results further on a Python benchmark. Retrieval from a private codebase's past fixes, and static analysis such as reachability and impact analysis to pull in related code across files, push results higher. The final stage is a planning agent that makes multi-step edits, with the speaker noting that real fixes often span several files and steps.

The closing argument is that fixes will still need checks: builds, existing tests and human review, since models can hallucinate or propose changes that do not actually fix the issue. The speaker suggests that future security tooling should be built for security staff who direct AI agents, rather than for developers who are reluctant to engage with security work. Practitioners should take away that the value lies in combining model fine-tuning, retrieval and classic program analysis, with validation kept in the loop.

talks.title: Scratch containers and the supply chain trouble
talks.teaser: Naveen S investigates Scratch containers and the supply chain trouble.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Naveen, a senior security engineer at Freshworks, explores the security implications, operational trade-offs, and supply chain challenges of building container images using the Docker `scratch` base image. While `scratch` containers significantly reduce image size and attack surface by removing extraneous OS packages and shells, they introduce serious blind spots for vulnerability scanners, creating a false sense of security regarding software supply chain health.

### Key Topics
- **Base Image Dilemmas:** Standard parent images (such as Ubuntu or Debian) are frequently oversized, outdated, and burdened with unpatched CVEs. While reducing images to only necessary dependencies limits exposure, standard multi-stage builds using `scratch` represent an extreme approach where no parent image layer is added.
- **Compiled vs. Interpreted Languages in Scratch:** Statically compiled binaries (such as Go) run naturally inside `scratch` containers once stripped of external C dependencies (`CGO_ENABLED=0`). In contrast, interpreted languages like Python require workarounds using packaging tools like PyInstaller and StaticX to bundle dependencies into a statically linked binary.
- **Scanner Blind Spots & Inconsistencies:** Traditional container scanners (e.g., Trivy) typically rely on OS package managers (`apt`, `dpkg`, `apk`) or language package manifests (`go.sum`, `pip`). In `scratch` containers lacking these package managers and metadata structures, scanners frequently report "zero vulnerabilities" despite the presence of known vulnerable application and system dependencies.
- **Distroless as an Alternative:** When `scratch` presents excessive build complexity or incompatibility, distroless base images (such as Chainctl/Chainguard Wolfi images or Bazel-built minimal images) offer a middle ground without package managers or shells while retaining required system dependencies.

### Technical Details
- **Go Application Test:** Naveen demonstrated a Go web server using a vulnerable Gin 1.4 dependency. Built on Debian Bullseye, Trivy detected 675 vulnerabilities (667 from Debian, 8 from the Go binary). Testing with Alpine showed zero base OS vulnerabilities and only the 8 binary vulnerabilities. Building into `scratch` also surfaced the 8 application vulnerabilities because Go language parsers can extract embedded module metadata from binaries.
- **Python Application Test:** Naveen packaged a Python application containing a vulnerable `requests` package (version 2.3) using PyInstaller and StaticX. On Debian Slim, Trivy detected 81 vulnerabilities; on Alpine, it reported 0. When placed in `scratch`, Trivy reported 0 vulnerabilities because it failed to recognize the bundled binary or package format, completely missing the known CVE.
- **Scanner Detection Mechanics:** Vulnerability tools detect packages via package managers, layer hashes from manifests, SBOM attestations, or language-specific decompilers/debuggers. Static linking of shared objects (`.so`) into standalone binaries hides system-level dependencies from tools that rely on OS package databases.
- **Exploitability vs. Compliance:** Even though missing runtime environments (like shells or utility binaries) can make remote code execution or injection exploits fail or simply terminate the container, underlying business logic and vulnerable dependencies remain unmonitored if scanners report false negatives.

### Takeaways
A report of zero vulnerabilities from a container scanner does not guarantee an application is secure or compliant. Organizations using `scratch` containers must perform due diligence, incorporate build-time SBOM generation before binary packaging, and be cautious of hidden vulnerabilities within statically linked shared objects.

talks.title: OWASP Dependency Check Project
talks.teaser: Explains how the OWASP Dependency-Check tool finds known vulnerable third-party libraries and how to manage its false positives.
talks.summary:
This session introduces OWASP Dependency-Check, a free software composition analysis tool that flags known vulnerable third-party libraries. The speaker, the project's founder, traces the field's history and explains that the tool began as an audit aid for Java and has since gained analyzers for other ecosystems, with some still marked experimental. Its main data source is the National Vulnerability Database, supplemented by OSS Index and wrapped audit tools for npm, Ruby and client-side JavaScript. Because the NVD now rate-limits requests, the speaker advises caching the data directory or mirroring the database.

The central challenge is matching a developer's Maven-style coordinates to the vendor and product identifiers used in vulnerability records. The tool gathers textual evidence from manifests, POM files, file names and package names, then searches it against an index of those identifiers. False positives are usually obvious and can be suppressed from the HTML report, preferably by package URL rather than by individual CVE. Build-plugin scans are generally more accurate than command-line or Docker scans, because they see transitive dependencies that a scan of a folder can miss. A live demo on a small HTML parser found no vulnerabilities, and a later example showed a vulnerable Commons Collections jar.

The question session covered multi-language support, vendor libraries and internal data sources. The speaker closed by urging teams to run the scanner early and often, including on pull requests, and invited contributors to help with roughly 350 open issues, an enterprise deployment guide and Gradle plugin work. The practical takeaway is to scan continuously, triage findings by real exploitability, and report misidentifications upstream.

talks.summary:
The talk argues that traditional appsec tooling is slow, produces PDF reports that get thrown over the wall at developers, and casts security as the team that always says no. Because skilled security staff are the critical resource, automating their repetitive work matters most. The goal is to give the business informed, consistent answers instead of blockers.

DefectDojo serves as the central point. It normalizes and deduplicates output from more than a hundred tools, tracks application and endpoint inventories, and pushes findings to Jira or summaries to Slack. Pipeline stages are fixed, much like ordering at a burrito line: intake, risk-based triage, testing, a vulnerability repository, then delivery. Three generations of pipelines are described. The first gets internal tooling in order. The second adds light hooks into developer pipelines that report results without breaking builds. The third is event-driven, launching containerized tools through a webhook when code is checked in. One friend's setup covered 15 repositories over four months.

In one earlier example, a team went from 44 assessments in 2014 to 224 in 2015 and 414 in 2016 while losing staff, which the speaker credits mostly to automation. Simple baseline metrics, such as how many repositories meet a standard, give executives a clear view. The main takeaways are that automation delivers breadth rather than rigorous testing, so scanners should not be made blocking gates, and results should land in the tools developers already use.

talks.title: Keynote: Data is a new security boundary
talks.teaser: Anastasiia Voitova examines Data is a new security boundary.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that data security should follow the data itself rather than individual databases or clouds, as modern systems spread sensitive information across many teams, tools and third-party services. The speaker, a cryptography engineer, walks through a five-step approach: identify sensitive data, map its flows through each component, threat model those flows, assess risk and trust, and then choose and implement controls. Encryption is presented as a strong safeguard because well-protected data limits the damage from mistakes elsewhere, and the talk points to regulations and OWASP guidance that expect it.

The middle section compares data-at-rest, data-in-transit and application-level encryption, including field-level and end-to-end variants, and explains that TLS and storage encryption still matter alongside them. Key management is highlighted as the hardest part, covering generation, rotation, revocation and recovery, with stories of products failing when a master key or key management service was lost. The talk also introduces zero-knowledge architectures, searchable encryption such as blind indexes and deterministic encryption, privacy-enhancing computation, and tamper-evident logging using hash chains and Merkle trees.

The closing part shows three real-world patterns: a document database's client-side field encryption SDK, where the application holds key material; a database-facing proxy that encrypts selected columns so neither the app nor the database sees plaintext; and a SaaS platform and a fintech that centralised field encryption in the data access layer, with per-customer keys and a decryption path for analytics. The takeaway is that encryption only works when surrounded by controls such as access control, audit logging, API protection and monitoring, so practitioners should design the key lifecycle and data flows together with those controls.

talks.title: Insiders Guide to Mobile AppSec with Latest OWASP MASVS
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP MASVS levels, the top mobile risk areas and practical testing guidance for mobile apps.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces MASVS, OWASP's mobile application security verification standard, as a shared baseline for developers and security teams. The speaker explains why mobile testing is harder than web testing: two operating systems, frequent platform updates, the need for physical devices, and an attack surface that spans the app, the device, the network and back-end APIs. The MASVS levels run from L1, a baseline for simple apps without regulated data, to L2, which adds defenses for personal or payment data such as certificate pinning. An R suffix adds reverse engineering resilience to protect intellectual property.

The speaker then walks through five areas that appear most often in the company's analysis of public app store apps. These are insecure data storage, found in about half of the apps; insecure network communication, such as plain HTTP, found in nearly half; insecure authentication, which appeared in a smaller share; extraneous functionality such as debug features left enabled; and weak reverse engineering and anti-tampering protections. For each, the talk offers development and testing tips, including encrypting sensitive data, enforcing HTTPS, expiring sessions and confirming release builds are not debuggable.

The closing point is that tamper protection cannot fix underlying bugs. It may deter reverse engineering but will not stop attacks on insecure network calls. Attendees are pointed to the MASVS and MSTG resources, open-source tools such as Frida and Radare2, and the CycloneDX standard for software bills of materials.

talks.title: How hackers can breach your C.I / C.D systems
talks.teaser: Walks through attacks against CI/CD pipelines, from leaked secrets and reverse shells to zip bombs and malicious actions.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how attackers can abuse software delivery pipelines, from source code through build servers, artifact repositories and deployment. The speakers introduce continuous integration and continuous deployment, then map a typical toolchain built around tools such as Jenkins, GitLab, GitHub Actions and Docker Hub, and identify the stages where an attacker could gain a foothold.

Early stages cover risks such as IDE files and sensitive data committed to repositories, overly broad roles that let a single developer change production code, and secrets exposed through pipeline environment variables. Live demos show a reverse shell opened from a Jenkins job, and a malicious GitHub Action that could forward environment variables to an outside server. Later examples include a Docker image published to a public registry with secrets inside, a zip bomb uploaded for deployment to Tomcat that exhausts memory, and memory and fork bombs that take down build agents. A shell alias replaced with a command that leaks environment variables is also shown.

The practical advice is to isolate CI/CD networks and restrict outbound internet access, use least-privilege service accounts instead of one all-powerful bot, and keep secrets in protected variables. Teams should rely on trusted, pinned actions and images, check Docker layers before publishing, validate API responses against their contracts, and apply resource limits to build agents so a single job cannot exhaust the machine.

talks.title: Data at Rest Encryption Going Beyond the Basics to Address Modern Attacks
talks.teaser: Explains why transparent data-at-rest encryption fails against modern attacks and how key-controlled encryption closes the gap.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on cryptography and key management and notes that the OWASP Top 10 2021 lists cryptographic failures as its own category. The speakers argue that TLS largely solves data in transit, but encryption at rest shifts the problem to key handling. A transparently encrypted database still returns plaintext to a SQL injection, because decryption happens for any query that reaches it.

The middle of the talk examines the central implicit trust model, where database administrators, cloud operators and hypervisor hosts can read plaintext. Insider misuse, a compromised cloud provider and attackers harvesting database credentials all get around these controls. Examples include a 2018 hotel group breach that began with spearphishing and led to database admin credentials exposing up to 500 million guest records, a retailer's SQL injection that exposed over 130 million card numbers, and a mobile payment app whose password reset required no authentication.

The speakers then propose encrypting higher in the stack using column-level, field-level and application-level encryption, so fewer components see plaintext. In a medical records example, each patient gets separate read and write keys, so an injected query yields only data that user could already access. The talk also covers trade-offs such as limited sorting and filtering on encrypted fields and performance cost, and it closes with key lifecycle guidance and the importance of getting implementation details right.

talks.title: Building Security Champions
talks.teaser: Explains how to recruit, engage, teach, recognize and sustain security champions to scale an application security program.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a shortage of security staff: a team cannot hire its way to full coverage, so programs need other ways to scale. A security champion is a member of a non-security team who advocates for security inside that team and acts as its first point of contact. The speaker argues that champions have to be built up rather than volunteered or ordered into the role, and presents a five-stage recipe covering recruiting, engagement, teaching, recognition and rewards, and consistency.

Recruiting relies on attracting people rather than assigning them. Useful tactics include asking for volunteers at lunch-and-learns, inviting frequent question-askers to take on the role, and getting each candidate's manager on board so the time is actually available. Engagement means involving champions in incidents within agreed limits, letting them see new tools and policies first, sending regular updates, and holding a monthly one-to-one with a standard set of questions. Teaching should stay narrow: threat modeling basics for designers, how to validate scanner output, how to find fixes for common bugs, and only the policies that apply to their work. Delegation has limits, and tasks such as approving tools should remain with the security team.

Recognition should happen in front of peers and in performance reviews, while rewards should reinforce security through training, books, time off or hardware keys. The speaker stresses that programs fade quickly without regular contact, so even a short monthly check-in keeps a champion program alive. Treat the program as a marathon, not a sprint.

talks.title: Web Application Honeypot Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Explains how ModSecurity probes with fake content and honey traps feed real web attack data into threat-sharing platforms.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the point that web traffic dominates internet activity and that web application firewalls sit in front of most serious deployments, so their logs are a useful source of threat intelligence. It argues that a WAF running the Core Rule Set on ModSecurity can act as a honeypot probe, even on a web server with no real content, because automated scanners keep hitting it.

The project described relaunches an earlier effort whose management console had been left to decay. The rebuilt proof of concept runs in Docker, with Apache and the rule set writing JSON audit logs into Elasticsearch, visualised in Kibana and pushed into MISP for sharing. To catch more manual attackers, it adds honey traps: fake listening ports, a disallowed robots.txt entry, fake HTML comments, hidden form fields and cookies. Any interaction with these baits is tagged as malicious and forwarded in the same way.

Next steps include converting MISP data into STIX or TAXII formats, building a management solution for fleets of VM, container or small-device probes, adding vulnerable content management systems as bait, and exploring machine learning to update probe rulesets automatically. The takeaway for practitioners is that inexpensive, deliberately exposed web decoys can produce shareable attack data, and the project invites contributions from students and collaborators.

talks.teaser: Adam Shostack details 25 Years in AppSec: Looking Back, Looking Forward.
talks.summary:
This keynote looks back roughly 25 years at application security, beginning with the speaker's own 1996 code review guidelines written for web-facing systems at a financial firm. It recalls a period with almost no tooling, few dedicated books, and an attacker-centred view of hardening networks, and it traces later milestones such as Microsoft's secure development lifecycle, the spread of commercial and open-source tools, the rise of bug bounties, and the change in how breaches are reported.

The middle of the talk covers how security features have moved into languages, frameworks, hardware chips, and formal methods used by cloud providers. It explains why insecure design was added to the OWASP Top Ten only in 2021, arguing that design trade-offs are harder to fix than injection flaws, and it presents threat modeling as the main way to address them. The speaker then discusses AI in two directions: its potential for finding bugs and reviewing code, and the security and fairness risks of machine learning systems. Abuse campaigns, deepfake-enabled phishing, and misuse of connected devices are described as harms that occur when systems work exactly as designed.

Looking ahead, the speaker expects C to remain dominant for kernels, attacks at the seams between components to grow, and ransomware to become more tailored to each victim. Practitioners are urged to learn from incidents through root-cause reporting, to demonstrate trustworthiness rather than bolt it on, and to build defenses that can favour defenders over attackers.

talks.title: Practical Threat Modeling for real-world and Cloud Situations in our hybrid and W...
talks.teaser: Compares STRIDE, PASTA and diamond threat models, then applies STRIDE to an AWS billing system example.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why threat modeling belongs in design and delivery work, using an everyday example of anticipating risks before a walk. The presenters tie this to shifting security left and to the changes remote and hybrid work brought to how teams build and run systems, which makes early, proactive review more valuable and gives teams a way to catch problems before they reach production.

The middle of the talk compares three approaches. STRIDE sorts threats into categories such as spoofing, tampering and elevation of privilege. PASTA is a seven-stage process that combines business context, threat intelligence and attacker-focused scenarios. The diamond model links an adversary, its infrastructure, its capabilities and its victims, and the speakers used a ransomware-as-a-service group that exploited exposed remote desktop access as an example. They then walked through a hypothetical billing application hosted on AWS, with a web interface, processing APIs, a file-upload path feeding a Lambda function and a database. Candidate threats included tampered uploads, spoofed users, disclosure of sensitive financial data, and a flood of files that could starve processing.

The talk closes with a five-step method: create the model, identify threats, address each one by eliminating, mitigating, transferring or accepting it, communicate results, and validate that mitigations work without introducing new threats. The main takeaway is to make threat modeling a routine part of the development lifecycle and to track whether it reduces findings and rework over time.

talks.title: Analyzing Google’s SLSA Framework for Securing Software Supply Chains
talks.teaser: Examines Google's SLSA framework for protecting build pipelines and artifact integrity, and the gaps it leaves open.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the rise of software supply chain attacks, which the presenters say have grown sharply, with one EU figure showing roughly fourfold growth from 2020 to 2021. Attackers increasingly target the CI/CD tooling behind software delivery rather than only production applications. The presenters argue that security teams often do not own the key delivery tools, such as source control, build servers and infrastructure-as-code, and that compromising source control can give an attacker control over the whole lifecycle.

The middle of the talk walks through Google's SLSA framework, which defines levels from zero to four for build provenance and artifact integrity. Level one requires a scripted, automated build that generates provenance. Higher levels add a hosted build service, signed and tamper-resistant provenance, and isolated builds, while the top level requires two-person review and reproducible builds. The framework's threat model covers source integrity and build integrity, and its requirements are grouped into source, build, provenance and common controls. The common controls include strong access control, multifactor authentication and limiting administrator access to delivery tools.

The closing section lists what SLSA does not cover: collusion between reviewers, administrator actions that temporarily remove protections, hash collisions, vulnerabilities in code and dependencies, infrastructure-as-code flaws, and secret exposure. For these gaps, the presenters point to complementary measures such as detecting rubber-stamp approvals from review activity, commit signing, continuous checking of provenance against deployed artifacts, and dedicated secret controls.

talks.title: OWASP Flagship Projects: OWASP DefectDojo
talks.teaser: Matt Tesauro examines OWASP Flagship Projects: OWASP DefectDojo.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, maintainers Matt Tesauro and Aaron introduce OWASP DefectDojo, an open-source security orchestration and vulnerability management platform. Originally conceived eight to nine years prior within Rackspace by its product security team, DefectDojo was open-sourced and later designated an OWASP Flagship project. The speakers describe how security teams frequently resort to spreadsheets like Excel or Google Sheets to track findings—an approach that fails as vulnerability volumes grow. DefectDojo addresses this problem by serving as a central source of truth for application and product security findings, offering consolidated deduplication, integrations, tracking, and an extensive ingestion engine.

### Key Topics
- **Origins and Purpose:** Built by application security practitioners to replace fragmented spreadsheets and disparate scanner web consoles with a centralized vulnerability repository and asset inventory.
- **Ingestion and Deduping:** DefectDojo ingests reports from more than 100 security tools across DAST, SAST, IAST, container scanners, and cloud tools. It normalizes findings and deduplicates repeat issues to keep data manageable.
- **Architecture and Modernization:** DefectDojo evolved from Python 2 and Django to Python 3 and Django 2, with efforts underway toward a React front end and API v2. Features from earlier internal tooling (such as the Bag of Holding metadata tool) were merged directly into DefectDojo.
- **The AppSec Pipeline:** The speakers detail the conceptual workflow of application security programs—Intake, Triage, Testing, pushing findings into DefectDojo, and Delivery (integrating with Jira, Slack, MS Teams, and GRC systems).
- **Deployment Options:** Deployments range from Docker Compose and Helm 3 on Kubernetes to Godojo, a single-binary installer for bare-metal/VM environments.

### Technical Details
- **Parsing Engine:** Parsing outputs from over 100 tools is made straightforward through lightweight Python parsers (often 20–40 lines). A template generator repo assists community contributors in authoring new tool parsers, with sample outputs fed directly into automated unit testing.
- **Integration and Automation:** The platform provides a Swagger-documented REST API (API v2) enabling automated ingestion in CI/CD pipelines. Supported notification and ticketing channels include Jira (with issue grouping to prevent ticket storms), Slack, and Microsoft Teams. It supports SSO via Okta, Google, Azure AD, and SAML, and incorporates standards like OWASP ASVS.
- **Scalability and Deployments:** Demonstrated production setups include a single EC2 `t2.large` instance with AWS RDS running Docker Compose, as well as massive deployments with a 21 GB database handling 5,000 ingested findings per day using Celery for deduplication processing. Metal/VM deployments are supported via `godojo`, which offers over 160 configurable options that can be set through environment variables.

### Takeaways
DefectDojo provides an automated, vendor-agnostic foundation for vulnerability management, freeing AppSec teams from manual tracking and enabling smaller teams to scale their assessment capacity significantly. The project relies heavily on an active open-source community, welcoming contributions in parser development, documentation, scanner test cases, and bug fixes. A public sandbox refreshed daily is maintained at demo.defectdojo.org.

talks.title: OWASP Flagship Projects: OWASP Dependency-Check
talks.teaser: Explains how OWASP Dependency-Check finds known vulnerable libraries and how to tune its results.
talks.summary:
This talk introduces software composition analysis, the practice of finding risk in third-party and open source components. The main focus is known public vulnerabilities, with licence risk a lesser concern. The speaker traces OWASP Dependency-Check from its Java origins to support for .NET, Ruby, Node, Python and other ecosystems, noting that some analyzers remain experimental.

The tool caches NVD data locally and matches evidence from each dependency, such as vendor, product and version, to CPE identifiers in a search index. Because a single library can carry different names in developer and security data, both false positives and false negatives occur. The speaker urges users to run the tool through build plugins, which expose more dependency information than the command line. The HTML report lets users generate suppression entries for false positives, while a hints file handles missed components. Some sources, such as the OSS Index and npm audit, send package details to outside services, which matters for privacy.

For deployment, the speaker recommends mirroring NVD data or preserving the data directory in ephemeral build environments to avoid rate limiting. Remote code execution issues should be patched quickly, since public exploit tooling tends to follow. The talk also notes that a free run can help prove a problem internally and test commercial products. It closes with requests for pull requests and help with an enterprise deployment guide and the Gradle plugin.
