talks.title: OWASP Flagship Projects: OWASP Dependency Track
talks.teaser: Shows how Dependency-Track analyzes SBOMs to find vulnerable, outdated, and license-risky components across many assets.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OWASP Dependency-Track, a flagship project built around software bill of materials (SBOMs). The speaker compares an SBOM to an ingredients label that lets an organization make risk-based decisions, such as spotting a prohibited or known-vulnerable component. Dependency-Track ingests SBOMs from build pipelines, vendors or manual uploads, then analyzes each component for security, operational and license risk. Every project is re-analyzed at least once a day, so a new vulnerability can trigger alerts against inventories that were uploaded long ago.

The demonstration walks through the dashboard, which tracks portfolio vulnerability counts and risk scores over time, and then through a single project's component list, showing version currency, first-party flags and license data. A dependency graph reveals how each component entered the build, separating direct from transitive dependencies. A critical Jackson Databind finding is used to show how an analyst can record an exploitability decision and suppress it with an audit trail. Components can be searched by package URL, CPE, SWID tag or hash, and a vulnerability page lists every affected project.

The speaker distinguishes this approach from traditional software composition analysis, since SBOMs also capture nested components, provenance and the full stack, including services and hardware. Service entries in an SBOM can expose endpoints and data flows, which the speaker suggests could feed threat modeling. Policy engines cover license and prohibited-component rules, and results can be pushed to chat, email and defect tracking tools. The takeaway is that fast, automated SBOM ingestion and alerting help teams make better risk decisions across large asset inventories.

talks.title: OWASP Flagship Projects: OWASP Security Shepherd
talks.teaser: Gives an overview of Security Shepherd, a gamified web and mobile CTF platform for classroom security training.
talks.summary:
Sean presents Security Shepherd, an OWASP project that works as a gamified capture-the-flag framework for web and mobile security training. Built on Tomcat, JSP and MySQL, it can be run as a prebuilt Ubuntu virtual machine, through Docker, or on a self-hosted server. Each lesson or challenge yields a key that players submit for points, and lessons explain the technique before the harder challenges arrive.

The walkthrough covers the administrator side and several exercises. Administrators can set up classes with separate scoreboards, enable a CTF mode that enforces linear progression with hints, and award medals to first finishers. In one lesson, a request is intercepted in ZAP and a user parameter is changed to admin to tamper with input the server trusts. A user search is shown to be injectable, where a stray quote triggers a database error, and a NoSQL challenge follows. Automated scanners are discouraged, since wrong key submissions can lower a player's score.

The talk closes with the project's roadmap: more translations, including a partial Irish version, UI improvements, new challenges based on newer vulnerabilities, bug fixes and a new release, with around 42 contributors so far. For educators and practitioners, the main takeaway is that a live scoreboard in a classroom drives engagement, and the project welcomes contributions.

talks.title: OWASP Standard Classification: How To Review Code For Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how to find common web vulnerabilities by manually reviewing source code, using keyword searches and data-flow tracing.
talks.summary:
The session, given by a developer and penetration tester, introduces security code review: finding vulnerabilities by reading source code manually. The speaker argues the skill helps developers write safer code and helps testers understand root causes. Before starting, a good editor should offer global search, regex matching and side-by-side file viewing, and a terminal helps test assumptions. Core vocabulary includes the source, where untrusted input enters, and the sink, where it causes harm.

The demonstration uses a deliberately vulnerable Java application. Keyword searches for terms such as key, secret and password exposed hardcoded AWS access keys. Searching for eval revealed a user-supplied parameter passed straight into code execution, a command injection. For deeper review, the speaker suggests starting with input-handling code and tracing data toward dangerous sinks. An order-status handler built a SQL statement from a raw order ID, and it also wrote full order objects, including card numbers and addresses, into logs.

Since no reviewer can read every line, the speaker recommends prioritising the riskiest functionality and using static analysis, dependency scanning and secret scanners to narrow the search. Scanner findings should then be checked manually, because tools are not fully accurate. The talk is presented as an introduction, with the OWASP Code Review Guide suggested for more vulnerable patterns.

talks.teaser: Cole Cornford details OWASP Standard Classification: Back to Basics: Looking for subtle bugs in beginne....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Cole Cornford steps away from advanced topics such as AI and complex flagship technologies to focus on core programming fundamentals. Emphasizing that mastering basics leads directly to more secure software, Cole illustrates how simple programming structures—such as basic control flow, variable initialization, and naming—often harbor subtle, high-impact security vulnerabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Code Clarity and Scrutiny**: Inscrutable or overly convoluted code prevents engineers and security reviewers from properly assessing its security posture. Automated tools can miss issues that are evident when code is clean and human-readable. Complex regular expressions pulled from third-party sources without understanding are common examples of unmaintainable, risky code.
- **Iteration and Resource Exhaustion**: Unbounded loops, deep recursion (such as the billion laughs attack in XML parsing), and missing rate limits allow applications to run indefinitely or consume excessive memory, leading directly to denial of service.
- **Selection Constructs and Logic Flaws**: Common control flow keywords like `if`, `else`, `switch`, and `try/catch` frequently hide business logic flaws. Seemingly simple linear logic can conceal unexpected paths or fail-open conditions.

### Technical Details
- **Fail-Open Logic**: Reviewing an example from Corsair source code, Cole demonstrates how having multiple authentication checks combined with an `else` branch resulted in a fail-open condition that static analysis tools failed to catch due to a lack of context.
- **Variable Default Initialization (OMIGOD Vulnerability)**: Examining code associated with the "OMIGOD" vulnerability affecting Azure management interfaces, Cole details how control flow combined with default variable initialization created a bypass. Specifically, an authentication handler checked whether an `auth_failed` variable was set; because the constructor initialized `auth_failed` to `false` by default, missing authorization headers bypassed the check and flowed directly into `process_authorized_message`.
- **Guard Clauses and Front-Loading Errors**: To eliminate these structural bugs, Cole advocates front-loading error handling at the beginning of methods. Structuring methods to explicitly validate input, authentication, and authorization requirements upfront prevents dangerous fall-through execution paths.

### Takeaways
- Write clear, readable code: readable code is easier to understand, safer to change, and far simpler to scrutinize during security reviews.
- Do not overlook basic building blocks: fundamental constructs like variables, boolean evaluations, loops, and conditional statements are primary locations where business logic vulnerabilities hide.
- Avoid deliberate or accidental obfuscation, as reviewing convoluted code consumes excessive time and increases the risk of missed flaws.

talks.title: Topics of Interest: Common NGINX Misconfigurations That Leave Your Web Server Open ...
talks.teaser: S. Pearlman examines Topics of Interest: Common NGINX Misconfigurations That Leave Your Web Server Open ....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Spencer, a security researcher at Detectify based in Stockholm, discusses common NGINX misconfigurations that leave web servers vulnerable to attack. Detectify operates an automated web vulnerability scanner using crowdsourced research from white-hat hackers worldwide, converting proofs-of-concept into continuously running modules. Spencer outlines how his team analyzed approximately 50,000 NGINX configuration files gathered from public GitHub repositories using Google BigQuery and command-line pattern matching tools to discover widespread real-world misconfigurations.

### Key Topics
- **Research Methodology**: Querying public GitHub datasets on Google BigQuery for repositories containing `nginx.conf` files, constructing raw download URLs using repository details, and parsing files with shell tools to locate pattern-based flaws.
- **Missing Root Directive**: The risks associated with declaring a global `root` directive without restricting it to specific location blocks.
- **Off-by-Slash Misconfiguration**: Directory traversal risks caused by omitting trailing slashes in alias configurations.
- **CRLF Injection via the `$uri` Variable**: Header injection and response body tampering enabled by automatic URL decoding in NGINX's `$uri` variable.
- **Proxy Pass with Regular Expressions**: HTTP request splitting and host header injection when regex matching allows newline characters into proxy requests.

### Technical Details
- **Missing Root Directive**: If a root directive is specified globally (e.g., set to `/etc/nginx`) without an explicit root location block, any unhandled request will default to serving files from that folder. Requesting `/test` or `/nginx.conf` allows attackers to retrieve sensitive files such as configuration files, access logs, or HTTP basic authentication credentials. The fix is setting specific, restricted paths for root directives without exposing sensitive directories.
- **Off-by-Slash (Alias Traversal)**: The `alias` directive replaces a matched path prefix. If a location prefix (e.g., `/static` or `/api`) lacks a trailing directory separator (`/`), appending a relative traversal like `..` in the request causes NGINX to map to a parent directory (e.g., traversing one folder above the intended path). In a demonstration on a sample application, this technique allowed reading a `secret.html` file stored alongside the target picture directory. The fix is ensuring trailing slashes match on both the location path and the alias target.
- **CRLF Injection via `$uri`**: The built-in NGINX `$uri` variable automatically decodes URL-encoded values, including carriage return (`%0D`) and line feed (`%0A`) characters. If `$uri` is used in a redirect or header reflection, attackers can inject custom HTTP headers or inject double CRLF sequences to supply an arbitrary HTTP response body. This enables cross-site scripting (XSS) and cookie leakage. The remediation is replacing `$uri` with `$request_uri`, which retains raw, unprocessed URI values without decoding.
- **Proxy Pass via Regex**: When `proxy_pass` uses regular expressions to capture paths and proxy upstream (e.g., to an Amazon S3 bucket), expressions that inadvertently match newline characters enable CRLF injection into upstream HTTP requests. Attackers can inject a custom `Host` header pointing to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket serving malicious JavaScript. This creates risks for web cache poisoning, XSS, and server-side request forgery (SSRF). The remediation is utilizing strict regex patterns that disallow newlines in proxy-passed inputs.

### Takeaways
NGINX powers roughly one-third of websites due to its speed, modularity, and load-balancing capabilities, but slight syntax oversights can cause severe vulnerabilities. Administrators should avoid global sensitive root paths, ensure symmetrical directory slashes when defining aliases, favor `$request_uri` over `$uri` in redirects, and sanitize regex inputs forwarded to upstream proxy servers.

talks.title: Learn to Exploit TOCTOU Race Condition Vulnerabilities with OWASP TimeGap Theory Abhi Balakrishnan
talks.teaser: Shows how time-of-check to time-of-use race conditions break web apps, through a deliberately vulnerable capture-the-flag style lab.
talks.summary:
Abhi Balakrishnan, a security consultant, introduces time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions in web applications. He uses a ticket-booking example to show how the gap between checking a condition and acting on it lets two simultaneous requests both succeed. He then presents OWASP TimeGap Theory, a free, open-source, intentionally vulnerable capture-the-flag style application with seven challenges that can run in Docker or on Heroku.

The challenges are walked through one by one. Parallel requests can create duplicate sign-up accounts with the same email address, and a login lockout can be sidestepped to brute-force a password. A reward-points transfer can be raced so the receiver ends up with more points than the sender held, and a year-end batch script can be exploited to award the same bonus to several users. A ratings feature that should allow only one like can be made to record several, though that attack also requires handling session, cookie and token details. Parallel requests can be sent from browser developer tools, from curl, or from a race-testing tool driven by a simple configuration file.

The speaker stresses that databases do not prevent these issues by default, that no sophisticated tooling is needed, and that the flaws are not tied to one language, since the PHP version of the lab inherits them from the web server. The practical takeaway is to design checks and state changes so they happen atomically, and to test sensitive endpoints for concurrency before attackers do.

talks.title: Keynote Presentation Blinded by “the weakest link” A New Perspective on Human Risk Masha Sedova
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Keynote Presentation Blinded by “the weakest link” A New Perspective on Human Risk Masha Sedova.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote presentation, Masha Sedova addresses one of cybersecurity's most persistent challenges: human risk. Rather than viewing employees dismissively as the "weakest link" or "problem between the keyboard and the chair," Sedova argues that security teams must stop relying on compliance-driven, one-size-fits-all annual training. Instead, organizations should treat the human element as a critical layer in the Swiss cheese model of defense by applying data analytics, psychology, and behavioral science to measure and actively influence security decisions.

### Key Topics
- **Beyond Security Awareness:** Awareness focuses merely on knowledge, but knowledge alone does not change behavior (citing studies such as LastPass showing poor password habits despite security awareness). Human risk is defined by the observable decisions employees make every day.
- **Security Debt and Enterprise-Wide Impact:** Risky choices—such as a developer shipping code without security reviews to meet a deadline—introduce security debt. Over time, accumulated debt across infrastructure, product security, and access control leads to security incidents.
- **Measuring Observable Behaviors vs. Underlying Mindsets:** Risk consists of impact (role and access permissions) and likelihood (user behavior and track record). Sedova illustrates how security tools already log employee behaviors (e.g., endpoint protection stopping unauthorized executable downloads) that reveal likelihood.
- **Influencing Behavior via Behavioral Science:** Applying Dr. B.J. Fogg's behavioral model, an action requires motivation, ability, and a prompt/trigger. Practitioners can improve security by either increasing ability (making tasks easier) or boosting motivation.

### Technical Details & Frameworks
- **Measurement Data Sources:** Security logs from endpoint protection, password managers, identity/MFA platforms, and web filtering reveal observable actions. For underlying mindset, beliefs, and values (the submerged part of the iceberg), Sedova references research from the Corporate Executive Board and recommends tools such as the Creative Commons-licensed Security Force Survey.
- **Increasing Ability:** Organizations should reduce friction for secure behavior by introducing password managers instead of expecting complex memorization, one-click phishing report buttons instead of manual email forwarding with headers, and automated security scanning tools for developers.
- **Motivational Levers:**
  - *Social Proof:* Demonstrating peer behavior significantly drives adoption (e.g., Facebook and Georgia Tech research showed highlighting friends using MFA made users 1.36 times more likely to enable it; "celebrity social proof" using executive adoption reached 80% password manager adoption in six months).
  - *Gamification:* Leveraging game mechanics such as security strength scorecards, department leaderboards for SLA adherence, and streak counters (e.g., "days since last successful fish").
  - *Positive Reinforcement:* Moving away from negative reinforcement (e.g., mandatory training or account lockout) toward celebrating and recognizing employees who report suspicious activity or exhibit strong security practices.

### Takeaways
Human risk directly affects every security domain, from incident response and compliance to product security and red teaming. Security teams must move away from the "department of no" mindset and instead leverage existing security telemetry to measure individual risk likelihood, reduce friction for good practices, and use positive behavioral science interventions to turn employees into effective security champions.

talks.title: Keynote Presentation Software Defined Security Governance John Steven
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Keynote Presentation Software Defined Security Governance John Steven.
talks.summary:
## Overview

John Stephen, Founding Principal of Edify Security and CTO at Zero North, presents a comprehensive framework for software-defined security governance in modern development environments. The keynote addresses how traditional application security practices have become misaligned with contemporary software delivery approaches, arguing that security must fundamentally evolve to remain effective as organizations embrace digital transformation.

## Digital Transformation's Five Pillars

Stephen identifies five interconnected waves reshaping development: (1) outsourcing of coding through open source and cloud platforms, (2) DevOps culture breaking down developer-operator boundaries, (3) automation emphasis in CI/CD pipelines, (4) microservices and containerized architectures, and (5) infrastructure-as-code enabling developer self-service. When combined, these create a "sea change" comparable to the shift from C/C++ to web development. Organizations are now self-servicing IT provisioning—EC2 instances, RDS databases, authentication frameworks—at scales that outpace traditional security governance models.

## The Governance Gap

A critical gap emerges between development's self-service capabilities and security's ability to govern. Development executives are deploying "pipeline-as-a-service" where teams instantly provision entire delivery platforms with built-in testing and quality checks. Meanwhile, security remains focused on integrating three to five scanning tools into CI/CD—a generational mismatch. This creates cascading challenges: developers can self-service infrastructure, containers, and cloud configurations faster than security can scan them; traditional vulnerability discovery tools find only a percentage of issues; and no single security product achieves comprehensive coverage across all technology stacks.

## Modern Framework Advantages and Gaps

Modern web frameworks (Django, Flask, Go, etc.) provide built-in security primitives—contextually aware output encoding, adaptive password hashing, authentication and authorization frameworks—reducing injection and XSS vulnerabilities. However, infrastructure-as-code tooling (Terraform, Ansible, Helm, Kubernetes) lacks robust security scanning comparable to source code analysis. Laurie Williams' research found infrastructure-as-code comprises 6-11% of public repositories with 29% monthly churn, yet commercial scanning tools rarely support these technologies. This represents a critical vulnerability discovery gap.

## From Shift-Left to Shift-Left-Right-Center

Stephen argues that traditional "shift left" approaches are obsolete given that modern software behavior emerges during orchestration, deployment, and runtime. Security must combine telemetry from three sources: IDE/build time (left), artifact repositories and orchestration (center), and production behavior (right). The center—containers, cloud configurations, and infrastructure orchestration—is where security initiatives are currently weakest. Effective programs must correlate findings across all three phases and attribute them to developers or teams.

## Policy-as-Code and Governance-as-Config

Instead of traditional gates and policy documents, security must evolve to governance-as-config—defining policies in the same configuration format as infrastructure. This enables:

- **Security Blueprints**: Hardened, verified snippets developers can reuse (solving cut-and-paste replication of both secure and insecure patterns)
- **Drift Detection**: Real-time alerting when deployed infrastructure deviates from approved blueprints
- **Guardrails**: Proactive, config-driven enforcement of security standards
- **Guard Rails vs. Gates**: Rather than blocking builds, guard rails enable self-service security compliance

Organizations like concourse labs are pioneering technology-independent policy languages, converting abstract security policies ("encrypt storage") into cloud-specific implementations (S3, RDS, etc.).

## Recommended Technical Approach

Stephen recommends a layered strategy:

1. **Modern Frameworks**: Migrate to languages and frameworks embedding security defaults
2. **Dependency Analysis**: Use Dependabot and OWASP Dependency-Track for composition analysis
3. **Configuration Scanning**: Leverage open source tools (Semgrep, SonarQube) to verify secure defaults in code
4. **Infrastructure Scanning**: Employ cloud-specific and multi-cloud tools (AWS Well-Architected tool, Scout) for cloud and infrastructure-as-code configuration
5. **Security Champions**: Enroll developers in self-governance and policy authorship
6. **Continuous Telemetry**: Replace point-in-time scan-and-report with event-driven, attributed findings

## Key Challenges Going Forward

- **Attribution**: Linking findings from infrastructure-as-code, containers, and runtime back to responsible developers
- **Measurement**: Transitioning from annual/quarterly reporting to continuous feedback loops while maintaining board-level visibility
- **Tool Coherence**: Gartner projects 10-30 tools needed for cloud environments; correlating and prioritizing findings is critical
- **Policy Enforcement vs. Enablement**: Balancing governance requirements with DevOps velocity; gates become obstacles without guardrails

## Takeaways

Security's future depends on meeting developers at scale through configuration-driven, self-service security controls rather than blocking gates. Organizations must focus on the "center" (orchestration, containers, cloud configuration) where technology gaps are largest. Governance and policy must become executable, version-controlled code. Telemetry must be continuously attributed across build, deploy, and runtime phases. Most critically, rather than resisting development's self-service imperative, security should enable it through hardened blueprints and automated guardrails, thereby embedding security into the developer experience itself.

talks.title: Enabling Message Level Protection at Uber Debosmit Debo Ray & Jovon Itwaru
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Enabling Message Level Protection at Uber Debosmit Debo Ray & Jovon Itwaru.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Uber, handling massive amounts of sensitive data—including rider and driver personal information, health records, credit card numbers, and government identifiers—requires robust safeguards as information moves across a complex microservice ecosystem. In this presentation, Uber security engineers Jovon Itwaru and Debosmit "Debo" Ray outline the motivations, architectural trade-offs, design, and implementation of **CryptoFX**, an internal client-side field-level encryption module developed to secure sensitive data at rest and in transit.

### Key Topics
- **Goals & Requirements**: Protecting sensitive data against threats such as rogue engineers or database breaches; enforcing strong cryptography defaults (e.g., authenticated encryption) while preventing developer mistakes like nonce reuse; providing an intuitive, low-friction API; ensuring cryptographic agility across algorithms and Key Management Systems (KMS); and satisfying regulatory mandates like PCI-DSS, PSD2, and GDPR.
- **Evaluation of Encryption Approaches**: Comparing volume/disk encryption, database transparent data encryption (TDE), column-level encryption, server-side encryption (e.g., S3 SSE), and client-side encryption. Uber determined that client-side field-level encryption was the only option providing adequate protection against network snoopers and compromised databases while remaining flexible enough for their infrastructure.
- **Architecture of CryptoFX**: A Go-based library leveraging dependency injection, envelope encryption, and configurable abstractions over ciphers and key providers.
- **Operational & Developer Experience Challenges**: Driving adoption via "white glove" onboarding, accommodating searchability requirements, managing legacy schema migrations, and handling API extensibility in a monorepo.

### Technical Details
- **Field-Level Envelope Encryption**: Rather than encrypting entire objects or volumes, Uber encrypts specific sensitive fields (e.g., address, SSN) to minimize performance overhead. For database storage, symmetric encryption using **AES-GCM (AES-GCM-256)** is employed via envelope encryption: a Key Encrypting Key (KEK) encrypts an ephemeral Data Encryption Key (DEK), which in turn encrypts the plaintext. Both the ciphertext and the encrypted DEK are stored together.
- **Flexible Deployment Models**: CryptoFX supports three modes depending on performance and security trade-offs:
  1. *Local Encryption*: DEKs and crypto operations remain local within the application process.
  2. *Remote Encryption*: Data is sent to a central remote service (e.g., HashiCorp Vault Transit engine), and the returned ciphertext only needs the key namespace and Base64 ciphertext.
  3. *Hybrid Model*: Services obtain DEKs from a remote KMS and cache/refresh them locally at configured intervals for high-throughput batch operations.
- **Configuration & Namespaces**: CryptoFX uses a concept of namespaces (similar to keyrings) specifying the KMS, cipher, key identifier, and key version. The `KeyProvider` abstraction enables seamless interoperability between local secret delivery (mounted files backed by `tmpfs`) and remote KMS solutions like HashiCorp Vault or AWS KMS without breaking callers.
- **Struct-Level Encryption & Search**: Using Go struct tags, developers can annotate struct fields (supporting strings, byte slices, and embedded structs) so that multiple fields can be encrypted in bulk under a single generated DEK. To support database search queries over encrypted fields without adopting leaky schemes, CryptoFX provides a `Hasher` interface generating deterministic **HMAC-SHA256** digests that are stored alongside ciphertexts.

### Takeaways
- **Avoid Building on Ad-Hoc Solutions**: Off-the-shelf tools and raw standard libraries often fail to fit complex, polyglot microservice environments or lead developers into misconfigurations like nonce reuse or weak ciphers. Sane defaults and centralized abstractions are critical.
- **Early Engagement & White-Glove Support**: Security teams driving crypto adoption must engage product teams early during design reviews and SDLC phases, providing direct onboarding assistance and establishing recognizable "happy path" code patterns.
- **Future Roadmap**: Ongoing work includes migrating legacy keys to HashiCorp Vault, adding high-level signer and verifier interfaces (navigating constraints like cloud CDN RSA verification limitations), and continuing to monitor searchable encryption techniques (noting that fully homomorphic, property-preserving, and functional encryption remain either too slow or vulnerable to inference attacks on low-entropy data).

talks.title: How the latest MASVS & MSTG Specs Make the Best Mobile Pen Testing Cocktails Brian Reed & Tony Ram
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for How the latest MASVS & MSTG Specs Make the Best Mobile Pen Testing Cocktails Brian Reed & Tony Ram.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Brian Reed (Chief Mobility Officer at Now Secure) and Tony Ramirez (Senior Application Security Analyst at Now Secure) present a comprehensive guide to mobile application security testing using the MASVS (Mobile Application Security Verification Standard) and MSTG (Mobile Security Testing Guide). The presentation emphasizes that 70% of digital traffic now occurs on mobile, yet mobile security testing capabilities lag significantly behind web security practices.

## Key Statistics & Context
Mobile apps present a substantially larger attack surface than web applications: 85% of tested apps fail one or more OWASP Top 10 mobile requirements, 70% leak GDPR-regulated data, approximately 50% exhibit insecure data storage (M2), 48% have insecure communication (M3), and 48% contain detectable extraneous functionality. The fundamental difference stems from architecture—98% of web code runs behind hardened perimeters, while mobile code executes on untrusted, easily-reversed devices in the wild.

## Anatomy of Mobile Attacks
Bad actors follow a predictable pattern: download apps from app stores, reverse them using tools like Radare2 and Frida, then interactively manipulate inputs/outputs. Nearly 99% of apps leak personally identifiable information; attackers can map API endpoints and discover network vulnerabilities. Approximately 50% of apps have certificate validation failures, enabling phishing endpoint attacks. This understanding drives the need for comprehensive testing frameworks.

## Tony's 10 Best Practices
1. **Understand MASVS/MSTG**: MASVS provides security requirements; MSTG supplies testing methodologies across iOS, Android, and hybrid frameworks.
2. **Use diversified tools**: No single tool covers all scenarios; leverage jailbroken/rooted devices, open-source tools, and eventually automation for high-risk scenarios.
3. **Inventory your apps**: Determine which apps require testing and their priority levels.
4. **Learn the attack surface**: Mobile encompasses code functionality, data at rest, data in motion, and backend APIs—broader than web.
5. **Data storage & encryption**: Verify how data is stored, accessed, and encrypted; test data wiping on failed authentication attempts.
6. **Client-side security**: Unlike web browsers, mobile platforms don't enforce certificate validation by default; developers must code this explicitly. Hardware-backed encryption and build settings are essential.
7. **Network security**: Test certificate validation, implement certificate pinning where appropriate, and verify HTTPS on all requests. Use proxies like mitmproxy to inspect TLS tunnels.
8. **Authentication & session management**: Both stateful and stateless models must be server-side enforced. Test biometric flows, multi-factor authentication, rate limiting, authorization, and logic flaws.
9. **Reverse engineering resilience**: These controls—tampering prevention, code obfuscation, device binding, payload encryption—must complement, not replace, security controls. Root/jailbreak detection alone cannot fix underlying vulnerabilities.
10. **Policy, privacy & developer partnerships**: Establish baselines using MASVS's AppSec Model (4 tiers: standard security, defense-in-depth, reverse engineering resilience, combinations). Privacy is now regulatory. Developers are allies—collaborate on secure coding practices, OS feature updates, and threat modeling.

## MASVS Specification Updates
Recent changes include enhanced WebView practices (content storage, loading source, device access), third-party keyboard support requirements, overlay detection (especially for financial apps), encryption for sensitive data, and evolving build settings (scoped storage, app signing keys). Data retention policies and memory-vs-storage decisions reflect maturation in platform capabilities.

## Testing Approach & Tools
Best-in-class testing combines four methodologies: static analysis, dynamic analysis, interactive testing, and API testing. Recommended tools include Frida, Radare2, Burp Suite, and mitmproxy. Test the binary rather than source code, since mobile involves multiple languages and development environments. For organizations with many apps, employ threat modeling and tiered risk strategies: automate lower-risk apps, manually pen-test higher-risk ones. Integration into the software development lifecycle via secure coding practices, software composition analysis (SCA), and secure code analysis (SAST) enables shift-left security. Monitor production behavior for bug fix releases and change requests that may introduce new vulnerabilities.

## Key Takeaway
Mobile and web security are fundamentally different disciplines requiring dedicated expertise, diverse tooling, and close developer collaboration. The MASVS/MSTG provide comprehensive guidance; the field faces a severe shortage of skilled analysts—making it a lucrative career path for those willing to master the attack surface and testing methodologies.

talks.teaser: Eva Galperin examines Who Deserves Cybersecurity? Expanding Our Circle of Care.
talks.summary:
Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, argues that the security field has concentrated on governments, large companies and wealthy institutions while journalists, activists and abuse survivors are left exposed. She starts with advanced persistent threat reports, noting that vendors published sophisticated cases for publicity, while simple campaigns against activists in Vietnam, Syria and Kazakhstan went largely unexamined. Drawing on her training work and her revision of the Surveillance Self-Defense guide, she makes the case for threat modeling and a harm reduction approach that meets users where they are instead of blaming them for using platforms like Facebook.

She then describes how a wave of abuse cases from survivors of sexual assault, worried about compromised devices, led her to test stalkerware against antivirus products. Her tests caught only about 60 percent of the leading stalkerware, so she worked with vendors such as Kaspersky, Norton and Avast to form the Coalition Against Stalkerware. The group shares samples and uses a definition built on concealment and lack of consent. Detection rates for many products have since climbed to roughly 95 to 99 percent.

She closes by urging security professionals to design for people on the periphery, including women, LGBTQ people, people under authoritarian rule, people with disabilities and abuse survivors, since those designs serve everyone. Because the industry faces a labor shortage, engineers are a tipping point and can decline to build harmful tools. In the Q&A she pointed to a recent FTC ban on a stalkerware maker and described covert monitoring of partners and children as abusive.

talks.title: OWASP Talk - HTTP3 Security
talks.teaser: Explains how QUIC and HTTP/3 change the transport and encryption stack and what that means for security teams and operators.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces HTTP/3 as HTTP/2 semantics carried over QUIC, a protocol that merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshake into one layer running on UDP. That combination cuts connection setup to a single round trip and allows encrypted early requests on resumed sessions. Nearly all of QUIC's packet contents are encrypted, which the speaker frames as a way to let the protocol evolve without middleboxes breaking.

The security consequences follow. Passive decryption at monitoring points no longer works, so inspection must be active or done on the endpoints. Firewalls can identify QUIC initial packets and filter UDP traffic, but Chrome only accepts custom root certificates when specific command-line settings are used, which complicates enterprise interception and internal sites. Packet captures reveal little without keys, and endpoint logging through QLOG is presented as an alternative with a performance cost. Connection IDs allow migration between networks, forcing load balancers to encode server routing into them, while amplification limits and stateless retry defend against abuse.

Near the end, the talk raises whether recent HTTP/2 request smuggling research applies to HTTP/3. The answer given is that such flaws stem from HTTP semantics and header handling, so new QPACK header code may be exposed. The takeaway is that QUIC deployments are complex and need careful planning, with HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 kept as fallbacks.

talks.title: OWASP Chair Update
talks.teaser: Corporate Memberships explores OWASP Chair Update.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this OWASP Chair Update, Sherif Mansour announces significant revisions to the OWASP Foundation's corporate membership program, presenting new packaging, tier structures, and regional pricing models. Speaking in connection with OWASP's Black Hat virtual booth presence, Mansour explains how the organization is aligning corporate benefits and pricing with geographic equity and organizational maturity, mirroring principles previously applied to individual memberships.

### Key Topics
- **Restructured Corporate Membership Tiers**: Introduction of Silver, Gold, and Platinum membership levels with standardized benefit matrices.
- **Geographic and Startup Pricing Adjustments**: Implementation of adjusted pricing tiers based on company location and startup status to broaden accessibility.
- **Trademark and Brand Licensing**: Tiered rights to use the OWASP logo and trademark across products and services beyond standard fair use.
- **Conference and Marketing Benefits**: Global AppSec discounts, early access to sponsorships, website branding rotation, and social media recognition.
- **Governance Participation**: Voting rights representation in global board elections for member organizations.

### Technical Details
- **Pricing Structure & Definitions**:
  - Standard pricing for organizations in developed nations is set at $25,000 for Platinum, $15,000 for Gold, and $5,000 for Silver.
  - Startup eligibility is specifically defined as companies within 24 months of their inception, with pricing set at $10,000 (or $4,000 for regional startups).
  - Regional eligibility applies to organizations headquartered in emerging markets or developing countries as defined by the IMF World Economic Outlook Table E, explicitly excluding designated low-tax jurisdictions and tax havens (such as the Bahamas or British Virgin Islands).
- **Benefit Allocations across Tiers**:
  - *OWASP Trademark License*: Silver tier allows licensing across 1 product or service; Gold permits up to 5 products or services; Platinum provides unlimited product/service trademark licensing.
  - *Event & Promotion Perks*: Includes corporate member support logos, discounts for staff registering for Global AppSec, early access to Global AppSec sponsorships, and participation in AppSec Days.
  - *Promotional Exposure*: Placement of corporate branding on owasp.org with rotation opportunities, news articles upon signing corporate sponsorships, and coordinated social media recognition.
  - *Governance*: Corporate members can designate an ambassador representative to cast a vote in the OWASP Global Board of Directors elections.

### Takeaways
The OWASP Foundation's updated corporate membership model aims to remove financial barriers for emerging companies and organizations in developing economies while maintaining structured, high-value tiers for larger enterprises. Prospective members can review tiers and submit requests directly through the corporate membership section on owasp.org.

talks.title: Being Powerful While Powerless: Elevating Security By Leading Without Authority
talks.teaser: Explains how a lone security engineer scales protection across a company through software, automation and cultural relationships.
talks.summary:
The speaker was the only member of the security team at a San Francisco payroll and benefits company, working as an individual contributor with no formal authority over roughly 100 to 150 engineers. Shifting priorities and new ventures kept adding risk, so the time available was the real constraint. The talk frames the problem as how to extend one person's reach across the whole organisation.

To multiply their output, the speaker leaned on software. Being able to write code and speak the engineers' language earned trust, and fixing reported bugs in code directly helped too. Static analysis run on pull requests gave developers instant feedback without waiting for security review, with a tool flagging suspicious exceptions for the speaker to check. Dependency management tooling replaced manual reviews of package files. Annual penetration tests served as evidence in vendor reviews and were benchmarked year over year, while a bug bounty program kept outside researchers testing the product after launch.

On the cultural side, the speaker built relationships with IT, legal and compliance, product management, engineering and infrastructure, sharing findings openly and having lunch with different teams. Teaching secure coding classes and running phishing training extended reach further. Goodwill built through small favours made later requests easier, and engineers who reported issues or fixed bugs on their own became allies. The main takeaway is that influence comes from building software and relationships rather than from a director or CSO title.

talks.title: Web Apps vs Blockchain DApps (Smart Contracts): Tools, Vulns And Standards
talks.teaser: Presents a verification standard for smart contracts, mapping common blockchain flaws to each stage of the development lifecycle.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how decentralized applications, which keep front-end code on blockchain-based storage and run business logic in smart contracts, differ from web applications in security terms. The speaker notes that web apps have well-known references such as the OWASP Top 10 and ASVS, while smart contracts lacked an equivalent checklist. To fill that gap, the speaker presents a smart contract verification standard modeled on ASVS, with 13 categories that follow the development lifecycle from analysis to maintenance.

Several contrasts drive the discussion. Everything on a public chain is readable, so confidential data should stay off-chain, and private variables offer no real secrecy. Every public function can be invoked by anyone, which enabled a wallet takeover when visibility was left unspecified. Predictable randomness, miner influence over transaction ordering, and unbounded loops that exceed gas limits have all caused losses. Integer overflows can mint tokens, reentrancy through external calls has drained funds, and an uninitialized shared contract was taken over and self-destructed, stranding the contracts that depended on it.

Recommended practices include simple, centralized access control, initializing contracts during deployment, safe arithmetic libraries, checking low-level call results, pull-style withdrawals, keeping balances held in contracts small, and pausing sensitive functions while still letting users withdraw. Automated scanners help, but manual review and formal verification of specifications are still needed. The standard is planned for open-source release, with a possible OWASP project and community contributions.

talks.title: The State Of Credential Stuffing And The Future Of Account Takeovers
talks.teaser: Explains how credential stuffing became cheap to run and how attackers evade defenses and bypass multi-factor authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that credential stuffing, the replay of breached username and password pairs across many sites to find reused passwords, is a far bigger problem than many security people assume. It cites yearly tracking of spilled credentials, with more than a billion recorded in 2018 and attack campaigns reaching billions of attempts. It then walks through the attack chain: sourcing credentials, automating logins, defeating defenses such as CAPTCHAs, and spreading traffic across cloud functions and residential proxies.

The central argument is economic. Breach dumps can be obtained for almost nothing, browser automation and CAPTCHA-solving services cost a few dollars per thousand solves, and cloud functions make distributed traffic cheap. Each attempt therefore costs a fraction of a cent against accounts with real resale value. The talk traces how attacks moved from scripted HTTP requests to automated real browsers, browser fingerprint spoofing, behavioral emulation, and residential proxies, and how malware marketplaces sell infected machines along with stored sessions and cookies.

The speaker argues that multi-factor authentication does not fully stop account takeover, because attackers can trick victims into reading out one-time codes once valid accounts are known. The closing takeaway is that this is a fraud problem rather than a simple bot problem, so every defense will eventually fail. Teams should plan for fast adaptation and bring developers, security and fraud teams closer together.

talks.title: WebAuthn: Strong Authentication vs Privacy vs Convenience
talks.teaser: Suby Raman investigates WebAuthn: Strong Authentication vs Privacy vs Convenience.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Suby Raman, a software engineer at Duo Security, discusses WebAuthn (Web Authentication API) as a modern public-key cryptography standard designed to replace traditional passwords while balancing strong authentication, user and developer convenience, and user privacy. He explains how WebAuthn removes shared secrets from authentication workflows and evaluates the real-world trade-offs between verifiable authenticator trust and user tracking protections.

### Key Topics
- **The Failure of Password-Based Authentication**: Passwords represent shared secrets that suffer from database leaks, lack of enforced transport security, unsafe reuse across sites, and susceptibility to phishing campaigns (with Duo's data showing 31% of users click phishing links and 17% submit passwords). Relying on user discipline or complex hashing/salting architectures presents systemic security risks.
- **Core WebAuthn Properties**: WebAuthn provides strong authentication backed by hardware-isolated modules (such as TPMs and Secure Enclaves), origin-scoped credentials that automatically mitigate phishing across lookalike domains, and attestation mechanisms to prove key origin.
- **User and Developer Convenience**: Eliminating passwords removes the mental burden on users and aids accessibility for mobility-impaired or elderly individuals using biometrics (fingerprints, facial recognition, palm scanning) or security keys. For developers, storing only public keys removes the operational complexity of managing password hashing, salting, and breach remediation.
- **Privacy and Trust Trade-offs**: Because hardware interactions could allow tracking or device fingerprinting, WebAuthn requires explicit user consent (physical interaction) before executing API calls. Furthermore, browsers limit silent probing of authenticators, and users can permit or deny sharing attestation certificates and device identifiers (AAGUID).

### Technical Details
- **API Registration Workflow**: A relying party calls `navigator.credentials.create()` asynchronously. The configuration contains a server-generated cryptographically random `challenge` (to block replay attacks), relying party info (`rp.id` scoped to the current origin), `user` metadata, and `pubKeyCredParams` (specifying accepted algorithms such as ECDSA represented by `-7`). The browser interacts with the authenticator to generate a private-public key pair, returning `clientDataJSON` and an `attestationObject` formatted using COSE (Concise Object Signing and Encryption).
- **API Authentication Workflow**: Authentication uses `navigator.credentials.get()`. The relying party supplies a challenge and an `allowCredentials` array listing registered credential IDs. The authenticator signs over the client data and authenticator data using the stored private key, which the server verifies against the stored public key.
- **Attestation Types**: 
  - *Direct Attestation*: Supplies full x.509 attestation certificates and the Authenticator Attestation GUID (AAGUID), identifying the exact make and model.
  - *None Attestation*: Returned when an authenticator lacks attestation private keys or when the user explicitly blocks sharing hardware details in browser prompts.
  - *Indirect Attestation*: The browser substitutes an anonymized certificate/AAGUID to protect privacy while attempting verification.
- **Device Loss and Recovery**: WebAuthn credentials do not sync natively across devices in Level 1; losing a platform authenticator or security key requires backup authenticators or identity proofing. Raman mentions early proposals, such as Yubico's backup authenticator restoration extension, to address account recovery.

### Takeaways
WebAuthn establishes robust, phishing-resistant authentication by moving security guarantees to hardware and cryptographic pairs rather than fallible human memory. However, relying parties must carefully balance security policies against privacy and UX constraints: strictly requiring direct attestation certificates will reject built-in authenticators (such as Chrome's Touch ID integration) or privacy-conscious users who block device telemetry. Implementing WebAuthn requires organizations to decide how much explicit device trust they mandate versus prioritizing frictionless user adoption.

talks.title: The Security We Need: Designing Usable IoT Security
talks.teaser: Damilare D. Fagbemi examines The Security We Need: Designing Usable IoT Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Daniel A. Oladimeji (introduced as Daniel / security architect at Intel Corporation) addresses the critical intersection of IoT design, usability, and security. As IoT adoption proliferates—expanding from a single household desktop to dozens of connected devices in smart homes and millions across smart cities and industrial settings—the burden of security configuration often falls on non-technical users. The speaker argues that security cannot rely on regular users behaving like security engineers. Instead, security practitioners must act like protective "Special Forces," designing systems that work securely by default with minimal user friction.

### Key Topics
The session centers around the "Five Cs" of security usability challenges and ten foundational design principles for usable IoT security:
- **The Five Cs of IoT Usability Challenges**:
  1. *Security doesn't make sense to regular users*: Users often assume that device manufacturers and experts have already secured systems (such as medical pacemakers) or suffer from the Dunning–Kruger effect.
  2. *Security is not the objective of the regular user*: Similar to seatbelt laws requiring enforcement because safety is not always front-of-mind, users prioritize core device functionality over security controls.
  3. *Cost of security is not measured*: Users do not know the actual cost/overhead of utilizing security features, and vendors lack sufficient research into lowering usability friction.
  4. *Barriers to necessary workflow*: Users systematically circumvent or disable security mechanisms (like TLS requirements on incompatible low-power sensor hubs) when they block intended workflows.
  5. *Conflicting views across stakeholders*: Disconnects exist between executive revenue vision, architect design, engineering implementation, and the end user's operational reality.

### Technical Details & Design Principles
The speaker outlines ten startup principles for designing usable IoT security:
- **Put on user hat**: Prioritize the user's primary objectives and workflow.
- **Secure defaults only**: Enforce secure defaults out of the box, such as HTTPS for smart home cameras (e.g., Ring devices) and secure boot mechanisms backed by hardware-protected cryptographic keys to verify trusted software periodically.
- **Assume no trusted networks**: Relying on NSA research guidance, systems must assume that corporate, factory, farm, and home networks are already compromised by sophisticated actors.
- **Targeted risk information**: When user choices are required, provide clear risk impact (e.g., explaining that pre-shared symmetric keys increase compromise risk across distributed endpoints).
- **Pre-configured configuration buckets**: Abstract complexity by offering predefined security tiers (e.g., medium vs. high risk) that automatically configure underlying parameters.
- **Design to scale & zero-touch provisioning**: Support out-of-the-box zero-touch provisioning where edge devices automatically establish authenticated mutual TLS connections with IoT cloud backends using factory-burned keys or pre-registered certificates.
- **Disallow intransitive authorization**: Require explicit active authorization grants by IoT administrators rather than cascading inherited permissions.
- **Runtime anomaly detection & device health checks**: Monitor baseline telemetry (such as unexpected CPU spikes from cryptocurrency mining malware or network interface cards handling 10x normal traffic volume) using machine learning.
- **Seamless authority revocation**: Enable administrators to deactivate device certificates easily to isolate compromised edge devices from the cloud.
- **Keep secrets secret & anticipate circumvention**: Store keys securely in hardware or software without forcing end users to manage cryptographic material, and analyze update failures rather than blaming users when slow deployment channels cause updates to be aborted.

### Takeaways
Secure IoT design is an art requiring simplicity and clarity ("keep it simple stupid" / "simplicity is the ultimate sophistication"). By removing configuration complexity, leveraging gateways for resource-constrained sensors, automating zero-touch provisioning, and enforcing strict secure defaults, designers can ensure security is resilient without relying on end-user intervention.

talks.title: How To Find And Prevent Entire Classes Of Security Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Explains variant analysis, a process for finding and preventing repeated classes of vulnerabilities using semantic code queries.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Sam, a developer advocate formerly at Semmle (recently acquired by GitHub), discusses how software projects repeatedly suffer from identical or closely related security bugs due to incomplete patching and shared architectural patterns. Rather than treating each reported vulnerability as an isolated incident, security teams need to practice variant analysis—a methodology used by organizations like Google and Microsoft to discover, investigate, and simultaneously fix all variations of a vulnerability across codebases before releasing patches publicly.

### Key Topics
- **Recurring Bug Patterns and Incomplete Fixes**: Real-world examples illustrate the systemic failure of one-off patching. In the Spring Framework (September 2017), user data concatenated into Spring Expression Language strings allowed remote code execution (RCE); pivotal patches were repeatedly bypassed until a major architectural refactor eliminated the vulnerability. Similarly, Apache Struts 2 suffered dozens of RCE vulnerabilities spanning multiple years (such as in 2013, 2016, and 2017) due to untrusted user input flowing into OGNL expressions. Even Apple's macOS/OS X XNU kernel packet mangler saw an initial RCE fix by Kevin Backhouse that left an exploitable bug in the exact same block of code.
- **The Shift from Manual to Automated Variant Analysis**: Historically, variant analysis relied heavily on manual data flow analysis, following call graphs in IDEs or Sourcegraph, and text searching with grep and awk. This manual approach is tedious, error-prone, and cannot scale as codebases grow and developer headcount dwarfs security staffing. Automating variant analysis allows security teams to query code syntactically and semantically (leveraging control flow, data flow, and call graphs) across entire repositories and multiple projects.
- **Ecosystem Knowledge Sharing**: When a vulnerability stems from standard library misuses or framework patterns—such as the "Zip Slip" path traversal vulnerability documented by Snyk—rules can be shared publicly. Microsoft and Semmle authored and open-sourced rules in languages like C# and Java to detect Zip Slip patterns where archive paths are concatenated to target directories without proper sanitization.

### Technical Details
- **ChakraCore Query Example**: Referencing a blog post by Microsoft's Stephen Hunter, Sam highlights a critical vulnerability in Microsoft's ChakraCore JavaScript engine. In C++ code exposed to JavaScript, a pointer and size to an ArrayBuffer (`pBuffer` and `bufferSize`) were extracted before calling `v8::ToPrimitive` / `valueOf`. Overriding `valueOf` in JavaScript allowed an attacker to free the buffer, leaving `pBuffer` as a dangling pointer leading to potential memory corruption or RCE. Microsoft modeled this pattern using a declarative SQL-like query language: selecting variables, ArrayBuffer pointer assignments, function calls, and variable accesses; filtering for calls that transitively reach `MethodCallToPrimitive`; and verifying that the call occurs after the assignment but before the variable use. This automated query identified the seed bug and four additional critical variants.
- **Integrating into Development Lifecycles**: A standard response workflow integrates variant analysis immediately following root cause diagnosis. Engineers write a semantic query, iteratively refine it against false positives, triage findings, and patch all variants simultaneously prior to public disclosure. These queries can then be integrated into continuous integration (CI), nightly builds, or code review tools (similar to Mozilla using Clang-Tidy on Phabricator for Firefox patches).

### Takeaways
- **Automate and Continuous Testing**: Variant analysis should be automated and run continuously against pull requests or nightly builds to prevent regressions and catch repeat mistakes.
- **Defense in Depth**: Variant analysis complements rather than replaces other disciplines. It does not replace sound software architecture (e.g., migrating to Rust for memory safety, avoiding raw expression languages, or using auto-escaping SQL libraries), exploit mitigations (ASLR, stack canaries), or practices like fuzzing, penetration testing, bug bounties, and red teaming.

talks.title: Fast Forwarding Mobile Security With The OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard and Testing Guide, with live bypass demos on iOS and Android.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) and the Mobile Security Testing Guide (MASTG), a project that has grown into a stable requirements set, translated versions, and compliance checklists that link each requirement to the matching guide chapter. The speaker argues that mobile security differs from web security, pointing to data leakage, insecure storage, weak authentication, inter-process communication, and reverse engineering as recurring problems. Requirements are split into baseline hygiene for ordinary apps and a stronger tier for apps where tampering carries real risk, such as banking or paid-content apps.

The middle of the talk covers network security and testing. Certificate pinning is shown being defeated on iOS in two ways: a tweak that patches the system-level trust methods on a jailbroken device, and a Frida-based tool that hooks a running app without changing the operating system. A biometric check is then bypassed by calling the local authentication policy method directly so that it always reports success, shown with Needle and objection. A similar pinning bypass is demonstrated on an Android emulator using objection and an Xposed-based module, with the speaker noting that emulators can be unstable.

The closing part outlines the guide's structure: general testing chapters, platform-specific sections, crackme challenges, and a playground set of sample apps. The main takeaway is to rely on well-tested pinning libraries rather than custom code, since hand-rolled implementations are easy to get wrong, and to use the checklists to point developers to specific guide sections. The speaker invites contributors to help expand the project.

talks.title: OWASP Based Threat Modelling: Creating A Feedback Model In An Agile Environment
talks.teaser: Presents a policy-driven threat modeling approach built on OWASP Top 10 mitigations that adds feedback loops for agile teams.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by explaining why threat modeling belongs early in the development lifecycle, then reviews common frameworks such as STRIDE, DREAD and PASTA. He questions whether these frameworks keep pace with changing threats, such as payment-card skimming through injected JavaScript, and with large volumes of modeling requests. He argues that a circular security process bolted onto agile does not really work, because lessons from one sprint never reach the next.

The proposed approach is layered. An information security policy sits at the base, security standards are written around OWASP Top 10 mitigations rather than individual attacks, and controls are chosen to match how critical each flow is. He walks through a library management system, decomposing the login flow and mapping controls to it. These include sign-in attempt limits and CAPTCHA, output encoding, subresource integrity for external scripts, masking sensitive data in logs, and upgrading a Node.js runtime with known vulnerabilities. He also shows how a residual risk from an earlier sprint raises the rating of a later finding, so a flaw that would be high on its own becomes critical.

To keep the cycle running, he describes an internal tool that takes onboarding answers from product teams, pulls in findings from scans and penetration tests, and produces dashboards of top threats and year-over-year trends. His takeaways are to keep short iterations inside the process, define a mitigation-focused top list for your own organization, treat threat modeling as the brain of the development lifecycle, and record residual risk in a tool rather than in long documents. He notes the tool was not yet publicly released.

talks.title: Secure Agile Development According To SAMM
talks.teaser: Shows how to fold OWASP SAMM security activities into Agile sprints using situational requirements, triggers and ready-made tests.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OWASP SAMM, a process-agnostic framework of security activities with maturity levels, and explains why teams struggle to apply it in Agile delivery. Common shortcuts fail: security handled in separate sprints, hundreds of rules kept on a wiki, a pen test months later, or one champion carrying all responsibility. These problems led to a set of Agile notes that extend SAMM with practical guidance, developed with a Dutch working group and practitioners.

The core approach is to reduce repeated expert work. Organizations prepare a baseline of requirements once, rule out those that do not apply to developers, record accepted risks, and rely on frameworks and libraries for much of the rest. Remaining requirements are linked to triggers, such as building a login form, which bring in ready-made instructions and tests for that task. The speaker contrasts this hygiene approach with analyzing every feature through threat modeling, using a password reset timing example. Tests become part of the story's acceptance criteria during refinement rather than sprint planning, and peer review checks whether developers actually use the framework.

The closing points focus on practice: automate verification where possible, review changes incrementally, and measure maturity and share metrics so teams can improve on their own. The speaker argues that the same mechanisms serve privacy and reliability, so security could become part of a wider software quality program. In audience questions, the speaker explained that the same approach is being applied to a Dutch baseline standard that does not yet have triggers.

talks.title: Attacking AWS: The Full Cyber Kill Chain
talks.teaser: Follows an attack on an AWS account from leaked keys and metadata SSRF through admin takeover, log evasion, and persistence.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how leaked access keys, often hard-coded into public repositories, give attackers a way into cloud accounts. Using a fictional software house as a case, the speaker shows a team running Jenkins on an EC2 instance whose attached role can deploy new machines. Instance metadata is reachable only from inside the instance, but a server-side request forgery flaw in a web application hosted there can expose the role credentials. The speaker then demonstrates the Pacu AWS exploitation framework, a Metasploit-style tool for AWS, to enumerate permissions with the stolen keys.

With those permissions, the attacker finds a stopped instance carrying an admin profile. Because user data can be changed while an instance is stopped, and a cloud-init boot hook makes it run on every start, the attacker injects a reverse shell, restarts the machine and collects admin credentials from its metadata. Further steps cover hiding activity by limiting CloudTrail to one region, persisting through Lambda functions or trust policies that let an outside account assume a role, and adding a second access key to a user, which is hard to spot in the console.

For defense, the speaker recommends separate accounts under an AWS Organization with service control policies, a metadata proxy that restricts credential use, CIS benchmark checks, centralized logging, and automated incident response. The assessment approach covers architecture, configuration, Lambda code and application review, and monitoring verification. The closing message is that cloud auditing should be a continuous, automated process.

talks.title: Making Continuous Security a Reality with OWASP’s AppSec Pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how an automated AppSec pipeline runs containerized scanners across many repos and feeds findings into DefectDojo.
talks.summary:
Matt Tesauro opens by arguing that traditional application security tooling is built to run slowly and does not suit teams that ship code many times a day. He proposes an AppSec pipeline as a repeatable roadmap for an internal security team: intake of requests, triage and orchestration of tools, and a vulnerability repository treated as the single source of truth. Normalized findings can then be pushed to defect trackers such as JIRA and to metrics or GRC systems.

The middle of the talk covers GASP, a Go library and command-line tool built to implement this model. Each scanner runs in its own Docker container that follows a shared specification, and a configuration file holds default profiles for each tool. Named pipelines chain tools through setup, main and final stages, and results land in DefectDojo. He reports that 36 GitHub repositories were cloned and scanned in just over three minutes on AWS. Aaron Weaver's implementation, triggered by commit web hooks, ran 15 repositories through roughly 5,100 runs over four months, with DefectDojo wired bidirectionally to JIRA.

The closing part gives practical lessons. A scanner profile usually needs two or three runs before it is stable, and legacy tools without APIs may need a shim inside their container. DefectDojo's deduplication and rules engine help cut false positives. The speakers stress getting the security team's own house in order first, so that it can then help development teams fix what the pipeline finds.

talks.summary: The speaker outlines Kubernetes security across the control plane, workloads, networking, and host systems. talks.title: XSS is dead. We just don't get it.
talks.teaser: Can the security community change its incentives enough to make fixing cross-site scripting the priority?
talks.summary: The speaker traces how cross-site scripting defenses have developed, from escaping and sanitization to browser restrictions and security policies, and explains why these measures still leave gaps. He argues that technical tools alone are not enough: incentives, business priorities and a focus on finding bugs over fixing them also affect whether vulnerabilities get resolved. Attendees hear proposals for rewarding fixes, improving regression testing and building motivation to prevent recurring flaws.

talks.title: Jumpstarting Your DevSecOps Pipeline with IAST and RASP
talks.teaser: Shows how IAST and RASP agents can find vulnerabilities and block attacks across development, CI and production.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the state of application security. The speaker argues that most vulnerabilities sit in custom code rather than libraries, that every application he protects was attacked, and that development and operations security have long been run separately. He proposes applying DevOps principles to security and focuses on automation with two techniques: interactive application security testing (IAST), an agent that runs inside the app, and runtime application self-protection (RASP), which sees data as the application handles it.

The demo follows a Java Spring pet clinic app through development, CI/CD and production. While a developer browses, the IAST agent reports a Hibernate injection, a path traversal and a stored cross-site scripting issue, each with a trace to the relevant line of code, and sends them to the IDE, Slack and a browser plugin. It also inventories open-source libraries and shows how much of each is actually invoked. In CI, scheduled test runs push findings into JIRA with two-way ticket closure, and JaCoCo measures how much code the tests exercised. In production, RASP blocks a SQL injection before it reaches the database and logs the request details, and it sandboxes deserialization, an attack that static tools cannot see.

The main takeaway is that instrumentation gives developers fast, accurate feedback and gives operations visibility into who attacks which applications. Library inventory lets teams respond to new vulnerabilities within hours, and RASP can protect applications while fixes are pending. The speaker argues that this approach scales across many applications without relying on scarce experts, and that policy changes such as retiring a weak cipher can be tested across the whole portfolio at once.

talks.title: Testing iOS Apps without Jailbreak in 2018
talks.teaser: Shows how to test iOS apps for security flaws without a jailbreak, using an injected Frida library on a re-signed app.
talks.summary:
Wojciech Reguła explains why iOS app penetration testing often depends on a jailbreak, and why that dependency is a problem. Jailbreaks cover only a narrow set of devices and firmware versions, and public ones are hard to find, so testers can lose time before an assessment even starts. Apple's FairPlay encryption also stops testers from reading an app package without a device.

As an alternative, the talk walks through injecting a Frida dynamic library into an app. The steps are to unpack the IPA, add the library to the frameworks folder, update the binary's import table, repack the app, and sign it with a free developer account, then trust it on the phone. The live demo used the Etsy app and the Passion Fruit client to inspect URL schemes, Info.plist, binary flags, caches, the app bundle, user defaults and the keychain. Keychain access crashed the client during the demo, so an objection-based dump was used instead.

The talk notes that certificate pinning is harder to bypass this way than with a jailbreak tweak, so it needs custom Frida scripts and extra time. It closes by stating that no single method is best and inviting better approaches. Attendees were offered a written walkthrough so they can repeat the setup at home.

talks.title: OWASP Serverless Top 10
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP Serverless Top 10, showing how injection and over-privileged functions differ from classic app attacks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Tal Melamed, Head of Security Research at Protego Labs, introduces the OWASP Serverless Top 10 project. The project provides a serverless-tailored interpretation of the traditional OWASP Top 10 application security risks. Melamed explains that while serverless architectures (such as AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions) shift infrastructure management to cloud providers, they also introduce unique security dynamics because code execution is triggered by diverse cloud events rather than traditional API or network perimeters.

### Key Topics
- **Nature of Serverless Computing**: Compute power executes inside ephemeral, stateless cloud containers that automatically spin up, execute code, and terminate. Execution environments are generally read-only aside from the `/tmp` scratch directory.
- **Shift in Attack Surface**: Traditional perimeters like network firewalls are absent. Serverless security is strictly code- and application-centric (AppSec), driven by event sources rather than purely HTTP/API endpoints.
- **OWASP Serverless Top 10 Mapping**: Adaptation of standard web vulnerabilities (injection, broken authentication, sensitive data exposure, XXE, broken access control, security misconfigurations, XSS, deserialization, vulnerable dependencies, and insufficient logging/monitoring) to serverless paradigms.

### Technical Details
- **Event Injections & RCE Realities**: Because standard servers and persistent shells are absent, traditional remote code execution (RCE) or OS hijacking does not function normally. Instead, attackers exploit event injection (via sources like MQTT, cloud storage events, or emails) to execute child processes, write to `/tmp`, archive source code, or exfiltrate backend application files via tunnels.
- **Broken Authentication Across Triggers**: While many teams secure API Gateways, roughly 30% of customer traffic enters through non-API triggers (such as AWS SES emails, cloud commit events, database changes, or IoT feeds). If functions assume internal triggers are trusted, attackers can bypass authentication by directly spoofing or generating triggering events.
- **Function Keys & Sensitive Data Exposure**: Sensitive application data is frequently written to the writable `/tmp` directory. Furthermore, cloud function environments expose session tokens, access keys, and environment variables (such as AWS credentials) via process environment variables. If an attacker extracts these keys, they can interact directly with cloud APIs (e.g., DynamoDB or S3) from their local machine without further interaction with the vulnerable function. In addition, container reuse for performance optimizations can allow leftover data in `/tmp` to persist across invocations.
- **Broken Access Control & Over-Privileged Functions**: Melamed highlights that 98% of thousands of reviewed functions are over-privileged due to developers using wildcard permissions (e.g., `s3:*` on all resources). Demonstrating the impact, Melamed shows how limiting IAM policies strictly to required actions on specific resources (e.g., `s3:PutObject` on a dedicated bucket) effectively blocks attackers from listing or compromising other buckets even if command injection occurs.
- **Dependencies & Logging Challenges**: Microservice functions often contain only ~100 lines of custom code but pull in thousands of lines of external dependencies, increasing the likelihood of known vulnerable components. Traditional network monitoring is impossible; teams must rely entirely on provider-level log streams, which can be overwhelming to parse across millions of distributed function invocations.

### Takeaways
Serverless architecture enables fine-grained least-privilege security at the function level, but realizing this benefit requires automated permission scoping, securing non-API triggers, monitoring cloud log services, and vetting third-party dependencies. Melamed points attendees to the OWASP Damn Vulnerable Serverless Application (DVSA) as an open-source project designed for practicing attacks and defenses in realistic serverless environments.

talks.title: Bringing Rapid Prototyping To The Threat Model Process GEOFFREY HILL
talks.teaser: Presents a methodology that speeds up threat modeling by prototyping lightweight models alongside agile sprints.
talks.summary:
Geoffrey Hill opens by explaining why traditional threat modeling struggles in agile and DevOps teams. Sessions often stall while people argue over threats instead of agreeing on mitigations, data flow diagrams drift away from the real architecture, and the model falls behind after a few sprints. He argues that a threat model should start a conversation rather than aim to be complete on the first pass.

He then presents rapid threat model prototyping, an open, Creative Commons methodology built on a consistent framework, a repeatable process and measurable data. The work starts with model storming in sprint zero, followed by applying STRIDE to a sample microservice system with a website, API gateway, uploader, message queue, analytics component and results store. Each element and flow gets a numeric trust score from 0 to 9, with anything outside the diagram's control scored at zero and data written to disk generally scored high. Analysts then walk the STRIDE categories in a fixed order, starting with elevation of privilege, and map findings to mitigations drawn from the OWASP Top 10 and OpenSAMM business functions so business owners can see the impact.

His closing advice is to iterate in small rounds, accepting a rough model that covers most of the risk early. Results can be packaged as JSON or XML, attached to build pipelines or pull requests, sent to dashboards such as ELK or Splunk, and tracked in a risk register. The method is published on GitHub so teams can download, adapt and contribute to it.
