talks.title: The Evolving Community of Appsec ASTHA SINGHAL
talks.teaser: Traces the history of application security from Microsoft's Trustworthy Computing to OWASP and argues for platform-team partnerships.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how application security grew out of early-2000s Microsoft problems. The speaker recalls worms such as the love bug, which abused hidden file extensions and spread through email contact lists, and the 2002 memo that launched Microsoft's Trustworthy Computing effort. That work produced the Security Development Lifecycle, which became the basis for many company AppSec programs.

Next, the talk covers vulnerability disclosure. Early on, researchers were often treated as adversaries, and anonymous zero-days and uncoordinated full disclosure were common. By the late 2000s, responsible disclosure matured, and in 2008 Microsoft said its research program would also cover third-party products and external reports, a shift that later helped the bug bounty industry grow. The OWASP story follows: founded in late 2001 to give developers guidance, it moved from pen-tester-focused material toward developer resources such as the Top 10 and dependency-check tooling.

The speaker argues that educating every developer does not scale. Instead, the community should work with platform teams that build CI/CD tools, container platforms, and base images, citing Netflix's Spinnaker, where secure defaults for load balancers reach every engineer. The takeaway is to build secure-by-default frameworks, hire engineers with platform backgrounds, and keep sharing lessons learned through meetups and communities.

talks.title: OWASP Top 10 for JavaScript Developers
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP Top 10 risks as they show up in JavaScript and Node.js code, with exploit demos and fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk goes through the OWASP Top 10 with a focus on Node.js back ends and the browser code that calls them. For injection, it shows a MongoDB login route that passes request fields straight into a find-one query. Sending a query operator such as not-equal or greater-than in the password field logs in without knowing the password. The suggested defences are schema validation with a library like Joi and parameterised queries, with validation paired with output encoding.

Broken authentication is illustrated with a hand-rolled Express session check that looked up cookie values on a plain object. A cookie value of "constructor" matched inherited object properties and was accepted as a valid session. The speaker recommends crypto.timingSafeEqual for comparisons and Map or hasOwnProperty checks for lookups. XXE examples show an XML parser with entity expansion enabled reading user-supplied input, and parsers that ignore entities by default are preferred. Access control is shown to fail when enforced only by client-side route guards, so server-side policy libraries such as CASL or role-checking middleware are advised.

The XSS section explains that DOM-based XSS is hard for static tools to catch and that browsers parse HTML differently. Framework templating, DOMPurify and a Content Security Policy are offered as layers of defence. The talk closes with vulnerable components, covering npm audit, Snyk, retire.js and GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. Pinning dependency versions through lockfiles is suggested to limit exposure to compromised packages.

talks.title: Black Clouds and Silver Linings in Node.js Security
talks.teaser: Traces malicious npm packages, compromised maintainer accounts and a template injection bug affecting Node.js projects.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of the npm registry, which is nearing a million packages and accepts submissions without automated security review. That openness attracts attackers, because compromising one popular package reaches many downstream users. The speaker groups malicious packages into three patterns: typosquatting, compromised maintainer accounts, and social engineering.

Several incidents illustrate these patterns. A typosquat of a popular environment-variable tool bundled the genuine package but sent environment variables to a remote host during installation. A backdoor called get-cookies was hidden several dependency levels deep and injected into a widely used mail parser, accepting commands through request headers and executing remote JavaScript. The eslint-scope compromise stole npm tokens, and its published code differed from the GitHub source. Research on maintainer accounts found weak and reused passwords. A live demo then showed how the dust templating engine's HTML escaping could be bypassed with parameter pollution, letting attacker input reach code evaluation.

The closing section covers defenses. Two-factor authentication is used by only a small share of packages, and token scoping is coarse, so one leaked token can reach every package a maintainer owns. Dependency trees often run more than four levels deep, and most vulnerabilities sit in indirect dependencies, so developers should audit their full tree. The speaker also pointed to developer-friendly tooling that runs in CI and opens automatic fix pull requests, plus the Node.js security working group's bug bounty and public vulnerability database.

talks.title: Can We Automate Security? SASHA ROSENBAUM
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Can We Automate Security? SASHA ROSENBAUM.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Sasha Rosenbaum, a program manager on the Azure DevOps team (formerly TFS) at Microsoft, explores the practical reality behind the question: "Can we automate security?" Her answer is that while parts of security can and should be automated, automation alone is far from sufficient. Grounded in her experience assisting a major US city recover from a devastating ransomware incident, Rosenbaum argues that modern security requires an "assumed breach" mindset. Rather than solely attempting to keep attackers out, organizations must focus on rapid detection, containment, and remediation, paired with deep cultural changes across engineering teams.

### Key Topics
- **The Reality of Breaches & Assumed Breach**: Rosenbaum shares her deployment to assist a major US city hit by ransomware via brute-forced weak passwords. The attack compromised 95% of city infrastructure—including courts and police databases—largely because 2,000 known security warnings had been ignored due to organizational fatigue, and no working recovery procedures or backups existed. Quoting former NSA/CIA director Michael Hayden, she stresses that determined attackers will inevitably penetrate systems; security teams must assume they are already breached.
- **Culture Change via Red Teaming & Gamification**: Developers frequently view security as an obstacle to shipping features. Microsoft addressed this by running internal Red Team exercises and capture the flag (CTF) events, demonstrating tangible proof of vulnerabilities (e.g., exploiting a cross-site scripting flaw to automatically upvote an internal bug ticket 280 times). Red Team operations operate under strict rules: do no harm, avoid impacting customer systems or availability, do not harass humans, and report findings responsibly. Microsoft eventually retired dedicated Blue Teams, embracing the model that every engineer must be a protector.
- **Protecting Credentials and Phishing Defense**: The two largest entry points for attackers are credential theft and known vulnerabilities. Internal phishing tests showed that 44% of employees clicked simulated promotional links, and spear-phishing disguised as manager requests remains highly successful. To mitigate this, Rosenbaum emphasizes mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) and link-wrapping in Office 365, which inspects targets at click time.
- **Open-Source Vulnerabilities & Supply Chain Security**: With ubiquitous adoption of open-source software, unpatched components pose severe risks, as seen in the Equifax breach involving an unpatched Apache Struts flaw. Defenses include automated dependency scanners (such as WhiteSource and GitHub's Dependabot), as well as routing external packages through scanned internal package repositories.
- **Preventing Lateral Movement**: Attackers think in graphs, hopping through exposed credentials in file shares or test environments to escalate privileges. Rosenbaum advises against treating dev or test environments as throwaways, avoiding default configurations on POCs (especially Kubernetes clusters), and enforcing zero standing admin privileges through Just-in-Time (JIT) access and secure admin workstations.
- **Automating Pipelines**: CI/CD pipelines can enforce automated secret scanning (such as CredScan) on pull requests to block secrets before merging into master. Furthermore, organizations should rotate secrets on every deployment using key vaults and adopt cloud infrastructure-as-code to prevent long-standing servers.

### Technical Details
- **Secret Scanning**: Implementing automated pull request build triggers using CredScan and similar repository tools to detect hardcoded secrets and block merges into trunk/master.
- **Access Control Architecture**: Implementing Just-in-Time (JIT) privilege elevation via temporary passwords or certificates, eliminating standing administrative permissions to production.
- **Pipeline Secret Management**: Storing all operational credentials in key vaults and rotating them automatically during every release to prevent breakage from stale secrets.
- **Threat Modeling Limitations**: Automated threat modeling tools tested by Microsoft generated high noise and false positives; threat modeling remains an effective human-driven whiteboard process for new feature designs, though it cannot cover every single code commit.
- **Bug Bounty**: Microsoft established an Azure bounty program offering up to $20,000 for documented, reproducible vulnerabilities.

### Takeaways
Automating security in CI/CD pipelines—especially secret detection, open-source dependency scanning, and automated credential rotation—is critical for modern engineering. However, automation cannot replace human vigilance and threat modeling. Organizations must eliminate standing privileges, deploy MFA, isolate environments, and use gamified exercises like Red Teaming to build a culture of security empathy among developers.

talks.title: Software Security War: your reports are dead! MATTEO MEUCCI
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Software Security War: your reports are dead! MATTEO MEUCCI.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Matteo Meucci addresses the limitations of traditional security reports and testing-centric approaches in modern application security. With massive codebases and high deployment frequencies (seen in organizations like Amazon, Google, and Netflix), relying on static vulnerability reports creates unacceptable latency in remediation. Meucci argues that traditional reports are effectively "dead" and advocates for shifting focus toward measuring security maturity, building an organizational security culture, and immediately integrating security flaws into developer issue trackers.

### Key Topics
- **The Limits of Testing and Reporting:** Emphasizing vulnerability counts or tool scans gives a false sense of security. Software is never finished, and security reports sitting on manager desks delay critical fixes.
- **OWASP Software Security 5 Dimension Framework (5D):** A lightweight assessment framework covering Processes, Testing, Team, Awareness, and Standards to identify gaps beyond basic testing.
- **OWASP SAMM & Maturity Assessments:** Historical assessment data shows industry maturity heavily skewed toward verification and security testing, while lacking in areas like awareness and dedicated security roles.
- **Industry Implementations:** Examination of how major organizations handle software security at scale, including Google's secure internal frameworks and automated testing, Facebook's modified PHP (Hacklang) and bug bounty/red teaming, and Comcast's culture-driven maturity model derived from SAMM and BSIMM.
- **Instant Feedback and Workflow Integration:** Treating vulnerabilities as standard bugs with high priority in issue trackers (e.g., Jira) to provide immediate feedback.

### Technical Details
- **Five Dimensions Framework Breakdown:**
  - *Processes:* Enforcing risk assessments (distinguishing critical software like online banking from low-risk internal applications), security requirements, threat modeling, secure code review, and penetration testing across SDLC phases.
  - *Testing:* Utilizing automated tooling (SAST, DAST, IAST, RASP) combined with external manual code review and penetration testing.
  - *Team:* Establishing dedicated roles such as Application Security Managers, security champions, satellite architects, and developers acting as security focal points.
  - *Awareness:* Ensuring software security education is distributed across top management and engineering roles.
  - *Standards:* Employing guidelines, threat modeling standards, architectural guidelines, and OWASP SAMM roadmaps.
- **Remediation & Supply Chain Verification:** Fixing vulnerabilities at the code level (e.g., using OWASP ESAPI to encode HTML attributes against XSS) must happen rapidly. For third-party vendors and outsourcers, Meucci notes that showing a retest report or a third-party maturity assessment certificate (e.g., SAMM Level 2/3) provides far better assurance than basic penetration test reports or HTTPS usage claims.

### Takeaways
- Testing is only the final verification step, not the entirety of software security.
- Static reports should be replaced with instant security feedback and issue-tracking integration.
- Security responsibility must extend across the organization rather than resting solely on developers.
- Organizations should focus on long-term security roadmaps and building security culture across all five dimensions rather than simply tallying vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Magecart - a growing threat to e-commerce sites
talks.teaser: Traces how Magecart groups skim card data from online checkouts, moving from compromised Magento stores to third-party scripts.
talks.summary:
Magecart is the name for several criminal groups that steal payment card data from online checkout pages, a campaign running since 2015 and gaining momentum recently. After chip cards made physical skimming harder, attackers shifted to e-commerce sites. The speakers from Trustwave describe how they estimate more than 50,000 websites were affected, either directly or through code they loaded from other services, with well-known brands such as British Airways and Ticketmaster among the victims.

The talk traces how the attacks evolved. In 2015 a study found that 40 percent of investigated compromises involved e-commerce sites, and 85 percent of those ran Magento open source, which had several critical flaws that many merchants left unpatched for long periods. Attackers then targeted Magento marketplace extensions, many of them vulnerable and from small vendors, with around twenty exploited by 2018. They next hit third-party web services such as chat widgets, whose scripts were fetched dynamically by merchant sites. One Australian merchant case showed card data posted to a freshly registered domain in Ukraine, a domain also found on 46 other sites.

Defenders should keep Magento and its extensions patched and remove unused ones, and keep checkout pages free of third-party scripts. Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity can block unexpected script loading, and blocking skimming domains helps.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 Welcome Address
talks.teaser: Richard Greenberg examines AppSecCali 2019 Welcome Address.
talks.summary:
### Overview
The AppSecCali 2019 Welcome Address opens the conference by acknowledging the collaborative efforts behind the event, which was organized by six California OWASP chapters alongside a volunteer-driven committee managing roughly 90 operational tasks. The conference chair emphasizes community involvement, the non-profit status of OWASP, and the vital role of event sponsors. The session also features brief overview presentations from diamond sponsors ShiftLeft and Netsparker prior to the morning keynote.

### Key Topics
- **OWASP Organization and Governance:** OWASP operates as an open, transparent, not-for-profit entity across the US and Europe, guided by core values of openness, innovation, global reach, and integrity. The chair introduced members of the OWASP Global Board, including Martin Knobloch, Chenxi Wang, Sherif Mansoor, Owen Pendlebury, Richard Greenberg, Gary Robinson, and Ofer Maor, as well as key staff members such as acting executive director Mike McCammon, director of community and operations Matt Tesauro, community manager Dawn Aitken, and director of projects Harold Blankenship.
- **Projects and Community Engagement:** The address highlighted prominent OWASP resources and standards, including the OWASP Top 10, the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS), WebGoat, CSRF cheat sheets, and mobile application checklists among over 110 active projects. Attendees were encouraged to contribute code, start or join chapters, and facilitate dialogue between security teams, developers, and executives.
- **Automated Vulnerability Discovery (ShiftLeft):** A representative from diamond sponsor ShiftLeft discussed the scaling challenges of modern vulnerability discovery. While manual penetration testing often lags behind rapid code changes, full automation cannot replace human expertise. ShiftLeft outlined their approach using a unified representation called a "code property graph" (CPG), which integrates data flows, call graphs, type hierarchies, and instruction-level information into a queryable graph structure.
- **ShiftLeft Ocular Tooling:** ShiftLeft presented Ocular, an interactive REPL shell designed for analysts to query code property graphs and discover vulnerabilities. It currently supports Java, C#, and C/C++, with the C/C++ module provided as open source.
- **Scaling Web Application Security (Netsparker):** Diamond sponsor Netsparker, represented by Joe, invited attendees to their upcoming talk on scaling web application security and encouraged engagement at booths 24 and 25.

### Technical Details
- **Code Property Graph (CPG):** A specialized data structure merging disparate code representations—instruction-level data, data flows, type hierarchies, and call graphs—into an accessible graph search engine for custom vulnerability pattern queries.
- **Ocular REPL:** A shell environment designed to query code property graphs, allowing practitioners to explore codebases and identify previously unknown security flaws.

### Takeaways
- Community engagement and cross-functional collaboration between developers, security practitioners, and leadership are fundamental to advancing software security standards.
- Practitioners can leverage over 110 OWASP initiatives, standards (ASVS), and tools (WebGoat) under free and open software licenses.
- Vulnerability analysis must modernize beyond manual penetration testing by utilizing graph-based representations like Code Property Graphs to automate deep structural inspection while enabling human-driven query exploration.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Authorization in Micro Services World Kubernetes, ISTIO and Open Policy Agent
talks.teaser: Traces how authorization grew harder across microservices and how Open Policy Agent moves access decisions out of application code.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how authorization became hard to manage as applications moved from client-server designs to three-tier web apps, service-oriented architectures and microservices. It reviews the common approaches: role-based and attribute-based access control, checks on web pages, firewalls and web access management products, API gateways, and hand-written checks inside each endpoint. The core problem is that rules end up scattered across layers and code, so changing a rule means a developer change and a redeploy, and centralized gateways become a bottleneck owned by operations teams.

The speaker then covers externalizing authorization, an idea that predates OPA in the XACML standard, whose XML policies were hard for developers to adopt. Kubernetes is used as an example: its webhook mode sends each API request's user, resource and verb to an external decision service that returns allowed or denied. Service meshes such as Istio still leave authorization local to each service. Open Policy Agent is then introduced as a general policy engine with its Rego language, where policies are evaluated against JSON input, loaded as bundles that can be updated without redeploying, and plugged into HTTP filters, gateways, SSH and Kafka.

The takeaway is to pull access decisions out of application code so that developers and security teams can agree on policy together, with decision logs available for auditing and troubleshooting. The speaker notes that OPA can complement an existing commercial gateway, and that service identities such as SPIFFE can support service-to-service authorization.

talks.teaser: Security leads from several large companies compare automation tactics, adoption hurdles and failed experiments in application security.
talks.summary:
Application security leaders from Dropbox, Netflix, DocuSign, Snap, Datadog and NCC Group discuss how they automate security across their development lifecycles. The panel is an unscripted discussion without slides, and the speakers deliberately highlight points of disagreement. Most describe internal tooling that scans new code pushes. Dropbox and Snap block on certain issues during code review and let developers mark false positives, which the security team reviews to tune rules. Others prefer post-commit audits so that engineers can move faster.

A recurring theme is that wrapper libraries and secure-by-default frameworks often beat scanning, because they eliminate whole bug classes. DocuSign built telemetry into its wrappers so engineers gained monitoring for free. Panelists also described failures: commercial dynamic scanners struggled with single-page apps, keyword monitoring of public Slack chats felt too invasive, a questionnaire-based review was gamed by developers choosing the shortest path, and a threat modeling form was disliked because it could not be worked on collaboratively. Several speakers argued that tools developers can understand and trust get better adoption than opaque analyzers.

For building a program, the advice was to build relationships with teams that own high-risk assets, gain asset visibility before automating, prioritize ruthlessly and make a decision quickly rather than stall. Panelists also discussed growing internal talent, giving researchers room to present, and treating attrition as normal. They closed by stressing that no silver bullet exists and that teams should start with their biggest risks and iterate.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Preventing Mobile App and API Abuse
talks.teaser: Walks through a courier app's attacks on mobile API keys, certificate pinning and OAuth, and how to harden each layer.
talks.summary:
The talk uses a courier app, Ship Fast, as a running example of how a mobile app and its backend API get abused. A driver's OAuth login alone proved insufficient: once a rogue client reused valid credentials, it could list every nearby shipment and claim the most lucrative one. Hardcoded API keys were a second weak point, exposed through an unzipped APK or a leaked backup file.

Each defence was then tried in turn. Certificate pinning blocked easy interception but is hard to maintain, and runtime hooks can bypass the trust check itself. Signing requests with an HMAC kept the secret off the wire, yet the computation is deterministic, so the secret was recovered from the app anyway. Obfuscation, anti-debugging and white-box cryptography only raise the cost. The speaker also explained the OAuth 2 code flow with PKCE, which keeps credentials away from the client, and advised short-lived access tokens and single-use refresh tokens.

The final design moves secrets off the device. A proxy holds the one remaining key, and a separate secret service issues short-lived tokens only after attesting that the app is untampered. Behavioral analytics and rate limiting remain a necessary backstop, since they yield statistical rather than certain decisions. The takeaway is to verify both the application and the user, and to replace long-lived secrets with time-limited stand-ins wherever possible.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Pose a Threat: How Perceptual Analysis Helps Bug Hunters
talks.teaser: Shows how perceptual hashing of screenshots helps testers triage huge sets of exposed web paths without writing signatures.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both longtime penetration testers, set out to find exposures across very large sets of cloud-hosted web targets, where IP addresses change constantly and manually reviewing responses does not scale. They focused on AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which many organizations of all sizes use. Their pipeline discovered domains and subdomains from open-source intelligence and certificate transparency data, requested a short list of common attack paths drawn from published scanning traffic, and captured headless browser screenshots of each response.

Instead of writing a signature for every path, they grouped the screenshots by visual similarity using a perceptual hashing algorithm, which gives visually similar images similar hashes. Blank pages sort to one end and visually dense pages to the other, so outliers stand out, and identical custom 404 pages can be discarded. Requests were spread across many IP addresses through cloud functions to avoid overloading or being blocked by any single host. Across roughly 88,000 targets, the process produced about 52,000 screenshots, narrowed to around 4,000 for review, and surfaced 321 critical exposures, including exposed environment files holding cloud and database credentials and large amounts of source code.

The talk contrasted this with older brute-force tools that took servers down and with manual screenshot review, which is inconsistent across a team. The speakers closed with next steps: using machine learning to classify pages, training models on historical bug bounty reports, and keeping discovery running so new targets are checked as they appear. The practical takeaway is that continuous discovery combined with visual triage can help a small team find issues that signatures would miss.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - (in)Secure Development - Why some product teams are great and others … aren’t...
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for AppSecCali 2019 - (in)Secure Development - Why some product teams are great and others … aren’t....
talks.summary:
Overview
Ken Hendrix, a Dutch development manager in Riot Games' security team, shares how his organization discovered why some product teams excel at security while others struggle. Riot Games, founded in 2006 and grown from 40–50 to over 3,500 employees, operates a highly autonomous engineering culture where every team maintains complete independence in how they build and organize their work. This autonomy, while powerful for product delivery, creates a core security challenge: traditional top-down mandates and gatekeeping fail because teams simply refuse to adopt them.

Key Topics
Maturity Model: Through observation of 50+ teams across 2017–2018, Hendrix identified a four-level maturity spectrum for security practices. Level 1 teams have limited security awareness and don't discuss it in planning. Level 2 teams treat security as a reactive pre-release phase, dependent on a single champion (e.g., a tech lead) who advocates for it—making security unsustainable when that person leaves. Level 3 teams integrate security into nearly every conversation and formal agenda, becoming a sustainable practice across the whole team. Level 4 teams practice security "like breathing," automatically and without prompting, typically in security-sensitive domains like authentication or payment.

Research Findings: By end of 2017, most teams clustered in Levels 1–2, with significant gaps before Level 3–4. Bug bounty data proved impact: a Level 4 team paid 55 cents per bounty dollar compared to Level 1's $1.00, and fixed high-risk issues in one-third the time. Security review data confirmed the pattern: Level 4 issues had severity valued at 58 cents versus Level 1's $1.00.

The Lightweight Solution: Rather than imposing heavy threat modeling (e.g., STRIDE taking 30+ minutes per sprint) or lengthy security checklists, Hendrix's team introduced a single security question per sprint story: "How can a malicious user intentionally abuse this functionality and how can we prevent that?" A brief 2–3 minute conversation ensures the team thinks about security without the overhead. The approach prioritizes scalability (not requiring security staff in every meeting) over perfection.

Practical Example: The Battlegrounds tournament-organizing tool team (5 engineers, designer, QA, product owner) applied this during sprint planning. One story about mass CSV tournament uploads surfaced the need for file validation and logging. Another about a tournament-help button revealed a denial-of-service vector when a team member asked what happens if someone clicks rapidly—prompting the product owner (non-technical) to raise the security question. Both conversations led to secure design choices and helped the team move from Level 2 to Level 3.

Technical Details
Implementation: The security question is integrated into the existing agile workflow (JIRA, Trello, etc.) rather than layered on top. Teams typically need 4–5 weeks to develop the "muscle" of thinking like an attacker. The process is intentionally imperfect—the security team acknowledges they could identify 20+ additional issues in a typical story but don't intervene, allowing the team's own conversation to drive lightweight solutions.

Challenges: Riot's decentralized model (20+ offices, 20+ programming languages, multiple frameworks) makes centralized code analysis difficult. Teams dropping in maturity occur, especially when a security champion or advocate leaves. Formal security training has struggled to be relevant and valuable across diverse engineering roles.

Metrics: By end of 2018, progress was observed with teams moving from Level 1→2 and Level 2→3. However, advancement from Level 3→4 is a multi-year journey with diminishing returns. The leadership in Level 4 teams consistently prioritized security, integrity, and trust—sometimes delaying releases for better security over additional player features.

Takeaways
Riot's core lesson is that security interventions must align with how teams actually work and operate. Preaching to teams already good at security moves the needle nowhere; focusing on teams at Level 1–2 is where impact happens. Lightweight, conversation-based tools that fit into existing agile workflows are far more adoptable than heavyweight processes. Security should not be a pre-release gate but an ongoing part of team thinking. Understanding team maturity and culture is essential before imposing solutions; understanding why teams reject mandates enables better engagement. Finally, observable, data-driven metrics (bug payouts, fix times, severity) help persuade teams and stakeholders that security practices yield tangible value.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Startup security: Starting a security program at a startup
talks.teaser: Describes how a first security hire can build a security program at a SaaS startup, from design reviews to incident response.
talks.summary:
Evan Johnson outlines a playbook for a first security hire at a SaaS startup, a role that spans production, corporate, business operations and unexpected requests, often with few people and little guidance. He stresses relationships first: internal teams are the security team's customers, so staying calm during incidents and building credibility with engineers matter. Priorities should follow whether the company sells to businesses or consumers, its size, product, shipping pace and culture.

For a starting set of tasks, he covers four areas. In security engineering, that means joining design reviews, learning the tech stack, and managing secrets and API keys, with a bug bounty only once its goals are clear. For detection and response, he recommends a basic incident plan and a simple reporting channel such as an email alias. For compliance, he suggests a public security page and early checks on customer commitments such as SOC 2. For corporate security, he points to identity and access management, endpoint protection, onboarding and offboarding, and office badges, most of which can be scoped to about a quarter. At Segment, removing engineers' day-to-day AWS keys and tying access to the identity provider reached full coverage in two to three weeks. A secrets tool called Chamber, by contrast, dragged on because people assumed the security team would own every secret.

He closes by urging teams to finish bounded, high-impact problems, avoid work that needs constant upkeep, and be able to show month-over-month security gains. Fancy solutions should wait until the basics are in place.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Open-source OWASP tools to aid in penetration testing coverage
talks.teaser: Shows how free OWASP tools map web application endpoints and measure code coverage during penetration testing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem in penetration testing: testers have limited time, and without a clear list of endpoints and the parameters they accept, testing turns into guesswork and brute-force probing. Knowing the attack surface lets a tester aim tests at the parts of an application that matter. The talk introduces the OWASP Attack Surface Detector, which analyzes source code rather than compiled binaries to list endpoints, HTTP methods and parameters. Its output can be saved as JSON or pushed directly into the ZAP proxy.

The live demo runs WebGoat in Docker and uses ZAP with Chrome. After a login context was configured so ZAP could authenticate, the spider found 139 URLs. Importing the detector's endpoints raised that to 174, exposing routes the crawl had not reached, and the detector listed parameter types such as strings that can be fuzzed. The second part covers Code Pulse, a tool that attaches a Java agent to JPetStore running in Docker and reports which classes and JSPs are exercised during testing. Two recorded sessions were compared: one tester browsed without signing in, and another logged in and bought an item. The comparison showed where their coverage overlapped and where it differed. Dependency-check results for the bundled libraries were also generated.

The main takeaway is that automated endpoint discovery and coverage tracking reduce guesswork and make it easier to see what has actually been tested. Authenticated contexts keep scans focused on the right pages, and per-tester coverage comparisons help teams spot gaps. The tools discussed are free and available from OWASP.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - A Seat at the Table
talks.teaser: Argues that security teams need consistent tools, threat modeling, and soft skills to take part in design discussions early.
talks.summary:
Security teams are often informed or consulted only after the important design decisions have already been made. This talk treats design as an ongoing dialogue that moves from exploratory "what if" discussion to firm decisions, and argues that security needs a place in the early part of that conversation.

The speaker proposes two things security needs in order to earn that seat. The first is tools that work in fluid discussions and give consistent answers. Threat modeling fits, since it asks what is being worked on, what can go wrong, what will be done about it, and whether the effort was worthwhile. Structured methods such as STRIDE or kill chains keep different analysts from producing very different results, and threat modeling can be split into small, automatable pieces. The second is soft skills: respecting speakers, inviting quiet voices, active listening, deferring judgment, and assuming good intent.

The closing argument is a business case. Behaviors that push colleagues away lead to escalations, weaker collaboration and hostile workplaces, while welcoming teams attract people who want to work with them. The speaker also connects this to diversity and suggests tracking rework and vulnerability counts to show the value of training. A practitioner should take away a consistent threat modeling practice, early engagement, and interpersonal habits that let security be invited to the table.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - Automated Account Takeover: The Rise of Single Request Attacks
talks.teaser: Surveys single request attacks behind account takeover, ticket scalping and carding, and the defenses that struggle against them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at single request attacks, automated attempts that get what they want from one request at a time, with account takeover as the main focus. The speaker explains how attackers take large breach lists of emails and passwords and test them against login pages at scale. They hide behind rotating IP addresses routed through compromised IoT devices. Browser fingerprints, user agents and mouse-movement biometrics are weak signals, since modified open-source Chromium and recorded input macros can imitate real users. Text CAPTCHAs fare no better, as optical character recognition and paid solving services handle both text and image challenges.

The talk then moves through other abuse cases built on the same technique. An airline had its seat inventory held during payment redirects for up to ten minutes, so flights appeared sold out while nothing was purchased. Ticketing bots buy inventory within minutes for resale, gift card balances are brute-forced, and stolen card numbers are tested on charity donation pages. Bots also got past an emulator check in Pokémon Go, records of deceased people were used to cast fake votes, and auction bids were inflated to block sales.

For defense, the speaker recommends rate limiting by both email and identity rather than IP address alone, and warns that locking accounts hurts legitimate users. Token-based multi-factor authentication is preferred over SMS, which the speaker says is now breached, and password managers and breached-credential checks help. The main takeaway is that client-side data cannot be trusted, so defenders should raise the cost of attacks until they are no longer worth the effort.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 - CISO Panel: Baking Security Into the SDLC
talks.teaser: Security leaders share practical lessons on building security into devops culture, tooling, training and hiring.
talks.summary:
A panel of security leaders discussed how to build security into the software development lifecycle and devops. The panelists agreed that the hardest obstacles are cultural rather than technical, since security staff who arrive pointing out flaws often meet resistance. Suggested fixes included spending a sprint or two building alongside developers, meeting engineering leaders early, and cultivating security champions inside product teams. Supplier trust was raised as an unresolved problem, linked to a government warning about third-party risk.

On tooling, speakers described running static analysis inside repositories and build pipelines, and dynamic scans that a security engineer reviews to remove false positives before developers see results. Penetration tests were framed as point-in-time assurance for customers and auditors. Bug bounties drew mixed reviews, with one speaker valuing researcher reports that prompted fast fixes and another pausing a program because submissions were low value. One team ran an internal capture-the-flag training built on a deliberately vulnerable web app, which led developers to hunt for bugs themselves.

For staffing and influence, the panel recommended looking internally for people with aptitude from outside technology, such as former call centre and teaching staff. To raise risk with executives, a developer was advised to compile metrics and demonstrate how flaws chain into a real exploit. The closing message was to treat findings as teachable moments rather than a hammer, mixing carrots and sticks to suit each culture.

talks.title: AppSecCali 2019 Keynote - Fail, Learn, Fix
talks.teaser: Traces security failures from electrical codes and medical device recalls to web TLS, arguing the industry must share lessons.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of electrical safety, from the 1880s World's Fair lighting contest between direct and alternating current to the National Electric Code that grew out of early failures. The speaker argues that engineering improves when failures are studied and fixed, and then applies that idea to computing. His main case is the Therac-25 radiotherapy machine, whose software-controlled design removed hardware interlocks while its documentation, testing and error reporting were weak. Repeated incidents were dismissed until the cause was found, and a later US law requiring failure reporting for medical devices is presented as a policy response.

In the middle section he turns to security, covering 1970s efforts to build multi-level secure systems, the Orange Book evaluation levels, and the finding that highly evaluated systems were not much more secure in practice. He points to growing botnet-driven DDoS bandwidth and repeated breach patterns, then grades the industry: strong at failing, middling at learning from failures, and weak at fixing them, because retrospectives rarely span organizations and security patterns stay tied to one company.

He closes by urging more cross-industry talk, shared models of systems, and packaged patterns that engineers can use without deep expertise. Examples include a configuration-driven approach to TLS at Netflix, the SPIFFE effort for app-to-app identity, browser auto-updates, and the rise of HTTPS across the top websites. The takeaway is to secure the whole system and make the fixes usable for smaller organizations.

talks.title: Battle Tested Application Security - Ty Sbano
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2018 analyzes Battle Tested Application Security - Ty Sbano.
talks.summary:
Ty Sbano presents a pragmatic guide to building and scaling application security programs based on his experience in financial services and startups. Rather than focusing on specific tools or frameworks, the talk emphasizes relationships, understanding organizational culture, and strategic positioning within engineering teams.

**Building an App Sec Program Fundamentals**: Sbano outlines three initial steps: learn your organization's technology culture and code delivery methods (IDEs, languages, tech stacks); ignore vendor hype in the first 30 days and listen to engineering teams instead to understand real pain points; and be willing to put in the work—showing up during releases, incident response, and high-stress moments to earn credibility.

**Key Relationship Areas**: Success requires engaging multiple stakeholders differently: development teams (present and empowering), operations (understanding CI/CD tools like Jenkins, Concourse, and how code moves to production), compliance (helping translate regulations into sensible practices), and legal (securing contractual language with vendors). Sbano stresses alignment with business mission—if you don't believe in what the company does, leave.

**SDLC and Risk-Based Approach**: Security gates are outdated; instead, be present in the code change process. Reject prescriptive 30-60-90 day remediation policies that don't align with actual release cycles. Risk-based prioritization matters more than tracking all static analysis findings—50,000 coding flaws require filtering and manual validation, not rigid compliance metrics. Different engineering teams have different release cadences, and policies must reflect that reality.

**Metrics and Measurements**: Sbano warns against measuring yourself to death with complex formulas (cosine and sine). Instead, track what matters: code coverage, portfolio risk, and application inventory. One example: early in his career, he learned that static analysis output produces "coding flaws," not "vulnerabilities," until validated—a lesson that changed how he educated auditors and regulators.

**Team Composition and Staffing**: Insourced programs are more rewarding and allow true partnership with engineers. Outsourced programs require careful contract language (Software Security Annex) and vendor management. Hybrid approaches work when your team deeply understands outsourced technologies—e.g., don't outsource static analysis unless you understand rule engines, tuning, and authentication.

**Training and Education**: Live coaching with individual engineers is the most impactful method. The example of explaining why null checks alone don't validate input—an engineer with a null check still couldn't prevent code injection until Sbano walked through the actual attack—illustrates the value of presence over CBTs and compliance trainings. Sneakernet (walking around) and building relationships matter more than lectures.

**Open Source Over Silver Bullets**: Embrace tools built into your tech stack (Java security modules, Kubernetes controls, OWASP Zap) before buying commercial solutions. Budget constraints are real; tools like Brakeman, OWASP proxy, and license checking via artifact registries provide significant value without enterprise spending.

**Asset Management and Risk Assessment**: Before starting a program, map all applications, data flows, and external attack surface. Move beyond questionnaires to automation—API analysis and stream analysis to detect if sensitive data flows in the clear or only appears encrypted, giving a reality check on true risk.

**Final Philosophy**: Hygiene over hype; dialogue over confidentiality (transparent reporting in backlogs); support and celebrate people doing great work rather than shaming mistakes; and always be learning. Risk management matters, but continuous learning is the core principle—no expert truly masters app sec.

talks.title: Threat Model-as-Code - Abhay Bhargav
talks.teaser: Presents a YAML-based approach that ties threat models to automated application security tests in CI/CD pipelines.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that threat modeling is often produced as a large, static document that is written once a year or less, goes stale in fast CI/CD environments, leans on generic high-level threats, and stays disconnected from engineering work. He contrasts this with infrastructure-as-code tools such as Kubernetes, Ansible and Terraform, where a declarative spec drives the whole deployment.

The proposed approach is ThreatPlaybook, an open-source framework that breaks a model down feature by feature. Each feature starts with a user story, linked to abuser stories describing how it could be misused, then to threat scenarios such as SQL injection or CSRF, and finally to security test cases and mitigations. These are written in YAML and executed through Robot Framework scripts that call tools for Node.js scanning, npm audit and ZAP. Results are correlated back to the threat scenarios by CWE. A recorded demo of an expense-management app showed the pipeline running, with the ZAP scan fast-forwarded. Diagrams and threat maps are generated from the spec rather than drawn by hand.

The takeaway is that a threat model can act as a playbook for application security, guiding test coverage, pentest prioritization and automation, and it can be updated incrementally as features change. The speaker presented this as one option rather than the only way, noted that the project is young, and said a CLI and better diagramming were planned.

talks.title: My journey through building an advanced bot detection product - David Senecal
talks.teaser: Traces how a web company built a bot detection product, from scraper defense to behavioral analysis and replay attacks.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a solution architect who has spent about twelve years dealing with automated traffic, describes how a large web infrastructure company built its own bot detection product, starting in 2015 with scraper detection. Early passive checks looked at headers, user agents, reputation and request rate. As bots adapted, the team added active checks such as cookie and JavaScript tests and browser fingerprinting, which caught headless browsers. Fraud such as gift card PIN guessing later led them to add behavioral analysis, acquired through a startup, followed by an SDK for native apps.

Bot operators responded by replaying recorded telemetry, reverse engineering client code, and spreading traffic across large botnets where each node sends only a few requests per minute. The speaker argues that no single method is enough, since each detection technique has blind spots, and that teams must balance false positives against false negatives. Response strategy also matters: serving stale or decoy data can keep bots busy for a while. Attackers have even probed the detection engine itself with floods.

For site owners, the advice is to build a separate login API for each client type, protect every endpoint equally because attackers go after the weakest one, and decommission old APIs. One case involved a retired API that was still live and under attack. Finally, blocking individual bot signatures works only briefly, so tuning detections and acting on them is the better long-term approach.

talks.title: The Anatomy of a Secure Web Application in Java Using Spring Security and Apache Fortress
talks.teaser: Shows how to layer role-based access control, Spring Security and the Java Security Manager in a Java web application.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2017 Equifax breach, which exploited a known Apache Struts flaw, CVE-2017-5638, whose patch had been available for months. Patching alone is not enough, the speakers argue, because unknown flaws always exist. They recommend least privilege and defense in depth, and suggest running a Java application under the Java Security Manager, which is hard to configure but reveals what the application really does.

The middle section covers role-based access control built on the ANSI standard model of users, roles, permissions, sessions, and static and dynamic separation of duty. Apache Fortress implements that model. A sample application applies controls at several layers: container login at the perimeter, Spring Security mapping pages to roles, and programmatic checks in the data access layer, so one layer can catch what another misses. Role constraints tied to a customer context avoid role explosion, where each customer would otherwise need its own copy of a role.

The live demo showed roles being activated to reach pages and data, with errors for out-of-policy access and for activating two roles that violate dynamic separation of duty. Selenium tests cover positive and negative cases. The closing advice is for builders to adopt a standard authorization model like this rather than rebuild it each time, and to test it. Time ran out before the internals were covered.

talks.title: Open Source Security Tools for Kubernetes Applications - Michael Ducy
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2018 details Open Source Security Tools for Kubernetes Applications - Michael Ducy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Michael Ducy from Sysdig presents an architectural and practical overview of open-source security tools for Kubernetes and containerized applications. The talk examines container security through multiple layers, emphasizing the build pipeline and runtime environments. Ducy frames modern container security challenges around the concept of shifting choice to the left, ephemeral container lifecycles, and shared-kernel resource isolation, while demonstrating how open-source tools can enforce policy and automate threat response.

### Key Topics
- **Layers of Container Security**: Security spans underlying infrastructure (host, network, cluster, container runtime), the build phase (source code, dependencies, artifacts), and the runtime phase (secrets, admission, anomaly detection, forensics).
- **Shift Left vs. Choice**: Shifting left should empower development teams with informed choices while establishing automated guardrails such as image analysis and admission controllers.
- **Infrastructure Hardening**: Utilizing core Kubernetes constructs including RBAC, pod security policies, affinity rules, seccomp, SELinux, AppArmor, resource constraints, and network policies.
- **Image Scanning & Build Security**: Employing Anchore Engine within CI/CD pipelines to scan container images, inspect OS/third-party dependencies, and block vulnerable or misconfigured images.
- **Runtime Security & Threat Detection**: Monitoring system calls and orchestrator metadata via Falco to identify abnormal behavior such as spawned shells, binary modifications, and crypto-mining activity.
- **Automated Response Engine**: Leveraging event streams, pub/sub messaging (NATS), and serverless functions (Kubeless) to autonomously remediate threats in real time.

### Technical Details
- **Infrastructure Verification**: Tools like kube-hunter pen-test clusters for exposed endpoints (such as dashboard or kubelet API vulnerabilities), kube-bench audits against CIS benchmarks, and kubesec analyzes deployment YAML manifests against best practices.
- **Network & Service Controls**: Cilium enables Layer 7 network filtering. Spiffe/Spire and service meshes address service identity and admittance, while HashiCorp Vault manages secrets delivery.
- **Anchore Engine**: Analyzes container native artifacts, evaluating OS packages, NPM/gem/Java dependencies, Dockerfile configurations, and hardcoded secrets. It integrates into Jenkins and works with Kubernetes admission controllers (including mutating controllers) to enforce image deployment rules.
- **Falco Architecture**: Falco utilizes a kernel module to capture low-level system call streams, which are filtered using Sysdig libraries and evaluated against rule files containing macros and lists. Out of the box, Falco provides 25 core rules detecting conditions such as writes to `/bin` or `/etc`, shell execution, namespace manipulation, or unexpected outbound connections.
- **Playbooks & SIEM Integration**: In an event-driven setup, Falco alerts publish to NATS topics categorized by severity. Kubeless serverless functions consume these alerts to execute remediation actions, such as killing an offending pod, tainting a worker node, or isolating a pod via network policy. Furthermore, events can be aggregated into an EFK stack (Elasticsearch, Fluentd, Kibana) for dashboarding and forensic review.

### Takeaways
Securing Kubernetes requires automated defense in depth across the build and runtime stages. By validating artifacts early with tools like Anchore and monitoring system calls continuously at runtime using Falco, security teams can establish baseline behavior and trigger automated, granular remediation using lightweight functions without disrupting cluster operations.

talks.title: SCORE Bot: Shift Left, at Scale! - Vidhu Jayabalan - Laksh Raghavan
talks.teaser: Walks through PayPal's deployment of a bot that flags company-specific vulnerabilities in pull requests during code review.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe the problem at PayPal, where more than 4,000 developers work across many languages and internal frameworks. Standard code review tends to focus on style and function, while generic scanners miss company-specific issues such as deprecated internal crypto APIs, problems in logging platforms, and deviations from internal security standards. IDE plugins were hard to keep consistent across many editors, and writing custom static analysis rules took weeks, so the team wanted feedback that arrives within seconds without developers installing or configuring anything.

The solution, called SCORE Bot, runs automatically when a pull request is opened. It scans the changed code and posts a comment that names the affected file, explains the issue in the context of the code, gives step-by-step fix instructions and reference documents, and sends an email with the same details. The merge button is disabled until the finding is fixed or a waiver is requested, and the security team can block releases that contain critical findings. In a live demo, the presenter ran the scanner locally through their developer pipeline tool, then opened a pull request that failed on a deprecated crypto utility and became mergeable again after a waiver was submitted.

The team reported end-to-end visibility across stacks, which lets them spot teams that lag on upgrades and run focused training. Roughly a thousand pull requests were tracked for a legacy C++ stack, with findings trending down over the period shown. The bot returns comments in under a second and runs about 25 checks. The main takeaways are to balance enforcement with developer empathy, to shift checks as early as possible using containerized tools, and to recognise that static checks suit company-specific rules better than dynamic issues. The team also plans to open source a generic rules engine later.

talks.title: Value Driven Threat Modeling - Avi Douglen
talks.teaser: AppSecUSA 2018 investigates Value Driven Threat Modeling - Avi Douglen.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Avi Douglen addresses the cultural and operational divide between security teams and software developers. With an industry ratio of roughly one security professional for every 100 developers, centralized security teams cannot scale to review every piece of code or architecture change. Traditional threat modeling methodologies—such as STRIDE, Attack Trees, and PASTA—are often too heavyweight, waterfall-oriented, and slow for modern agile sprints. Douglen argues that if security is to scale, developers must perform threat modeling themselves. To make this feasible, threat modeling must shift toward an agile, lightweight approach centered on business value rather than exhaustive attacker modeling.

### Key Topics
- **The Security-Developer Disconnect**: Traditional security approaches demand deep attacker mindset analysis, heavyweight documentation, and weeks-long turnaround times, conflicting with fast two-week agile sprint cadences.
- **Traditional Threat Modeling Frameworks**: Methodologies like STRIDE (Microsoft), Attack Trees, and PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) provide high assurance and thoroughness but do not fit smoothly into lightweight developer workflows.
- **Reframing the Four Core Questions**: Adapting Adam Shostack's four foundational threat modeling questions into value-focused developer questions:
  1. *Why are we building this?* (Identifying business value, revenue, or safety impact rather than just re-analyzing known architecture).
  2. *What needs to happen to make sure we achieve that value?* (Defining explicit conditions and failure states for success).
  3. *How do we ensure those conditions actually happen?* (Translating security countermeasures into explicit functional assumptions, validations, and unit tests).
  4. *Did we do a good enough job?* (Evaluating sufficiency within the agile retrospective).
- **Embracing Useful Imperfection**: Embracing the aphorism adapted from modeling philosophy: "All threat models are wrong, some are useful."Douglen argues teams should lean into this reality by prioritizing immediate usefulness to delivery over unattainable theoretical perfection.

### Technical Details & Implementation Techniques
Douglen outlines concrete integration points for developers within existing agile workflows:
- **Baseline Knowledge & Threat Libraries**: Avoid wasting modeling time on standard code hygiene issues (OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities like SQLi or XSS, or basic transport layer security) that should be handled by templates, baseline libraries, or training.
- **User Story Integration**: Threat modeling occurs directly during discovery or sprint planning per user story/feature rather than as a standalone document.
- **The "Without" Clause**: Adding a constraint clause directly into the standard user story template: *"As a [role], I want [action], so that [value], without [security catastrophe / loss of value]."*
- **Acceptance Criteria & Definition of Done**: Embedding threat models and explicit security acceptance criteria (e.g., account lockouts after specific failed attempts) directly into user stories and automated unit tests.
- **Abuser Stories & Value Piracy**: Reorienting abuser stories to protect core business assets (e.g., stealing customer orders/juice boxes).
- **Threat Pyramids**: Prioritizing defenses logically—addressing high-impact risks (remote code execution, direct monetary theft) before lower-tier concerns (denial of service, spam).
- **"Sorry Points" for Risk Escalation**: Using a relative risk-scoring mechanism ("sorry points") to measure how disastrous failure would be, helping developers determine whether a story can be modeled independently or requires escalation to security champions or dedicated specialists.
- **Translating Vulnerabilities to Business Impact**: Communicating findings in terms of value (e.g., translating CSRF into "unallocated cash transfers" or authorization bypass into "diverted product shipments").

### Takeaways & Trade-Offs
Value-driven threat modeling offers speed, scalability, native agile integration, and better alignment with developer priorities. However, Douglen acknowledges clear trade-offs: it does not produce complete threat models, lacks high assurance, and may miss subtle threats. High-consequence environments like banking core systems or defense projects will still need rigorous formal reviews. Nevertheless, for day-to-day agile development, empowering developers to perform imperfect, value-focused threat modeling is far superior to performing no threat modeling at all.

talks.title: OWASP Amass Project
talks.teaser: Shows how the Amass project maps an organization's external attack surface through DNS enumeration and network graph visualization.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads the OWASP Amass project, explains why it exists. After repeatedly being asked for network diagrams that customers could not provide, he wanted a single way to see an organization's external footprint as an adversary would. Amass focuses on in-depth DNS enumeration to map an organization's namespace. It combines name permutation, reverse DNS sweeping and scraping the internet for names, and it runs passive data sources first before moving to active techniques such as zone transfers, certificate grabbing and brute forcing.

The talk walks through the tool suite, which now includes the core discovery tool, a local transform for an external graph tool, a database handler with Neo4j support, and a visualization tool. A live example shows how each discovered network can feed further discovery, and how the output can be rendered as interactive graphs where structure hints at shared services and relationships between organizations. Recent changes include adaptive rate limiting per resolver and a default mode that needs no API keys.

The closing section covers the roadmap: more consistent results, broader package support, better documentation and video material, and more contributors. Audience questions touched on who uses the tool, with bug bounty hunters, red teamers, OSINT analysts and blue teams all reporting value. The main takeaway is that knowing your external attack surface is a prerequisite for both defending it and assessing it.

talks.title: OWASP IoT Top 10
talks.teaser: Walks through the draft OWASP IoT Top 10 list and the room's feedback on how its ranking should change.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces the OWASP IoT security project, an umbrella that includes the IoT Top 10, general IoT vulnerability lists, recommendations, an ICS-focused effort and a planned reference architecture. The Top 10 is meant as a list of practices to avoid rather than a strict ranking of vulnerabilities, threats or risks. The draft was built from real-world vulnerabilities gathered from public databases, bug bounty data and contributors' internal findings, weighted by how often each appeared, and checked against many recent IoT guidance documents.

The draft currently leads with weak passwords, followed by insecure network services, insecure access interfaces, insecure outdated components, lack of a secure update mechanism, privacy protection, data transfer and storage weaknesses, physical hardening and device management. Compared with the 2014 edition, passwords moved to the top, cloud, mobile and API access were merged, and storage was folded into transport. The audience pushed back on several points: updatability was argued to be the most important foundation, impact may matter more than ease of attack in industrial settings, access methods could be split again, and supply chain should be named explicitly. Physical hardening and insufficient security configurability were questioned, while root of trust and least privilege were suggested as missing items.

The team treats the list as an open draft and invites further feedback through its OWASP Slack channel. The main takeaway is that the ranking is still changing, with ordering, category merges and manufacturer-focused items all under discussion.

talks.title: Making Security Approachable for Developers and Operators - Armon Dadgar
talks.teaser: Shows how platforms, middleware and frameworks can take security burdens like secrets and encryption off application developers.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why application developers feel security is effortless, and argues that the traditional castle-and-moat model hid network trust from them. That model assumes insiders are trustworthy and the perimeter filters perfectly, and the speaker says both assumptions fail at scale. The Equifax breach, which began with an outdated dependency on a public-facing application, and the Target breach, which spread from an HVAC system across a flat network to databases, show how one foothold can lead to lateral movement.

Zero trust shifts work onto applications. Secrets must be centralized, encrypted and audited rather than scattered across code and wikis, and sensitive data should be encrypted at the application layer, since transparent disk encryption still decrypts for any authenticated query. Services also need caller identity, explicit authorization and encrypted traffic. The speaker shows how cipher documentation overwhelms newcomers with jargon about modes and padding, and notes that code using a zero initialization vector still compiles.

The proposed answer is to split concerns across layers and specialists instead of expecting a super developer. Platforms can deliver secrets and enforce mutual TLS through proxies, key management services can offer encrypt and decrypt APIs so keys never reach application code, and frameworks guard against common web flaws. Security teams can write rules about logical services rather than millions of IP firewall rules. The takeaway is to motivate security by explaining real risks and to accept simpler explanations when people are new.

talks.teaser: Walks through OWASP's chapter and project network, finances, staff roles, and process changes for its leaders.
talks.summary:
This OWASP leaders workshop at AppSecUSA 2018 opened with a level-setting overview of the foundation for chapter and project leaders. It covered the core purpose and values, the three pillars of tools, education and community, the roles of the staff team, and the size of the chapter and project network. Income was shown to come mostly from global conferences and membership, while operating expenses ran above income.

Much of the session focused on money and process. The presenters explained that regional event income is split 90/10 in the foundation's favor, a change from an earlier 60/40 arrangement, and asked the community to help set the right level. They described monthly reconciliation of JIRA tickets and chapter and project balances, accrual accounting that recognizes revenue when invoices are issued, and a planned cleanup of the many event platforms in use. Requests were moving from Salesforce cases into JIRA service desk.

Questions from the floor covered out-of-date wiki entries, a request for a shared email alias for leadership changes, which could not replace named approvers for reimbursements, and a proposal to limit each chapter to three official points of contact. Leaders were told to update the wiki or send changes through the contact form. The takeaway was to keep chapter and project records current and route requests through official channels while the foundation consolidates its systems.

talks.title: Exploiting Unknown Browsers and Objects
talks.teaser: Shows an inspector that enumerates browser JavaScript objects to surface cross-domain and Java bridge flaws.
talks.summary:
Gareth Heyes, a researcher at PortSwigger, starts from a common problem: when a browser or embedded rendering engine ships without developer tools, it is hard to see which objects are exposed and which security protections apply. He presents an Inspector built on his earlier capability-testing page. It ranks interesting objects first, detects window and cross-domain window objects, and identifies function and object constructors, since these can lead to arbitrary code execution or access across origins.

He then goes through bugs that this approach helped uncover. In Safari, overwriting the location host property sent the query string to another origin, and replacing parent and top with alert allowed cross-origin calls. A Microsoft flaw leaked the closed property across constructors, enabling universal XSS. Firefox failed to check the location of a Twitter list page, which exposed user IDs, and a Safari about:blank issue let a local file read content from other sites. For Java bridges in an embedded browser, the Inspector checks for getClass and hashCode, tests whether it can create a socket, and generates a proof of concept. He also showed how a missing annotation check on a referenced object still allowed remote code execution.

Heyes ran live demos of the Java bridge and a Safari exception that leaked an origin. He noted that some checks still need manual analysis, and he described a blind mode for pages that cannot be interacted with, plus uses for probing sandboxes. The takeaway is to enumerate objects systematically and test cross-domain boundaries when no developer tools are available.

talks.title: Prepare(): Introducing Novel Exploitation Techniques in Wordpress
talks.teaser: Shows how design flaws in WordPress core's database helpers enable SQL injection and PHP object injection through plugins.
talks.summary:
WordPress powers a large share of websites, and its core is well covered by a bug bounty program, so the speaker looks at design flaws in the core that plugins can expose. He starts with the built-in defenses, including CSRF tokens, context-aware sanitizers, and WordPress's own prepared-statement implementation. Many plugins depend on that custom implementation because moving them to PDO would require rewriting a lot of code.

The first technique is a "double prepare" pattern, where the output of one prepare call is passed into a second one. In WordPress versions before 4.8.3, a placeholder inside user input could break out of the quoting applied by the second call and inject SQL. WordPress's fix replaces percent signs with a long random token before queries are built. The speaker then shows a second technique that depends on that patch. WP_Query results are cached by serializing the object into the database. A WooCommerce product-list shortcode passes user input into a WP_Query argument, so the token survives serialization and the stored string length no longer matches its contents. By adjusting the length fields, an attacker can inject a PHP object, demonstrated as authenticated remote code execution, and similar patterns were reported in unauthenticated plugins.

The talk closes with a short video of an author-level flaw in media deletion, where thumbnails stayed on disk after the original file was removed, and the speaker explains how this could be abused to reset an installation. For plugin developers, the takeaways are to avoid hand-built SQL with user input, avoid unserialize on user-controlled data, and prefer JSON encoding where possible. Caching whole objects is a core design issue that is hard to remove because of backward compatibility.

talks.title: Serverless Security: Functions-as-a-Service (FaaS) by Niels Tanis
talks.teaser: Explains how Functions-as-a-Service changes the attack surface, monitoring, secrets handling and deployment risks for developers.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from how software architecture has moved from monolithic applications to microservices and then to Functions-as-a-Service, where small, stateless, short-lived functions run in response to events and are billed per execution. The speaker sets out these definitions so the audience shares the same vocabulary, then reviews the benefits, such as no servers to maintain and vendor-managed patching.

The security discussion covers the downsides. A compromised function may only keep persistence for the short lifetime the platform allows, but data can still be exfiltrated. Denial of service shifts from the infrastructure to the application, where heavy event load drives cost and pressure on downstream services. Event-driven chains are harder to map, log and correlate than a single monolith. The speaker points to insecure code in sample applications, including unsanitized log input and SQL injection, and to risky third-party dependencies, such as a compromised npm package. Storing secrets in environment variables exposes them to anyone who compromises a function, so a vault that grants each function only the secrets it needs is preferable. Encryption at rest and in transit, and least-privilege roles instead of wildcard access, are also highlighted.

The closing message is that deployment-as-code pipelines are part of the attack surface and need gates. Threat modeling, isolating environments, monitoring for anomalies and automating configuration help teams act quickly when something changes. The platform abstracts the infrastructure, but it does not remove the need for security design.

talks.title: APPSEC Cali 2018 - Robots with Pentest Recipes
talks.teaser: Shows how to wrap ZAP, Nmap and Selenium tests in Robot Framework keywords to automate application security checks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why application security struggles to keep up with continuous delivery pipelines. The speaker describes small AppSec teams being overwhelmed by security reviews, threat modeling and bug bounty triage across many agile teams. Security tools are also hard to automate, since their APIs are often poorly documented or behave differently than described. Custom flaws tied to business logic, such as authorization problems, are usually missed by standard scanners and end up as PDF reports or tickets.

As a proposed answer, the speaker introduces Robot Framework, an open-source keyword-driven test framework, and argues that QA and engineering teams can run security checks alongside their Selenium tests. Tools are wrapped as keywords, with integrations for ZAP and Nmap and others in progress. A demo test suite started ZAP as a proxy, ran login and functional steps through it, launched an active scan, then wrote out a JSON report. A web service example showed the same approach for APIs, where spidering does not work well. Results come out as HTML and JSON with pass or fail status for each step.

The later part covered a pentest pipeline that chains Nmap, a browser login through ZAP and report generation, and the idea of converting a pentester's custom authorization finding into a regression script that fails until the bug is fixed. The speaker also said a large Selenium suite was converted to Robot in a short time and that the scripts can run from Jenkins on a schedule. The takeaway is that teams can turn one-off findings into repeatable checks and lower the barrier for engineers to test for security.

talks.title: Threat Modeling Toolkit
talks.summary:
The talk presents a practical threat modeling toolkit for application security work. The speaker treats threat modeling as a design-stage activity that clarifies how a system works for reviewers, and stresses that it should be collaborative, since talking through a model with other people is what surfaces mistakes and gaps.

The first component is a simplified flow diagram, drawn with Microsoft-style notation of actors, processes, data stores, flows and trust boundaries. Rather than diagramming everything, the speaker focuses it on the attack surface, labels protocols and adds notes on open questions. A security control checklist sits alongside, marking each control as done or missing so teams can see the gaps against the diagram. The worked example is a personal cryptocurrency setup with a software wallet, a browser, a mobile app and an exchange website and API. While mapping the wallet, the speaker found a JSON-RPC endpoint that answered requests without authentication.

The second component is an attack tree. The attacker's goal sits at the root, sub-goals branch below it with AND and OR gates, and concrete vulnerabilities form the leaves. The example goal is stealing cryptocurrency, which splits into wallet access, exchange access and market manipulation, and the speaker stops digging once a branch is deep enough. Trees can be written as code with PlantUML, which makes them easy to rearrange, and controls from the flow diagram can be mapped onto the sub-goals they mitigate. The main takeaways are to keep the scope narrow, accept that any model will be incomplete, and use these artifacts to bring developers, architects and security staff into the same conversation.
