talks.title: AppSec EU15 - Simon Bennetts - OWASP ZAP: More Advanced Features
talks.teaser: Explains OWASP ZAP 2.4.0's new features and the planned move toward a multi-user service version.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OWASP ZAP, a free and open source web application security scanner aimed at beginners as well as professionals and developers. The speaker covers common usage patterns, from point-and-shoot scanning to manual proxying before scanning, and automated security regression tests run in continuous integration.

The main section walks through version 2.4.0. Changes include a startup prompt to persist sessions, fewer default tabs with pinning, and a context dialogue for scope and application characteristics. Attack dialogues now offer advanced options, scan policies give fine-grained control over thresholds and attack strength, and a new Attack Mode keeps scanning newly discovered content as the user browses. The fuzzer was reworked around fuzz locations, payload sources and processors, including scripts. The API can run several spider and scanner jobs concurrently, and alpha add-ons cover access control testing and sequence scanning.

The closing section outlines the next steps: a bug fix release, new scan rules, a GitHub migration, and a planned ZAP as a service direction with an enterprise database, multiple users and roles, a web interface, and a 99.99% uptime target. Database independence work already in the trunk adds a low memory option and MySQL support that can be used before the service is finished. Desktop ZAP will continue. Practitioners should update to 2.4.0 and can start using the API and shared databases now.

talks.title: AppSec EU15 - Greg Patton - The API Assessment Primer
talks.teaser: Explains a practical approach to assessing APIs and the common flaws that turn up in them.
talks.summary:
APIs now sit behind phones, connected devices, enterprise thick clients and service-oriented back ends, and security is often an afterthought in rushed releases. The session outlines a high-level assessment approach: gather source code, documentation and known-good requests, capture runtime traffic, and map every method the API exposes. Testers need one tool to capture traffic and another to craft and resend requests, and should try other HTTP verbs and content types, since responses can change.

The bulk of the talk covers recurring flaws. Mobile backends often skip authentication, run outdated frameworks, or keep sessions alive with no logout. Information leakage appears when responses return whole datasets or detailed errors. One conference app exposed every attendee's personal details through a single method, and a mobile app returned other customers' password hashes when IDs were enumerated. Undocumented verbs reveal hidden functionality, missing object-level checks expose other users' orders, and plain HTTP logins leak credentials. Injection still applies to APIs, and hardcoded keys in app binaries or public repositories get abused quickly. One developer's cloud keys, pushed to GitHub for only five minutes, led to a bill over 2,000 dollars.

The takeaways: think like an abuser, return only the data a client needs, validate parameters on the server, guard API keys, and lean on OWASP resources.

talks.title: AppSec EU15 - Matt Tesauro - Lessons From DevOps: Taking DevOps Practices Into Your AppSec Life
talks.teaser: Shows how DevOps workflow, automation and feedback loops can make application security faster and more useful to the business.
talks.summary:
Matt Tesauro opens with the problem facing application security teams in fast-moving software shops. At Rackspace, one product group averaged 75 deploys a week, which left no dedicated security testing window, and end-of-cycle testing stopped working. Python and OpenStack code offered little static analysis, and many REST APIs were hard to test programmatically.

He argues that AppSec should borrow DevOps thinking, framed around the workflow, feedback and experimentation ideas from The Phoenix Project. He describes an AppSec pipeline he built at Pearson. Requests enter through an inventory app, are triaged by risk into automated and manual activities that run in parallel, and feed into ThreadFix, which deduplicates and normalizes findings and serves as the source of truth for metrics. Tool setup is scripted, and the process is designed to grow over time so that bottlenecks can be found and automated.

Practical habits include turning manual steps into repeatable scripts, giving developers small tests to verify their own fixes, filing findings directly into bug trackers instead of PDF reports, and setting SLAs for a mitigation plan rather than a fix date. Overdue findings are escalated through management. He also covers hardened configuration management recipes, post-deployment checks, host audit tools and tracking vendor security announcements. The takeaway is to fix workflow paper cuts first, reduce false positives, and learn to speak developers' language.

talks.title: AppSec EU15 - Christian Schneider - Security DevOps
talks.teaser: Shows how to wire open-source web scanners such as ZAP and Arachni into Jenkins builds for automated security checks.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a bottleneck in agile and DevOps releases: security teams cannot manually test every rollout, so routine checks need to run automatically inside the build chain. The speaker presents a security DevOps maturity model with belt-style levels and focuses on two axes, dynamic depth and consolidation of findings. Manual penetration testing remains necessary; automation is meant to free testers for harder problems.

For dynamic depth, the first level scans the public attack surface from a nightly Jenkins job using the ZAP plugin, with Arachni, BDD Security and Gauntlet as alternatives. The next level covers authenticated areas: a ZAP context stores login form details and logged-in indicators, the saved session file is kept in the repository, and Arachni's auto-login or a Selenium-based login class in BDD Security achieves the same result. Higher levels cover backend REST and SOAP calls by proxying traffic between the application and its services, and targeted workflow scanning by routing existing Selenium tests through ZAP while triggering attacks via its API.

For consolidation, the speaker suggests publishing HTML reports to the build first, then failing builds only on high-severity, high-confidence XPath matches to avoid alert fatigue. The final step is deduplicating results from several tools with ThreadFix before pushing them to bug trackers. The main takeaway is that the early levels are cheap to adopt, and that recordings of existing QA tests can make deeper scans practical.

talks.title: AppSec EU15 - Joshua Corman - Continuous Acceleration: Why Continuous Everything Requires A Suppl...
talks.teaser: Argues that software supply chain hygiene and fast patching are needed to keep cars, medical devices and industrial systems safe.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software is spreading into cars, medical devices and industrial control systems faster than it can be secured. The speaker points to Heartbleed, where about 600,000 servers responded as vulnerable on the first day and many were still unpatched more than a year later, and to embedded devices that cannot be patched at all. He likens the problem to building codes: the harm from a failure depends on the protections in place, not only on the size of the threat.

Using automotive examples, he presents a five-part framework from the Cavalry group covering safety by design, third-party coordinated disclosure, evidence capture, prompt updates, and segmentation with isolation. He cites BMW fixing a remotely exploitable flaw over the air before customers were harmed, and notes that many automakers cannot update vehicles quickly. On the software supply chain side, a Bouncy Castle flaw fixed years earlier was still pulled into about 650,000 applications, and an Apache Struts bug affected many banks at once. A study of open source dependencies found that only 41 percent of known vulnerable components were ever fixed, with a mean time to repair near 390 days.

He connects this to DevOps, arguing that fewer, better-vetted suppliers and traceability of which parts went where, borrowed from Toyota's manufacturing approach, can cut unplanned work and speed remediation. Practical steps include tracking the components and versions you ship, patching known vulnerabilities first, and planning for updates from the start, as in proposed US federal rules requiring a bill of materials.

talks.title: Building a Modern Security Engineering Organization - Zane Lackey
talks.teaser: Explains how a security team can keep pace with continuous deployment by building trust, feedback loops and goal-driven attack simulations.
talks.summary:
Drawing on about three years building security teams at Etsy, the talk looks at how deployment has moved from slow, gated releases to near-instant pushes, with more people holding production access. The speaker argues that sign-off gates get routed around, and that continuous deployment is made safe by visibility: graphs of business and error metrics displayed where the wider engineering organization can see them, including a TV showing attack spikes.

On culture, the advice is to treat developers with empathy, reward good security behaviour, explain why an issue matters rather than listing raw counts, and build relationships with informal team leads who can route questions to security. For production access, the method is to take away access without taking away capability: find out why engineers SSH into servers, such as to read error logs, build a safer alternative like central logging, then alert on and gradually restrict the old path. Bug bounty programs are presented as a way to invite safe reporting and shorten remediation time, though the first few weeks are intense and money is rarely the main motivator.

For testing, the talk contrasts vulnerability-enumerating pentests with goal-oriented attack simulations, where a red team pursues objectives such as reaching domain admin, with a cutout to manage risk and varied attacker profiles. Practitioners should record expectations before a program launches, track bug counts and remediation time against them, and record attack paths to guide monitoring and detection investment.

talks.title: Fixing XSS with Content Security Policy - Ksenia Dmitrieva
talks.teaser: Explains how Content Security Policy can limit cross-site scripting and what it takes to deploy it on existing sites.
talks.summary:
The talk covers why cross-site scripting remains hard to stop with input validation and output encoding alone, especially DOM-based XSS, where the payload never reaches the server. It walks through reflected, stored and DOM-based examples, including inline script, third-party script injection and eval-style code, to show how the browser ends up trusting attacker code.

Content Security Policy is introduced as a server-sent HTTP header that lists allowed sources for each resource type, such as scripts, images, frames and connections. The browser enforces the list, or falls back to the same-origin policy when the header is unsupported. The speaker explains default-src behavior, violation reports sent to a report endpoint, and report-only mode for testing a policy without breaking pages. Differences between browsers in report formats and in how Firefox exposes full URLs are noted, along with the privacy concerns that follow.

Adoption is still low: a 2013 study of the top websites found only a few hundred using CSP, and most of those kept unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval, which largely undermines protection. Twitter was cited as an example that loaded all its scripts from a single domain. The main obstacle is externalizing inline JavaScript and replacing inline event handlers with listeners, which is costly for legacy code. Nonce and hash sources in the CSP 1.1 draft help but do not cover eval or DOM-generated script, so practitioners should start with report-only policies, remove unsafe keywords and plan the refactor.

talks.title: Node.js application (in)security - Ilja van Sprundel
talks.teaser: OWASP AppSec California 2015 investigates Node.js application (in)security - Ilja van Sprundel.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how Node.js applications go wrong, seen through a security reviewer's eyes. Node runs server-side JavaScript on Google's V8 engine, and a basic app takes only a few lines. The speaker frames the bugs as familiar vulnerability classes showing up in a new environment.

Web issues come first. Cross-site scripting needs output escaping, which a community validation module can supply. SQL injection is rarer because many apps choose NoSQL stores, yet MySQL drivers fed concatenated input still fall to it, and a Yahoo Query Language injection turned up on GitHub. Cross-site request forgery has no built-in defense, so a maintained library beats custom token code. Response splitting only works through header names. Classic problems include eval on user strings, command injection via child_process exec, argument injection through spawn, and path traversal in file serving.

The platform-specific part covers pseudo-random bytes, which the docs label non-cryptographically strong, and token libraries that rely on them, a mismatch the speaker traced to OpenSSL wrappers with no easy fix. Logging untrusted data through console.log can inject terminal escape sequences, so hex-escaping non-printable characters is the suggested wrapper. Buffer allocations can expose uninitialized heap memory, a Heartbleed-style risk, and out-of-bounds float and double writes succeed despite the docs. The takeaway: validate input, use prepared statements, keep untrusted data away from eval and shell calls, and handle Buffer carefully.

talks.title: .NET Reversing and Exploitation for Cool Kids - Kelly Lum
talks.teaser: OWASP AppSec California 2015 investigates .NET Reversing and Exploitation for Cool Kids - Kelly Lum.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces .NET reverse engineering and exploitation for an audience already familiar with Java and web bugs. It explains how code written in any .NET language compiles to Common Intermediate Language, stored in easy-to-parse metadata tables, which makes decompilation straightforward. The speaker then surveys common obfuscation techniques such as string encryption, control flow changes, symbol renaming, tamper detection and assembly encryption, and notes that strong name signatures are rarely checked by default.

The middle of the talk covers .NET-specific attack surface. Reflection lets runtime changes to types, properties and methods alter program behavior when untrusted data influences them. The legacy Code Access Security model decides permissions by walking the call stack, while .NET 4 adds security transparency levels (transparent, safe critical and critical), with Global Assembly Cache code always running at full trust. A worked example shows a trusted call chain in the security exception code, where a failed permission demand converts objects to XML and can run attacker-supplied code at full trust. Other historical bugs mentioned include a remoting type filter check, IRI parsing, a ClickOnce installer communication flaw, and framework assemblies without ASLR.

To close, the speaker modifies the IL of a Global Assembly Cache image, turns off the strong name bypass registry setting, and precompiles a replacement native image, then shows the altered output on a compromised machine. Practitioners should take away the value of validating strong names, auditing reflection that depends on user input, reviewing where transparent code reaches critical code, and watching for changes to the strong name bypass setting as a sign of tampering.

talks.title: Catch me if you can: Building a Web Malware Analyzer using Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Walks through using machine learning to classify web malware, from honeypot sample collection to clustering and classification tools.
talks.summary:
A Cloudflare researcher explains why signature-based antivirus struggles with web malware on small and medium business sites. Injected JavaScript, PHP and iframes change shape on every infected site, and shared hosting limits how often scans can run. Web malware is framed as the delivery mechanism for later payloads, reaching sites through themes, plugins, outdated CMS installs and weak FTP credentials.

The middle of the talk covers collection and detection. A honeypot runs containerized WordPress, Joomla and Django instances, and a file watchdog sends newly dropped files to a Cuckoo sandbox to record their behaviour. The detection pipeline combines reputation checks on IP and hosting data, antivirus, static analysis of JavaScript structure and variable naming, and dynamic analysis with Rhino JS that follows redirect chains. PyBrain is suggested for clustering unlabelled samples and scikit-learn for classification, with tree-based methods such as random forests recommended as a starting point.

The closing points stress that labelled training data is scarce and costly, and that models need regular retraining by people. Adding features without enough data leads to overfitting. The speaker reports that the approach catches fuzzed iframes and encoded scripts well but is weaker against targeted binaries. Practitioners are urged to harden hosting environments with packaged CMS installs and timely updates.

talks.title: Static Analysis for Dynamic Assessments
talks.teaser: Shows how dynamic web testers can run static analysis tools on the client-side files they collect while browsing a target.
talks.summary:
Greg Patton, a dynamic web tester at HP Fortify on Demand, starts from a gap he sees often: static and dynamic assessments are usually run by different teams at different times, and dynamic testers rarely receive source code. Dynamic scanners also tend to miss DOM-based and other client-side JavaScript issues, while static tools can flag some of them without a full codebase.

He presents Ripa, a Windows utility he wrote with a colleague. The workflow is to browse the target through Burp Suite, save the selected items as an XML file, and let Ripa parse that file, strip the HTTP headers and write the response bodies to local folders grouped by file type, such as JavaScript, HTML, PDF and DLL. In a demo against a conference website, the extracted files were run through Fortify SCA. The results included insecure randomness from Math.random calls, possible hardcoded passwords that were mostly in comments, and a login password field with autocomplete enabled. He also showed searching the extracted files for customer-specific strings.

He says the approach has helped most with DOM-based cross-site scripting and with pulling out Silverlight XAP packages for decompilation. His advice is that testers should run static tools on the presentation-layer files they already collect, and use those results to guide content discovery before testing. He closed by asking for feedback on whether the technique should become a Burp or ZAP extension.

talks.title: Cloud Security at Scale and What it Means for Your Application
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix secures a large AWS environment using chaos tooling, immutable images and open-source security tools.
talks.summary:
Ben Hagen, engineering manager of the cloud security tools and operations team at Netflix, describes how the company secures its large Amazon Web Services footprint. He explains the scale involved, with hundreds of developers pushing code to production many times a day, and why Netflix leaves security decisions to application teams rather than using release gates. Services are deployed as immutable images with an average instance lifetime of under three days, so changes are made by building new images instead of altering running servers.

The middle of the talk covers the tooling. Chaos Monkey randomly terminates instances, and larger chaos exercises take down an entire availability zone so that teams build resilient services. Security Monkey records configuration changes over time and alerts on risky settings, such as security groups open to the internet or users without two-factor authentication. Other projects were presented for scanning at scale through chained plugins, ranking application risk from dependencies and data access, tracking IP intelligence, auditing security groups across regions and accounts, monitoring mentions of the company online, and taking screenshots of unknown sites safely.

To close, Hagen summarized the theme: make developers face failure, keep configurations consistent, and maintain an audit trail. Many of the tools are open source, while the scanning framework was still internal. Audience questions covered network segmentation for compliance, console access through federated single sign-on, and predictive autoscaling.

talks.title: DevOps and Security: The Facts, The Myths, The Legend
talks.teaser: Busts common myths about DevOps and security, covering separation of duties, change management, and auditor concerns.
talks.summary:
The talk takes on the widespread belief that DevOps undermines security. The speaker argues that many of the concerns are myths and focuses on which risks deserve attention. He says automated deployment does not break separation of duties, because no one logs into servers to push code by hand. The real issue is change management: automated pipelines give a far tighter record of who changed what and when, and pre-approved automated actions can be broader but still controlled. He also argues that security does not disappear in DevOps but moves into the pipeline, where security tests can be built into unit, functional and integration testing.

The middle of the talk covers code complexity and release size. Small, frequent changes keep code simpler, which makes vulnerabilities and bugs easier to find, and make failures easier to troubleshoot and roll back. Fast feedback from automated tests also lets developers fix problems while the context is still fresh. The speaker separates ITIL's bureaucracy from its principles, and points to Facebook's process, where every change is code reviewed and a release team schedules deployments through an automated check-in. Configuration management tools such as Chef and Puppet can serve as an auditable inventory and reverse unauthorized changes.

The closing section addresses auditors. The speaker says the friction is largely an education problem: teams should explain automated controls, show audit trails, and confirm early that auditors have authority to accept compensating controls. His takeaway is to treat DevOps as a cultural shift to engage with rather than resist, and to automate repetitive work so security staff can focus on harder problems.

talks.title: Hacking the Oracle Application Framework
talks.teaser: Shows how reverse engineering a huge Java web application's code can expose hidden features and session data.
talks.summary:
David Byrne presents a case study in deep-dive penetration testing, an approach that examines an application's underlying code rather than relying only on surface scanning. The motivating finding came from an engagement against Oracle E-Business Suite: a cookie named OA Developer or OA Diagnostic, set to one, enabled a hidden feature that listed active sessions, including administrator sessions, without any authentication. An attacker could wait for an administrator to log in and then hijack that session. The speaker suggests the flaw survived for years because no one had examined the core of the product.

The talk walks through the workflow on a virtualized test environment with access to the software. Early steps included checking the database, where some password columns were stored in plain text, and inventorying the files behind running processes. Scripts were used to extract archives, drop open-source libraries by matching file hashes against public Maven artifacts, reorganize the hundreds of thousands of classes, and decompile them. Several analysis strategies were compared: hunting for suggestive filenames, an advanced grep that flagged unvalidated request parameters and surfaced about 150 cross-site scripting cases in JSPs, and static analysis with FindBugs, which reported a path traversal that proved hard to reach. Other approaches included working backward from database calls to spot SQL injection candidates and reviewing application logs during testing.

The main takeaway is that source access lets testers find flaws that black-box scanning misses, but each method carries trade-offs in false positives, dead ends and time. Because a large application cannot be tested exhaustively, target selection largely determines what a tester will find.

talks.title: Clientside security with the Security Header Injection Module SHIM
talks.teaser: Shows how the SHIM module adds security headers to ASP.NET sites through web.config, with live demos of the attacks they block.
talks.summary:
The OWASP Secure Headers project aims to make people aware of HTTP response headers that harden browsers against common attacks. This session presented SHIM, an HTTP module for ASP.NET that sets these headers from web.config, with no custom code. A demo site first showed a cached page reappearing after navigating back, an injected remote script running, and a page framed by a malicious site. With the module enabled on the safe pages, the cached page was re-requested, the script was blocked by Content Security Policy, and the frame was refused.

Each header was then covered in turn. Cache-Control, Pragma and Expires keep sensitive pages out of caches. X-Frame-Options defaults to deny, with same-origin and allow-from options, though allow-from has weak browser support. HSTS requires HTTPS for a year and can include subdomains, which blunts SSL stripping. X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff and X-XSS-Protection add browser-side checks. Content Security Policy took the most time, and ASP.NET web forms need unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval allowances. Per-path exclusion lists let vulnerable or static content be handled differently.

The main takeaway is that these headers are defense in depth and do not replace output encoding. Their value depends on the browsers a site's users run, so a policy should be built gradually, tested in report-only mode, and checked against real traffic before enforcement.

talks.title: Stephen de Vries - Continuous Security Testing in a Devops World
talks.teaser: Shows how security scans and checks can be written as plain-language tests that run automatically in a CI pipeline.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the gap between continuous delivery and traditional application security. In a pipeline that deploys features many times a day, the usual model of requirements kept in documents and manual scanner runs cannot keep pace. The speaker argues that security testing is close enough to quality testing to attach to the same pipeline, and that tests with explicit pass criteria can serve as living requirements.

The middle of the talk covers the BDD Security framework, an open-source tool that writes security tests as plain-language given/when/then statements backed by Java code. It wraps scanners such as ZAP and Nessus, and adds functional checks for behaviour like case-sensitive passwords, HTTPS login, account lockout and server-side logout. A demo app shows a ZAP scan with a false-positive file, and an access control test that catches one user viewing another user's profile. Navigation logic sits apart from the tests, so the same specifications can be reused across applications. A Jenkins job then rebuilds the app and runs the tests on each commit, linking any new failures to the commit that caused them.

The talk closes with limitations: CSRF tokens hinder automated access control tests, email-driven actions are not supported, and navigation code needs guards that flag unexpected pages. The takeaway is that security checks become repeatable and self-verifying, with false-positive handling and acceptance criteria recorded in code. Two similar tools, Gauntlet and Mittn, are mentioned as scanner-only alternatives.

talks.title: Mark Graham - Cloud-based Detection Techniques for Botnets and Other Malware
talks.teaser: Explains how botnets evade signature antivirus and how DNS and NetFlow traffic analysis can expose them.
talks.summary:
Mark Graham, a PhD student at Anglia Ruskin University, opens by tracing malware from the 1971 Creeper virus, which spread over ARPANET, through worms and trojans to botnets that coordinate thousands of compromised machines for spam, denial of service, banking theft and click fraud. He explains why signature-based antivirus lags behind new malware: a sample must be captured, reverse engineered and fingerprinted, and trivial recompilation or padding can defeat an existing signature. Heuristic scanning fills some of that gap but produces many false positives.

The middle of the talk follows botnet command-and-control design. Early IRC-based bots were easy to block by port, so authors moved to HTTP, then from centralised servers to peer-to-peer and hybrid designs that survive takedowns. Evasion methods such as fast flux, which rapidly rotates IP addresses, and domain generation algorithms, which produce large numbers of throwaway domains, make DNS record analysis harder. Flow protocols such as NetFlow, IPFIX and sFlow are presented as a traffic-based alternative, with vertical correlation favoured over horizontal correlation to cut noise. Graham then described his group's early work: running Zeus in a virtual environment, cloning infected virtual machines, detecting the spread from flow data, and tracing the command-and-control virtual machine so it could be removed.

The talk closes by noting that signature antivirus still helps against known malware, while traffic-based and cloud-assisted detection is gaining ground. Open questions include where flow probes should sit, how to manage the volume of flow data in real time, and whether big-data services could help. Graham leaves the audience with the question of whether end users or ISPs should be responsible for stopping botnets.

talks.title: Seba Deleersnyder Bart De Win - OpenSAMM Best Practices Lessons from the Trenches
talks.teaser: Shows how the OpenSAMM maturity model guides application security in the SDLC, with lessons learned from real rollouts.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces OpenSAMM, the Software Assurance Maturity Model, as a way to build application security activities into the software development lifecycle step by step rather than through a single top-down push. The speakers argue that many organisations only test for security just before release, which is reactive and misses design flaws. The model groups security practices under business functions such as construction and verification, and each practice has activities across maturity levels with defined results, metrics, costs and dependencies.

The middle of the talk covers applying the model. Assessments work best as interviews or workshops with managers, operations staff and developers rather than questionnaires sent by email, and answers need checking because people respond differently when their manager is present. Goals should follow business drivers such as regulation and risk appetite rather than aiming for top level everywhere. Planning should start with quick wins such as awareness training and match release cycles. Implementation should begin with high-risk applications, leave legacy code for later, and use a central competence group that trains champions instead of becoming a bottleneck.

The closing part gives budget guidance, noting that improvement projects may add roughly 5 to 15 percent in startup costs, with lower ongoing costs once activities are in place. The speakers point to upcoming QuickStart guidance, mappings to other standards, and a self-assessment tool. The main takeaway for practitioners is an iterative approach that starts with assessment, uses scorecards for gap analysis, and tracks measurable results over time.

talks.title: Mark Denihan Sean Duggan - OWASP Security Shepherd
talks.teaser: Mobile Web Security Awareness analyzes Mark Denihan Sean Duggan - OWASP Security Shepherd.
talks.summary:
## Overview

OWASP Security Shepherd is an educational platform created by Mark Denihan and Sean Duggan to teach application security to students. Mark developed the project as a final year project at Dublin Institute of Technology after undertaking a pentesting internship at IBM under Jason Fl, where he struggled to find learning resources geared toward students rather than experienced practitioners. Sean, a year behind Mark in his studies, joined the effort to expand Security Shepherd into mobile platforms as his own final year project. The platform was designed to address a significant gap in computer science education, as top courses in the USA do not adequately cover application security.

## Technical Architecture

Security Shepherd runs on a straightforward stack: Tomcat application server (handling up to 1,700 concurrent users with default settings), MySQL database, ESAPI for encoding, Anti-Samy for XSS prevention, and OWASP CSRFGuard. Every vulnerability implemented is real but with restricted privileges—users complete challenges with credentials that only access the specific level, preventing them from compromising the broader platform. For vulnerabilities like cross-site scripting where real detection is difficult without browser virtualization, Anti-Samy is deployed instead.

## Educational Methodology

The platform employs a graduated learning approach. When students encounter a topic for the first time, they receive a comprehensive lesson written in layman's terms, followed by a simple challenge that essentially walks them through the solution. As progression continues, each subsequent challenge provides less help and introduces bad fixes (security implementations with flaws), forcing students to deepen their understanding. Students learn that reading lessons is necessary to progress, and the reinforcement of concepts through increasingly complex variations is effective—particularly for difficult topics like CSRF.

## CSRF Teaching Example

The CSRF progression demonstrates this approach: Level 1 introduces image-tag attacks with simulated immediate execution; Level 2 escalates to POST requests using iframes; Level 4 introduces weak CSRF tokens that are highly predictable (only values 0, 1, 2), requiring students to send multiple requests to guarantee success. This real-world reflection of broken protections is significantly more effective than theoretical lectures.

## Gamification and Administration

Administrators can enable leaderboards and point systems, where students gain points for completing levels with bonus points for first completion. This gamification dramatically increases engagement, though it sometimes shifts focus from learning to competition. To prevent cheating, keys are user-specific—encrypted with the user's username and a random base key—so sharing answers fails. Administrators can configure the experience granularly: enable/disable module categories, set module blocks to pause progression, provide or hide cheat sheets, and view real-time student progress to identify those struggling.

## Mobile Security (Mobile Shepherd)

Sean created Mobile Shepherd by packaging vulnerable Android applications on Android x86 VirtualBox images. This approach avoids requiring individual app downloads, Android SDK setup, or reliance on slow emulators. Mobile levels cover insecure storage (plain-text credentials in SQLite databases), client-side injection (SQL injection in login fields), and reverse engineering (extracting hardcoded keys from APK files using dex2jar and Java analysis).

## Operational Success

The platform successfully supported major CTF competitions, including ABC Ireland 2012, OWASP Lads online CTF (approximately 600 users), AbstE EU, global CTF, and on-premises competitions in Dublin, Facebook, and Ireland. One instance generated 200 GB of application logs without being compromised.

## Current State and Needs

Security Shepherd currently covers all OWASP Top 10 web application risks and approximately 60% of OWASP mobile risks across roughly 50 levels, progressing from novice to expert difficulty. The project urgently needs community contributions: more bad fix examples, localization/translation support, expansion to iOS and Windows platforms, and improved tooling for custom content integration. The platform is available live at the time of the talk for hands-on exploration.

talks.title: Lorenzo Cavallaro - Keynote - Copper Droid On the Reconstruction of Android Malware Behaviors
talks.teaser: Explains how CopperDroid rebuilds high-level Android malware behavior from system call traces collected in an emulator.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a university researcher, starts from the rapid growth of Android malware, which spans adware, premium SMS and call abuse, fake apps and exploits of the operating system. Signature-based detection no longer keeps up, and dynamic analysis is a practical alternative. Existing dynamic approaches that introspect the Dalvik virtual machine are costly to maintain because the runtime changes between Android versions, as the move to ART shows.

The core idea is to observe only the system calls made by an app, using an emulator based on QEMU that is modified just enough to add instrumentation. The system ties each call to its process and thread by walking kernel structures, then parses Binder ioctl transactions to recover the arguments of inter-process calls. Complex parcelable objects are unmarshalled by a helper emulator that uses Java reflection to find the creator field. A dependency graph links related calls, such as open, mmap and ioctl on the same shared memory, so low-level sequences collapse into higher-level actions like creating a file or sending an SMS.

To improve coverage, the approach triggers components declared in the manifest, such as an SMS receiver or a boot-completed event. Across about 2,900 samples this surfaced around 25 extra behaviors on more than 60 percent of them. On a set of roughly 1,300 malware samples, the share accessing personal information rose from about 40 percent to about 66 percent after stimulation. The speaker stresses that dynamic analysis only sees the paths that get executed, and that the work is an early step. A later release is planned, and the output is meant as a base for machine learning or policy enforcement.

talks.title: Steven Murdoch - Keynote
talks.teaser: Surveys how anonymous communication systems evolved from remailers to Tor and the censorship and sustainability problems they face.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why people need anonymous communication, from activists, journalists and whistleblowers to ordinary users who want to avoid being profiled. It argues that encryption alone is not enough, because traffic metadata such as who talks to whom, when, and how much can still expose them. The speaker traces the history of anonymous systems, starting with early email remailers whose single operator became a tempting target. Cypherpunk and Mixmaster designs then added layered encryption, batching and reordering of messages, and Mixminion added replies, but all of them suffered from long delays and too few users to hide among.

For the web, the talk compares open proxies and VPNs with Tor, describing how each relay removes one layer of encryption as traffic passes through the entry, middle and exit nodes. It then covers censorship. China's attempts to block Tor by fingerprinting its traffic and blocking published relay addresses are described, along with the bridge-distribution methods, such as CAPTCHAs, email and social networks, that work in some countries but not others. Abuse of exit nodes and hidden services is also discussed, including Nymble as an approach to anonymous blacklisting.

The closing sections cover funding and sustainability, including reliance on a single government funder, the risks of paying relays, and the tragedy of the commons when volunteers run the network. The main takeaways are that metadata protection is a hard problem and that Tor will likely need a more peer-to-peer architecture to grow to internet scale.

talks.title: Jerry Hoff - Getting a Handle on Mobile Security
talks.teaser: Argues that server-side risk often outweighs mobile device risk, then covers transport, storage and business logic pitfalls.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Jerry Hoff addresses the growing industry obsession with mobile device security and contrasts it with the reality of application risk. Organizations and executives often overemphasize securing the physical mobile client—likely because it is a tangible, handheld item—while continuing to neglect vulnerable backend server infrastructure. Hoff argues that while mobile security matters, server-side flaws generally pose far greater organizational risk, and security teams must adopt a practical, risk-based approach rather than chasing extreme controls or relying blindly on top-ten compliance lists.

### Key Topics
- **Client vs. Server Risk Allocation**: Evaluating where development time and security budget should actually be spent. Hoff notes that search trends and client demands focus heavily on mobile security, even though server backends remain brittle and harbor severe vulnerabilities.
- **Mobile Development Frameworks & Attack Surfaces**: Mobile apps are built across diverse stacks, from native platforms (Objective-C, Swift, Java, C++) to web-container hybrids like PhoneGap using HTML5 and JavaScript. Technologies that wrap native phone APIs in JavaScript introduce unique risks.
- **App Store Realities & Decompilation**: Exploring the false sense of security provided by app store review processes. Decompiling mobile apps is trivially easy (e.g., using `dex2jar` and `jad` on Android, or analyzing binaries and plist files on iOS), showing that client-side code cannot hide secrets or enforce security rules.

### Technical Details
Hoff highlights three critical foundational areas developers must focus on before considering advanced controls like anti-jailbreaking mechanisms:
1. **Insufficient Transport Layer Protection**: Mobile traffic should strictly use TLS/HTTPS. Developers frequently fail to properly validate certificates or fail to prevent insecure connections in thick clients. Intercepting traffic using local proxies like OWASP ZAP demonstrates widespread insecure communication and data leakage to third parties. Hoff also mentions a PayPal vulnerability involving fetching JavaScript over non-HTTPS connections, which creates remote code execution risks when native wrappers interpret unencrypted scripts.
2. **Unsafe Data Storage on the Device**: Mobile apps routinely scatter data across local storage mechanisms—SQLite databases, SD cards, local file systems, iOS Keychain, user defaults, plist files, and log files. Tools like iFunBox reveal that apps often leave sensitive artifacts accessible on un-jailbroken devices. Hoff references the public reaction to Starbucks storing unencrypted passwords locally. Unless required by strict business models, sensitive data should not reside permanently on lost-prone mobile devices.
3. **Business Logic & Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) on the Device**: Developers often trust client-side state, storing flags like `isPaid` locally in editable plist files or delegating access control choices to client requests. Because client parameters are easily altered via proxies or binary tampering, access control and business logic validation must remain on the server.

Hoff compares these issues against common web vulnerabilities, emphasizing that high-impact threats like SQL injection, broken authentication, and session flaws execute on the server. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is typically less prevalent in native mobile clients than web apps, though hybrid apps using PhoneGap can elevate XSS impacts.

### Takeaways
Security programs should prioritize securing the backend server where the highest organizational damage occurs before over-engineering client-side protections. When developing mobile apps, teams should master the fundamentals—transport encryption, avoiding sensitive local storage, and enforcing business logic and authorization strictly on the server. Developers should view checklists like the OWASP Mobile Top 10 through a risk-based lens, tailoring defenses to their specific risk tolerance rather than treating generic lists as absolute dogma.

talks.title: OWASP Global Webinar - Jack Mannino
talks.teaser: Shows the upcoming GoDroid 1.0 release, its Android flaws such as insecure storage and exported components, and the roadmap.
talks.summary:
The session previews the upcoming 1.0 release of GoDroid, an intentionally vulnerable Android training app from OWASP, and its roadmap. The speaker explains what changed since the first release: documentation was expanded, the Swing front end became a web application, and a PhoneGap app was added beside the native apps. Learners can follow guided lessons with hints and solutions or explore the apps freely.

The demos covered several weaknesses. A login feature stored the password in plain text in a world-readable preferences file. Certificate validation was switched off globally, so a proxy could intercept traffic silently. Cross-site scripting in a web view reached a JavaScript interface that could send SMS without user input. A broadcast receiver sent texts for callers lacking the SMS permission because it had no permission check. Hardcoded admin logic could be recovered by decompiling the app. The PhoneGap configuration enabled powerful plugins and a wildcard origin.

The roadmap includes a preconfigured virtual machine, support for other JavaScript frameworks and languages such as .NET and Ruby, and NFC exercises built on Open NFC. Contributions can be code, feature requests, bug reports or promotion. The takeaway: the OWASP Mobile Top 10 is a starting point, not a full security program, and the master branch remains buggy until 1.0.

talks.title: OWASP Global Webinar - Josh Sokol
talks.teaser: Explains practical risk prioritization and walks through SimpleRisk, a free open-source risk register for tracking and reviewing risks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with personal risk management, using a home burglary and a house fire as examples of risks paired with mitigations such as alarms and smoke detectors. It then moves to business settings, where risks are ranked by likelihood and impact, and the speaker explains why a fixed formula may need weighting to suit an organization. The speaker also separates a risk from an individual vulnerability, noting that several cross-site scripting findings might roll up into one risk about user compromise.

Next comes risk evaluation: deciding whether a risk is acceptable, transferable through insurance, or reducible through controls, with avoidance as the answer when none of those apply. Reviews should recur on a schedule, with high-level risks revisited more often than low ones, and higher-severity items escalated to executives. The speaker argues that enterprise GRC platforms are hard to justify for smaller teams, which is why many organizations fall back on spreadsheets and word documents.

The closing demo walks through SimpleRisk, a free open-source risk register. It shows configurable formulas and review intervals, user roles, an audit trail, CVSS-based scoring on a zero-to-ten scale, mitigation planning, management review, and assignment of risks to projects. The takeaway is that a dynamic, database-backed register works better than static documents, and the tool can be self-hosted or used as a hosted service.

talks.title: OWASP Global Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how the Passal project estimates password strength from detected patterns and ties that estimate to a password policy.
talks.summary:
Cam Morris, project leader for the OWASP Passal project, argues that character-composition rules such as requiring uppercase letters, digits and symbols do not measure real password strength. He presents Passal as a possible replacement for password policy. The analyzer looks for patterns in a password, including dictionary words, dates, leetspeak substitutions, keyboard runs, misspelled words and reversed words. It measures each pattern by how many candidates fit it, then chains the patterns together and picks the weakest combination as a worst-case view in which the attacker already knows the pattern types.

That candidate count is converted into an estimated time to crack, which depends on the hash function protecting the passwords and on the attacker's hardware. In a live demo, a 16-character keyboard-run password that would pass a typical policy scored only about 8 billion candidates. Raising the hash to 100,000 rounds of SHA-512 greatly lengthened the estimate, while a single hash round cut it to about four months. A policy can then be written as a minimum pattern size, based on an assumed attacker and hash and a chosen risk window. Cam also showed a passphrase built from a city name and common words, which scored much higher than the complex-looking string.

He covered the code as well: a Java core library, a JSON service, a command-line interface and an applet, so a password can be analyzed on the user's own machine rather than sent to a server. Planned work includes frequency-ranked wordlists, international keyboards, a JavaScript build and a Linux PAM module. Cam suggested that random words make strong passphrases and invited developers, Linux administrators and other contributors to get involved.

talks.title: Mantra OS: Because the World is Cruel
talks.teaser: Presents Mantra OS, a virtualized sandbox platform for security testing, and demos a certificate-spoofing man-in-the-middle attack.
talks.summary:
Gregory Disney-Leugers, who leads the OWASP Mantra OS project, introduces Mantra as a sandbox attack platform for testing and development that runs on virtualized and cloud hosts such as vSphere and OpenStack, distributed as ISO, OVF and OVA images. It bundles tools from the Mantra security toolkit and the OWASP WTE repository, including ZAP, Metasploit, sqlmap, Wireshark and Ettercap. The speaker describes its layered isolation: grsecurity and OpenVZ containers with LXC, KVM as a second virtualization layer, AppArmor and SELinux, and an IDS with a honeypot for attackers who strike back.

The main demo is Search Stealer, a script the speaker wrote to show how certificate fields can be abused. Using the example of an Akamai-hosted government site, it copies the genuine certificate and root CA, creates a fake certificate authority, and packages the original certificate with a new key into a PKCS12 file to produce a certificate that looks legitimate. Traffic for google.com is then redirected to a fake page carrying a BeEF hook. Chromium still shows a broken-certificate warning, but it lets the connection through because the subject alternative name and issuer key identifier match the real certificate. Each session is logged for later analysis.

In the Q&A, the speaker compares Mantra with BackTrack, noting that Mantra offers similar tools but adds virtualization and sandboxing meant to protect the tester and suit enterprise deployment. The practical takeaway is that browsers may not reject spoofed certificates that reuse matching identifiers, and that isolating offensive tooling matters when testing inside an organization.

talks.title: Michael Coates
talks.teaser: Argues that application security should shift toward secure-by-default frameworks, shared security programs and better metrics.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by reflecting on more than a decade in security, describing the cycle of excitement, alarm and eventual acceptance that many practitioners go through. He points to the Verizon data breach report, which found that most compromises were opportunistic and that most exploited issues were low difficulty. His argument is that teams spend too much effort on exotic threats while basic fundamentals such as injection flaws are still not reliably addressed. He also says the industry lacks published guidance on building a security program, and that application security teams often work in silos, ignoring malware on point-of-sale systems in breaches like Target's because it sits outside their layer.

The middle of the talk makes the case for changing how security is delivered. Developers are measured on features shipped, so asking them to code securely on top of that is misaligned. He proposes pushing security as far left as possible: secure-by-default frameworks first, then security libraries that make the right approach easy, and secure coding guides last. Security teams should only do work that cannot be automated, and any control they add must scale. He also calls for real metrics to show what works, and for pragmatic threat-model thinking rather than absolutist demands for perfect security.

The closing section turns to OWASP as a volunteer-run community with chapters in many countries, a small paid staff, and open projects, including a planned framework security project. Attendees are encouraged to edit the wiki, join local chapters, share what their programs are doing, and volunteer to speak at chapter events.

talks.title: Privacy vs Security Intricacies
talks.teaser: Explores where privacy and security conflict, using everyday examples to show why the two are not the same.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that privacy and security are routinely confused, and that a single technology can help one while harming the other. HTTP Strict Transport Security serves as the main example: it blocks downgrade attacks, but it can also be used as a tracking identifier and can expose referrer data. Judging such a feature requires separating its effects instead of calling it simply good or bad.

The speaker then sorts everyday cases into consumer privacy, consumer security, corporate privacy and corporate security. Searching for financial trouble at work versus at home, updating software, persistent login state, DRM with back doors, and using Tor for anonymity each produce different winners and losers. Advertising incentives, browser ad-blocking disputes, and social media data resold through commercial firehoses show how business models shape the privacy arguments that reach the public, while historical cases of persecution show that exposure can be a safety issue.

The closing advice is to ask who benefits from any position, to be explicit about trade-offs when speaking to journalists, and to build clearer shared vocabulary for privacy and security. The speaker leaves the audience to decide where they stand on conflicts such as corporate livelihood versus consumer privacy.

talks.title: 7 Deadly Sins: Unlock the Gates of Mobile Hacking Heaven
talks.teaser: Walks through intercepting mobile app traffic and the seven recurring authentication flaws behind real app case studies.
talks.summary:
The talk looks beyond the mobile app itself to the web services behind it, which carry the data that matters. The speaker shows how to position a portable Wi-Fi access point as a man-in-the-middle, then inspect traffic in a proxy. Formats such as JSON, REST-style XML, and AMF can look unfamiliar, but classic injection still works against them once decoded and edited.

A fantasy football app serves as the main case. Its web version held up, but the mobile traffic exposed a roster XML document that could be edited to move bench players into starting slots mid-season. Other examples include a replayable unencrypted Twitter request, a backup app that sent hard-coded credentials and used the SIM identifier for authentication, a word game whose dictionary check could be bypassed by replaying a response, a Starbucks app storing credentials in plain text on the device, a Snapchat lookup that allowed phone number enumeration, and a Bump exchange that accepted spoofed locations.

The speaker groups these flaws into seven deadly sins: trusting the client, not requiring encryption, long-lived sessions, not keeping secrets on the device, allowing repeated requests, no time limit on requests, and failing to prevent altered requests. Recommended defenses include TLS with certificate verification, short session lifetimes, nonces, timestamps, and request signing with a key kept on the device, with the server validating every request.

talks.title: HTML5 JS Security - maty siman
talks.teaser: Shows how HTML5 features make old XSS tricks more dangerous, from iframe screenshots to sandbox quirks and client-side game logic.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with cross-site scripting, a long-known flaw, and shows how HTML5 makes it more dangerous. An injected script can keep a vulnerable page running in a hidden frame and use a canvas library to capture screenshots of other pages, including a password field that the presenter briefly switched to plain text during rendering so the captured image revealed it. A WebSocket-based network scan run from the victim's browser can also map internal hosts behind a firewall.

The sandbox attribute comes next. A sandboxed frame is treated like third-party content and cannot run scripts unless allow-scripts is granted. Adding allow-same-origin lets that script reach the parent page, and the presenter showed that Chrome blocked a resulting top-navigation attempt while Firefox allowed it, so the outcome depends on the browser. Client-side logic fared poorly as well: a browser game stored its score in local storage and a cookie, and an intercepting proxy let the presenter change its JavaScript in transit. A final demo tricked a user into granting camera, microphone and location access by placing a decoy cursor over the permission prompt.

The takeaway is that same-origin rules and sandboxing do not guarantee safety, because browsers behave differently. Developers should treat client-side code as user interface only and keep scores, rules and other business logic on the server.

talks.title: Application Security at DevOps Speed and portfolio scale
talks.teaser: Argues that application security must become continuous, automated verification that scales across large application portfolios.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that application security practice has not kept pace with modern development. Annual reviews, penetration tests and scanners struggle with heavy frameworks, dependency-rich builds and non-HTTP protocols, so results arrive long after the code has changed. The speaker proposes continuous, portfolio-wide verification at the speed of DevOps, with the goal of showing that defenses are present, correct and used properly in every application.

The core idea is a "sensor": a small check that tests one positive security property and runs in a test or CI environment. Examples include verifying an X-Frame-Options header against clickjacking, analyzing authorization annotations to build an access control matrix, flagging known vulnerable libraries with OWASP Dependency Check, and confirming CSRF tokens are enforced by replaying requests with ZAP scripts. Test suites for encoding and canonicalization were presented as a way to keep security controls correct, and runtime data flow instrumentation was suggested for finding injection. Sensor data feeds a central warehouse that reports scores per application.

Practitioners are advised to break business concerns down into defense strategies and concrete controls, then compare the expected model with what is actually verified to find untested risks and wasted effort. Start small with the most critical controls, deploy sensors where developers already work, and turn penetration test findings into reusable checks rather than static reports.

talks.title: Revenge of the Geeks: Hacking Fantasy Sports Sites
talks.teaser: Shows how intercepting mobile app traffic exposes weak session handling in fantasy sports and other apps.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many mobile apps expose more risk in the server-side APIs they call than in the app itself. The speaker shows how to watch that traffic by placing a portable Wi-Fi access point between a phone and the internet, then forwarding ports 80 and 443 to an intercepting proxy such as Burp. He covers the data formats that appear along the way, including JSON, REST responses, XML payloads and AMF, and explains that each can be decoded and altered once captured.

Framing the analysis around seven session-management mistakes, he covers trusting the client, skipping encryption, allowing lifetime sessions, storing no secrets, accepting replayed requests, never expiring requests and leaving requests unsigned. A fantasy football app sent plaintext traffic with long-lived session tokens, so a captured token could change another player's lineup. A backup app authenticated devices with an identifier and a shared password, a word game leaked valid words through its responses, and a proximity contact-exchange app could be abused with spoofed coordinates and a race condition.

The closing advice is to authenticate over TLS with certificate validation, keep sessions short, add nonces and timestamps, sign request contents with a key shared at login, and let users list and revoke active sessions. He notes that some vendors fixed the flaws, but older API versions stayed reachable, so practitioners should test every interface an app uses.

talks.title: Contain Yourself: Building Secure Containers for Mobile Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how iOS secure containers wrap existing apps with injected code and where their encryption and authentication fail.
talks.summary:
The talk examines secure containers for iOS, which protect corporate data inside apps on bring-your-own-device phones where the employer cannot enforce device policies. It defines a container as application-layer security and explains application wrapping, where a commercial tool injects a dynamic library into an existing app package, re-signs it, and leaves the original source code untouched. The speaker compares the binary before and after wrapping and shows how the injected library is loaded at launch.

Next the talk covers method swizzling in Objective-C as the mechanism for replacing functions such as the app launch handler, with a demo that inserts a login screen into a sample banking app. It then turns to attacks. A consumer finance app's passcode screen was bypassed on a jailbroken device by dumping class names, hooking the method that dismisses the lock, and calling it from a live interpreter. A password vault that derived its encryption key by hashing the password with SHA-256 was shown to be far faster to brute force than a PBKDF2 setup. Other cases included files copied by document interaction APIs that stayed unencrypted, and cookie storage that a data wipe never cleared.

The closing takeaways are that encryption keys must only be released after successful authentication and never stored beside the data they protect. Offline designs should wrap a master key with a passphrase-derived key using a slow key derivation function. Policy checks should run server-side where possible, since client-side controls can be bypassed. Jailbreak detection raises the effort required but cannot stop malware, and iOS background limits complicate remote wipe.

talks.title: Case Study: 10 Steps to Agile Development without Compromising Enterprise Security
talks.teaser: Shows how a SaaS company embedded security checkpoints and reusable controls into its agile sprints without slowing releases.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the belief that a security development lifecycle cannot fit into agile delivery, where fuzzing seems too slow and fast release cadences seem to leave no room for controls. The speaker presents a case study from LivePerson, a SaaS platform that handles chat data for large regulated customers, with about 22 scrum teams and roughly 200 developers. The approach begins with discovery: mapping how requirements move from sales and product through the software and system architects into the scrum teams, so the security team takes part at every checkpoint instead of reviewing at the end.

During release planning, a high-level security design review looks beyond standard issues such as input validation and session handling to business and compliance concerns. One example is a geolocation feature that would conflict with European data-transfer rules. During development, teams are steered to shared validation utilities instead of writing their own regular expressions, and static analysis checks that code uses them. Each build is scanned for open-source licence problems and known CVEs, and the final artifact is scanned for runtime configuration issues. The CI pipeline fails a build on any high or medium finding, and a tab added to TeamCity points developers to the offending line. Heavier scans on large projects move to nightly builds, and customer-run penetration tests are accepted as a form of transparency.

The takeaways are to engage early, reduce friction with reusable components, automate policy enforcement in CI, and be open with customers. The speaker advises starting with a small project, cutting false positives quickly, and tying security to business needs such as bank customer requirements, which helps management back the decision to break builds.

talks.title: Mobile app analysis with Santoku Linux
talks.teaser: Shows how Santoku Linux supports Android and iOS forensics, app data analysis and malware reverse engineering.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from a mobile security company, introduces Santoku Linux, an Ubuntu-based distribution that bundles open-source tools for mobile forensics, app security testing and malware analysis. He frames data acquisition in three levels, logical, file system and physical, and explains how each trades data depth against the privileges and device changes it requires.

For iOS, he creates a logical backup, which needs the passcode, and browses the output with iPhone Backup Analyzer. For Android, he demonstrates AF Logical, an open-source tool that exports call logs, messages and other content provider data to the SD card without root, then pulls it over ADB. A Texas case shows why physical images matter, since a deleted fake-messaging app and its records were recovered from one. He then turns to popular apps, noting that many failed man-in-the-middle checks and some stored passwords in plain text. In a demo, he pulls an app's data directory and captured traffic and finds credentials in preferences, databases and journal files.

The malware section covers reverse engineering with apktool, dex2jar and JD-GUI. It shows a sample that sideloads further apps, and a Korean banking trojan that altered zip encryption flags to disrupt analysis tools. The main takeaway is to combine static review, data inspection, network capture and dynamic observation when assessing an app, and the tools are open source for others to extend.

talks.title: AppSec at DevOps Speed and Portfolio Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how continuous, positive-model sensors can verify web defenses across large application portfolios at devops speed.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that traditional application security methods, such as periodic penetration tests, manual code review and static scanning, cannot keep pace with modern frameworks, custom protocols and fast release cycles. Framing the problem as public health, the speaker aims to eliminate common flaws across a whole population of applications. The target is confidence that defenses are present, correct and used properly everywhere, with feedback arriving continuously.

The main demonstration is a clickjacking sensor: a passive monitor in a test environment checks responses for a proper frame-options header and feeds results into a shared store with per-application dashboards. Other examples include a build-time tool that extracts authorization annotations to produce an access control matrix, a dependency check that flags vulnerable libraries on every build, a proxy that verifies anti-CSRF tokens during existing browser tests, and unit suites that confirm encoders and cryptographic controls actually work. A quick header checker also showed that a set of top internet sites generally fared better than 140 financial sites.

The speaker argues that many findings are noise because the expected security model is not aligned with what is actually measured, and that sensors should verify good behavior rather than search for bad patterns. Practical advice is to start by building one simple sensor with open tools, publish the results in a basic dashboard, then add sensors and refine the model as new threats appear.

talks.title: Hacking Web Server Apps for iOS
talks.teaser: Shows how file-sharing web server apps on iOS expose files through path traversal, cross-site scripting and missing encryption.
talks.summary:
Bruno Oliveira presents research into iOS apps that turn a phone into a file-sharing web server, a popular way to move files without cables. The talk explains that many of these apps serve plain HTTP with no encryption, offer authentication that is optional or off by default, and advertise themselves over mDNS, which makes them easy to find on a local network.

The talk then walks through the flaws found across several apps. Reflected and persistent cross-site scripting were shown, including a stored payload in an album name that ran when the page was opened. The most serious issue was path traversal in one app, where a crafted request reached files outside the shared folder. On a non-jailbroken phone this exposed the app's own data. On a jailbroken phone it reached the system password file, where the hashes were visible, and the folders of other apps. In a live demo over a public IP address, a PHP web shell was uploaded to a web server running inside another app, which gave file access as the mobile user. Only one vendor responded and fixed its issue. On iOS 7 the platform restricted access so that the app could only reach its own folder.

The takeaway is that developers of these apps need to encrypt traffic, enforce authentication and validate input before serving files. Users should treat file-sharing apps as untrusted, check the ones they install, and understand that a jailbroken device widens the impact of any flaw.

talks.title: HTML5: Risky Business or Hidden Security Tool Chest?
talks.teaser: Examines which HTML5 browser features can strengthen web authentication and where they add new security risks.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether HTML5 is a liability for web applications or a useful set of security tools. The speaker's starting point is that developers do not control the browser their users run, so an application is exposed to browser-side risks whether or not it uses the new APIs. Mobile authentication, where typing a password is awkward, serves as the main thread for judging the options.

Storage came first. Local storage persists far longer than cookies and holds more data, but it lacks the Secure and HttpOnly protections cookies offer, and any script on the page can read it. Keeping a session token there does defend against cross-site request forgery, because the browser does not attach it automatically. Other ideas were demonstrated and assessed as supplements rather than standalone factors: canvas-drawn patterns that users tend to choose in predictable shapes, geolocation checks that can be spoofed, face recognition and motion-based input that proved too noisy, and notifications that alert users to logins from unfamiliar places. A client-side password hashing demo using the crypto API, with a server-supplied nonce, showed how the cleartext password need not leave the browser, though a captured hash can still be replayed.

The main takeaway is to judge each HTML5 feature by the threat it addresses and by browser support across the user base. Client-side code can be altered, so server-side controls and TLS remain necessary.

talks.title: Why is SCADA Security an Uphill Battle?
talks.teaser: Maps SCADA vulnerabilities across field devices, protocols and control-room software, and outlines defensive steps for operators.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by clarifying what SCADA covers, since the term is stretched across distributed control systems, industrial control and critical infrastructure. It explains why the topic suits an application security conference: control systems now run web servers, databases and off-the-shelf operating systems. The speaker proposes a four-part model of these environments: field sensors that acquire data, PLCs, IEDs and RTUs that convert it, communication protocols such as Modbus and DNP3, and the SCADA master or HMI where operators watch alarms.

Mapped against this model, almost no reported vulnerabilities sat in field sensors, about 11 percent in conversion devices and about 22 percent in communication, while roughly two-thirds fell in the SCADA master. One example was an RTU that broadcast its location and kept a debug port open with a hard-coded password. A PLC showed a similar exposed debug port, and several protocol implementations suffered denial-of-service or memory-corruption flaws. Master software showed familiar web bugs, including cross-site scripting, SQL injection and directory traversal, because operators now use browsers and databases.

The talk then turned to recurring weaknesses: control networks joined to corporate networks or the internet, protocols with little built-in authentication, rare patching, default or shared passwords, and equipment that stays in service for decades. Recommendations included scanning only during maintenance windows, since low-powered devices can crash, checking for accidental internet exposure, segmenting networks, and planning patches with the vendor. Where possible, a test environment should be used before changes reach production.

talks.title: BASHing iOS Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how scripted binary and on-device checks can cover several mobile top ten risks in iOS apps without source code.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how to assess iOS apps cheaply when only the compiled binary is available. The presenters argue that full mobile assessments are costly, and that many checks for common mobile risks, such as insecure data storage, weak transport protection and leaked sensitive data, can be pulled from the app itself without source code.

The workflow starts by decrypting a store-downloaded app on a jailbroken device, then uses otool to read architecture, header flags such as PIE and stack protection, and linked frameworks. Running strings on the binary exposes method names, URLs, parameter names, SQL queries and possibly embedded secrets, and grep can flag patterns such as non-parameterized queries or deprecated crypto. After the app is launched, file system artifacts are examined for data protection classes, plist and database contents, credentials that end up in the URL cache, and logs.

The speakers wrap these steps in a bash framework that runs the checks automatically and reports the results, including ad libraries, developer paths left in binaries, and whether endpoints use HTTPS. They also note that Android analysis is in progress and that their tool is offered through a web front end rather than as released code. The takeaway is that simple scripted checks give quick coverage of several mobile top ten categories, though each finding needs context before it is treated as a confirmed vulnerability.

talks.title: Big Data Intelligence
talks.teaser: Shows how Akamai measures WAF accuracy with precision, recall and MCC, and tunes the OWASP Core Rule Set with big data.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how Akamai relates to the OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set. Akamai's cloud WAF runs ported versions of the rules rather than ModSecurity code itself. The speakers then describe Akamai's Cloud Security Intelligence platform, which gathers security events from servers worldwide into a Hadoop and HBase store and offers a query engine for moving from broad rule trigger views down to individual events.

Next, the talk explains how to measure WAF accuracy using true and false positives and negatives, then precision, recall, accuracy and the Matthews correlation coefficient. It argues that plain accuracy misleads when attacks are rare, so MCC gives a better picture. To test the rules, Akamai built a framework that replays large sets of valid traffic recorded from popular sites alongside attacks from scanners, SQL injection tools and public exploit databases.

The tuning lessons follow. A single anomaly score threshold suited some attack types poorly, so scoring was split into risk groups per attack type. HTTP protocol violation rules fired billions of times on real clients, so they received their own threshold. Complex cookies caused false positives, and scores spread across several cookies or parameters were treated as likely false positives. Redundant regular expressions and some useless rules were trimmed or disabled. They close by urging the project to adopt these ideas and evaluators to weigh false positives too.

talks.title: OWASP Zed Attack Proxy
talks.teaser: Walks through the ZAP web testing proxy's new features, browser integration, scripting and the experimental Zest language.
talks.summary:
The session introduces ZAP, a free and open source web application testing proxy aimed at newcomers and professional testers alike. It covers core capabilities such as an intercepting proxy, active and passive scanners, traditional and AJAX spidering, and WebSocket support. Developers can also drive ZAP through its API to run automated security regression tests in build pipelines.

The middle of the talk shows newer work. Plug and Hack lets Firefox control ZAP from its developer toolbar, allowing breakpoints on traffic and quick switching between logged-in sessions to test access control. Embedded scripting supports targeted scripts and active and passive rules, shown with a rule that flags redirects carrying a body and another that strips a Content Security Policy header. Zest, an experimental tool-independent JSON scripting language, records request sequences with assertions and handles anti-CSRF tokens, so a finding can be handed to a developer as a reproducible script. A work-in-progress second phase monitors and fuzzes browser post messages, revealing a DOM XSS in widely copied example code.

The closing portion covers the project's direction: community-driven, permanently free, and designed so its components can be reused by other tools. Attendees were encouraged to try the features, complete the user questionnaire and join the next day's hackathon. In the Q&A, the speaker explained that sensitive values can be redacted from Zest scripts before they are shared with vendors.
